title: 嘉靖二十二年順天府鄉試錄
text:
往典文事臣鳴夏拜
命驚惕竊伏自念雖嘗以譾薄謬
當
甄拔置之史局然兹唯承
任使之初其何以稱塞
詔旨翌日
陛辭入院則府尹臣擢府丞臣廷
===
赦先事經畫百需罔弗裕御史
臣鏞臣宗魯寔監臨之其知縣
臣希學學正臣希賢教諭臣南
金臣鎬臣熈臣繼宗臣澋臣純
仁臣英選則遠近遴選充分經
校閱之任彬彬然業應聘至矣
乃相與誓戒就列合提學御史
alt_text:
往典文事〔臣鳴夏〕拜
命驚惕竊伏自念雖嘗以譾薄謬
當
甄拔置之史局然茲唯承
任使之初其何以稱塞
詔旨翌日
陛辭入院則府尹〔臣〕擢府丞〔臣〕廷
試光事經畫百需罔弗裕御史
===
〔臣鏞臣宗魯〕寔監臨之其知縣
〔臣希學〕學正〔臣希賢〕教諭〔臣南〕
金〔臣鎬臣熈臣繼宗臣澯臣純〕
仁〔臣英選〕則遠近遴選充分經
校閲之任彬彬然業應聘至矣
乃相與誓戒就列合提學御史
punctuated: 往典文事。臣鳴夏拜命驚惕，竊伏自念：雖嘗以譾薄謬當甄拔，置之史局，然兹唯承任使之初，其何以稱塞詔旨？翌日，陛辭入院，則府尹臣擢、府丞臣廷赦先事經畫，百需罔弗裕。御史臣鏞、臣宗魯寔監臨之。其知縣臣希學、學正臣希賢、教諭臣南金、臣鎬、臣熈、臣繼宗、臣澋、臣純仁、臣英選，則遠近遴選，充分經校閱之任，彬彬然業應聘至矣。乃相與誓戒就列，合提學御史
translation_en: …to go and oversee the literary examination. Your servant Mingxia received the command with trepidation. I humbly reflected: although, despite my shallow learning, I had previously been undeservedly selected and placed in the Historiography Office, this was the beginning of my service on such an assignment. How could I adequately fulfill the intent of the imperial command? The following day, after taking leave of Your Majesty at court, I entered the examination compound. Prefect Zhuo and Vice Prefect Tingshe had planned matters in advance, amply providing for every requirement. Investigating Censors Yong and Zonglu served as Supervising Officials. County Magistrate Xixue, Confucian School Instructor Xixian, and Confucian School Instructors Nanjin, Gao, Xi, Jizong, Hong, Chunren, and Yingxuan had been selected from near and far to examine the papers, each taking responsibility for a particular Classic. These cultivated men had already arrived in response to their invitations. We then took the oath together, received the admonitions, and assumed our respective stations, assembling [the candidates selected by] the Investigating Censor for Education …

title: 嘉靖二十二年順天府鄉試錄
text:
臣謝九儀暨六館諸曹所簡士
三千二百有竒三試三校之獲
其雋百三十有五人遵
成制為錄以
獻臣鳴夏竊惟賢才國家楨幹人
主之自為社稷計者罔不欲培
植而長養之至其昌熾蕃碩則
===
有非人力所能強致者夫固時
使之也臣觀今日之才可謂極
盛然嘗遡而求之效斯可覩洪
惟我
太祖高皇帝混一函夏首崇教化酌
古建制盡善全美嘗仰觀奎壁
間以卜文運將興其所以克享

三千二百有奇三試三校之獲
其儁百三十有五人遵
成制爲録以
獻臣鳴夏竊唯賢才國家楨幹人
主之自爲社稷計者罔不欲培
植而長養之至其昌熾蕃碩則
有非人力所能强致者夫固時
使之也臣觀今日之才可謂極
盛然嘗遡而求之效斯可覩洪
===
惟我
太祖高皇帝混一函夏首崇教化酌
古建制盡善全美嘗仰觀奎璧
間以卜文運將興其所以克享
punctuated:
臣謝九儀暨六館諸曹所簡士三千二百有竒，三試三校之，獲其雋百三十有五人。遵成制，為錄以獻。
臣鳴夏竊惟：賢才，國家楨幹。人主之自為社稷計者，罔不欲培植而長養之。至其昌熾蕃碩，則有非人力所能強致者，夫固時使之也。臣觀今日之才，可謂極盛，然嘗遡而求之，效斯可覩。洪惟我太祖高皇帝混一函夏，首崇教化，酌古建制，盡善全美。嘗仰觀奎壁間，以卜文運將興，其所以克享
translation_en:
…more than 3,200 scholars selected by your servant Xie Jiuyi and the officials of the Six Colleges and the various offices. We examined them in three sessions and assessed their work three times, obtaining 135 outstanding candidates. Following established regulations, we compiled this record for presentation to the throne.
Your servant Mingxia humbly reflects: worthy and talented men are the pillars of the state. Every ruler who plans for the welfare of his realm wishes to cultivate and nurture them. Yet their flourishing and abundant growth involve something that human effort alone cannot compel: it is indeed the times that bring this about. Looking at the talent of today, your servant would call it supremely flourishing. Yet when one traces its origins, the effects of earlier efforts become apparent. Reverently considering how our Emperor Taizu Gao united all the Chinese realm, he gave foremost importance to moral instruction, drawing upon antiquity to establish institutions that were wholly good and complete. He once looked up at the constellations Kui and Bi to divine the coming rise of literary fortunes. The means by which he was able to enjoy…

title: 嘉靖二十二年順天府鄉試錄
text:
天心有明徵矣我
成祖文皇帝則又從而振飭之表章
六經折衷諸子聲教之訖於斯
盛焉
聖子
神孫重華協德比至
今日不懈益勤
===
八葉相承之間盖已衍百七十餘
年之慶矣若乃維
皇建極萬物快覩二十餘禩以来
至仁達孝倫制兼盡禮備樂和
天地為昭而况
敷言之訓所以勅示膠庠者又皆
精一執中之微傳乎然則和氣
alt_text:
天心有明徵矣我
成祖文皇帝則又從而振飭之表章
六學折衷諸子聲教之訖於斯
盛焉
聖子
神孫重華協德比至
今日不懈益勤
八葉相承之間蓋已衍百七十餘
===
年之慶矣若乃維
皇建極萬物快覩二十餘禩以来
至仁達孝倫制兼盡禮備樂和
天地爲昭而況
敷言之訓所以勅示膠庠者又皆
精一執中之徵傳乎然則和氣
punctuated: 天心有明徵矣。我成祖文皇帝則又從而振飭之，表章六經，折衷諸子，聲教之訖，於斯盛焉。聖子神孫，重華協德，比至今日，不懈益勤。八葉相承之間，盖已衍百七十餘年之慶矣。若乃維皇建極，萬物快覩，二十餘禩以来，至仁達孝，倫制兼盡，禮備樂和，天地為昭。而况敷言之訓，所以勅示膠庠者，又皆精一執中之微傳乎？然則和氣
translation_en:
…there is clear evidence that he enjoyed Heaven’s favor. Our Emperor Chengzu Wen then carried forward this work, reinvigorating and ordering it, honoring and elucidating the Six Classics, and weighing the teachings of the various philosophical masters. The reach of his civilizing influence attained its fullest flourishing at this time. His sage sons and divine grandsons continued his glory and matched his virtue; down to the present day, their diligence has increased without slackening. Through eight successive generations, these blessings have now extended for more than 170 years.
As for Your Majesty’s establishment of the supreme standard, all beings behold it with delight. For more than twenty years, your consummate benevolence and far-reaching filial piety have fully embraced both human relationships and institutions. Ritual is complete and music harmonious, with Heaven and Earth bearing witness. Moreover, are not the instructions you proclaim to the schools all subtle transmissions of the teaching to remain discerning and undivided and hold fast to the Mean? Thus, the harmonious vital force…

title: 嘉靖二十二年順天府鄉試錄
text:
之所甄陶
神機之所斡運皆有不期然而然
者是故星露呈祥河岳獻瑞觀
于物而人可知矣比屋可封羣
黎為德觀于凡民而士可知矣
學有淵源辭尚體要羞桓文而
慕堯舜雖羈丱之童不少讓焉
===
觀于
京邑之士而四方可知矣猗歟盛
哉雖然才非時罔萃時非才罔
與保終文運治化其交相成也
久矣唯爾多士亦嘗思所以答
明時乎人亦有言太上有立德其
次有立功其次有立言夫古之

黎爲德觀于凡民而士可知矣
學有淵源辭尚體要羞桓文而
慕堯舜雖羈丱之童不少讓焉
===
覲于
京邑之士而四方可知矣猗歟盛
哉雖然才非時罔萃時非才罔
興保終文運治化其交相成也
久矣唯爾多士亦嘗思所以答
明時乎人亦有言太上有立德其
次有立功其次有立言夫古之
punctuated:
之所甄陶，神機之所斡運，皆有不期然而然者。是故星露呈祥，河岳獻瑞，觀于物而人可知矣；比屋可封，羣黎為德，觀于凡民而士可知矣。學有淵源，辭尚體要，羞桓文而慕堯舜，雖羈丱之童不少讓焉。觀于京邑之士而四方可知矣。猗歟盛哉！
雖然，才非時罔萃，時非才罔與保終。文運治化，其交相成也久矣。唯爾多士，亦嘗思所以答明時乎？人亦有言：「太上有立德，其次有立功，其次有立言。」夫古之
translation_en:
…what that harmonious influence molds and what the wondrous workings of imperial governance direct all come about without deliberate contrivance. Thus the stars and dew display auspicious signs, and the rivers and mountains offer favorable omens: by observing these things, one may understand the condition of the people. Every household has someone worthy of enfeoffment, and the common people practice virtue: by observing the common people, one may understand the condition of the scholars. Their learning has deep roots, and their writing prizes substance and essentials. They disdain Duke Huan of Qi and Duke Wen of Jin and aspire to Yao and Shun; even boys with their hair still bound in childhood tufts yield nothing in this regard. By observing the scholars of the capital, one may understand those throughout the realm. Ah, how flourishing it is!
Yet talent cannot gather without a favorable age, and an age cannot be sustained to its end without talent. The fortunes of letters and the transforming influence of government have long fostered one another. You many scholars, have you ever considered how to repay this enlightened age? As the saying goes: “Highest is establishing virtue; next is establishing meritorious achievements; next is establishing enduring words.” Now, in antiquity…

title: 嘉靖二十二年順天府鄉試錄
text:
立言固非若今之言也抑亦以
爲次者君子學成而行其蘊藉
典墳根極理要夫固爲參賛彌
綸之具也及其時之不遇然後
筆之於書則爲之闡性命之原
合天人之會明王伯之辨嚴義
利之分以詔後世盖非其所得
己也是故孔孟皇皇濂洛關閩
諸儒其所遇可知矣爾多士生
逢
堯舜千載一時繼自今其尚以古人
之所立言者體之爲德措之爲
功浚亮咸事以弼成
雍熙太和之治於有永斯其足尚
alt_text:
立言固非君子之言也抑亦以
爲次者君子學成而行其蘊籍
典墳根極理要尤固爲參賛彌
綸之具也及其時之不遇然後
筆之於書則爲之闡性命之原
合天人之會明王伯之辨嚴義
利之分以詔後世蓋非其所得
===
已也是故孔孟皇皇濂洛關閩
諸儒其所遇可知矣爾多士生
逢
堯舜千載一時繼自今其尚以古人
之所立言者體之爲德措之爲
功浚亮咸事以邇成
雍熙太和之治於有永斯其足尚
punctuated: 立言固非若今之言也。抑亦以爲次者，君子學成而行，其蘊藉典墳，根極理要，夫固爲參賛彌綸之具也。及其時之不遇，然後筆之於書，則爲之闡性命之原，合天人之會，明王伯之辨，嚴義利之分，以詔後世，盖非其所得己也。是故孔孟皇皇，濂洛關閩諸儒，其所遇可知矣。爾多士生逢堯舜，千載一時。繼自今，其尚以古人之所立言者，體之爲德，措之爲功，浚亮咸事，以弼成雍熙太和之治於有永，斯其足尚
translation_en:
…establishing enduring words certainly did not mean speaking as people do today. Yet why was it ranked below the others? When a gentleman has completed his learning and puts it into practice, his grounding in the ancient classics and his thorough grasp of essential principles equip him to assist in the work of transformation and bring all things into harmonious order. Only when he fails to find his opportunity does he commit his thoughts to writing. He then elucidates the origins of human nature and destiny, brings together the points at which Heaven and humanity meet, clarifies the distinction between true kingship and hegemony, and strictly distinguishes righteousness from profit, thereby instructing later generations. This is surely something he cannot help doing. Thus Confucius and Mencius restlessly sought opportunities to serve; the circumstances encountered by the Confucian masters of Lian, Luo, Guan, and Min can likewise be understood.

You scholars have been born into an age of Yao and Shun, an opportunity that comes once in a thousand years. From this time forward, may you embody in your own virtue what the ancients established in words, and put it into practice as achievements. Diligently assist in every affair, helping to bring about an enduring reign of concord, prosperity, and supreme harmony. This would indeed be worthy of esteem…

title: 嘉靖二十二年順天府鄉試錄
text:
也已夫君子不能違時亦不負
時若乃志卑行劣竊古人糠粃
不啻自足及見諸用併所得而
棄之斯其為負也不以甚乎孟
軻氏曰天下之善士斯友天下
之善士爾多士
帝畿之選也行且友天下士矣其尚
===
思所以為天下倡哉臣承乏竣
事不能無厚望於多士故相與
懋戒之以謹其始云
右春坊右中允兼翰林院修撰
秦鳴夏謹序
alt_text:
也已夫君子不能違時亦不負
時若乃志甲行劣竊古人糠粃
不啻自足及見諸用倂所得而
棄之斯其爲負也不以甚乎孟
軻氏曰天下之善士斯友天下
之善士爾多士
帝畿之選也行且友天下士矣其尚
思所以爲天下倡哉臣承乏竣
事不能無厚望於多士故相與
懋戒之以謹其始云
右春坊右中允兼翰林院修撰
秦鳴夏謹序
punctuated:
也已。夫君子不能違時，亦不負時。若乃志卑行劣，竊古人糠粃，不啻自足；及見諸用，併所得而棄之，斯其為負也，不以甚乎？孟軻氏曰：「天下之善士，斯友天下之善士。」爾多士，帝畿之選也，行且友天下士矣，其尚思所以為天下倡哉！臣承乏竣事，不能無厚望於多士，故相與懋戒之，以謹其始云。
右春坊右中允兼翰林院修撰秦鳴夏謹序。
translation_en:
…indeed. The gentleman cannot act against his times, nor does he fail them. But those whose aspirations are low and whose conduct is base pilfer the mere husks of the ancients’ learning and consider themselves more than satisfied. When it comes to putting that learning into practice, they discard even what they have acquired. Is this not an excessive failure of their times? Meng Ke said: “The good scholars of the realm befriend the good scholars of the realm.” You scholars are the chosen men of the imperial capital region, and soon you will befriend scholars from throughout the realm. May you consider how to set an example for all under Heaven! Having served for want of someone better and completed my duties, I, your servant, cannot but hold high hopes for you scholars. Thus we earnestly admonish you to exercise care at the outset.
Preface respectfully composed by Qin Mingxia, Right Mentor in the Right Secretariat of the Heir Apparent and concurrently Senior Compiler in the Hanlin Academy.

第壹場

四書

子曰：「無爲而治者，其舜也與？夫何爲哉？恭己正南面而已矣。」

詩云：「伐柯伐柯，其則不遠。」執柯以伐柯，睨而視之，猶以爲遠。故君子以人治人，改而止。

夫義，路也；禮，門也。惟君子能由是路，出入是門也。詩云：「周道如砥，其直如矢。君子所履，小人所視。」

易

上九，何天之衢，亨。

六五，或益之十朋之龜，弗克違，元吉。

制而用之謂之法，利用出入，民咸用之謂之神。

天地定位，山澤通氣，雷風相薄，水火不相射，八卦相錯。

書
translation_en:
First Session

Four Books

The Master said: “Was it not Shun who brought order without acting? What did he do? He merely held himself reverently and sat facing due south.”

The Book of Odes says: “In hewing an axe handle, hewing an axe handle, the model is not far away.” Yet when one holds an axe handle to hew another and glances sideways at it, one still considers the model distant. Thus the gentleman governs people according to their own human nature, stopping once they have corrected themselves.

“Righteousness is the road; ritual propriety is the gate. Only the gentleman can follow this road and pass in and out through this gate. The Book of Odes says: ‘The great road is like a whetstone, straight as an arrow. The gentleman treads it; the common people look to it.’”

Book of Changes

“Top nine: How open is the thoroughfare of Heaven! Success.”

“Six in the fifth place: Someone augments him with a tortoise worth ten pairs of shells; its favorable oracle cannot be gainsaid. Supreme good fortune.”

“To fashion things and put them to use is called a standard. To make their use beneficial in going out and coming in, so that all the people use them, is called numinous efficacy.”

“Heaven and earth take their fixed positions; mountain and lake communicate their vital energies; thunder and wind impel one another; water and fire do not oppose one another. The eight trigrams interweave.”

Book of Documents

punctuated:
帝曰：「來，禹！汝亦昌言。」禹拜曰：「都！帝，予何言？予思日孜孜。」皐陶曰：「吁！如何？」禹曰：「洪水滔天，浩浩懷山襄陵，下民昏墊。予乘四載，隨山刊木，暨益奏庶鮮食。予決九川距四海，濬畎澮距川，暨稷播，奏庶艱食鮮食，懋遷有無，化居，烝民乃粒，萬邦作乂。」皐陶曰：「俞！師汝昌言。」
若虞機張，往省括于度，則釋。
歲月日時無易，百穀用成，乂用明，俊民用章，家用平康。
亦惟有若虢叔，有若閎夭，有若散宜生，有若泰顛，有若南宮括。
詩
有匪君子，充耳琇瑩，會弁如星。
方叔率止，鉦人伐鼓，陳師鞠旅。顯允方叔，伐鼓淵淵，振旅闐闐。
既醉以酒，既飽以德。君子萬年，介爾景福。
既醉以酒，爾殽既將。君子萬年，介爾昭
translation_en:
The emperor said: “Come, Yu! You too should offer excellent words.” Yu bowed and said: “Ah, Emperor, what can I say? My thought is to work diligently every day.” Gao Yao said: “Ah! How so?” Yu said: “The floodwaters rose to heaven; vast and surging, they encircled the mountains and overtopped the hills. The people below were overwhelmed and submerged. I used four kinds of conveyance, cut trees as I followed the mountains, and, together with Yi, provided the people with fresh meat to eat. I opened channels for the nine rivers to reach the four seas and dredged the field ditches and larger channels to reach the rivers. Together with Ji, I sowed grain, providing the people with food won through toil as well as fresh meat. I encouraged exchanges between those who had supplies and those who lacked them, putting stored goods into circulation. Thus the multitudes obtained grain to eat, and the myriad states became well governed.” Gao Yao said: “Yes! We shall take your excellent words as our guide.”
Be like a forester with his crossbow cocked: before advancing, check that the arrow’s nock is properly aligned, and only then release it.
When the years, months, days, and hours do not depart from their proper order, the hundred grains ripen, government becomes enlightened, worthy men become illustrious, and households enjoy peace and well-being.
There were also men such as Guo Shu, Hong Yao, San Yisheng, Tai Dian, and Nangong Kuo.
Book of Odes
There is that cultivated gentleman: his ear pendants are of gleaming stone, and the ornaments joining his cap shine like stars.
Fang Shu leads them; the gong players beat the drums. He arrays the troops and assembles the host. Illustrious and trustworthy is Fang Shu! The drums resound deeply; the troops are marshalled amid a mighty din.
Already drunk with wine, already filled with virtue. May our lord live ten thousand years; may great blessings attend you.
Already drunk with wine, with your dishes of food already served. May our lord live ten thousand years; may there attend you radiant…

translation_en:
Heaven’s mandate—how profound and unceasing! Ah, how illustrious was the purity of King Wen’s virtue! May it be bestowed upon us in abundance; may we receive it. Let us fully follow our King Wen; may his descendants hold firmly to his example.

Spring and Autumn Annals
In spring, in the first month, the duke hunted at Lang. 〔Fourth year of Duke Huan〕
In autumn, men of Song besieged Cao. 〔Nineteenth year of Duke Xi〕 In the third month, on the bingwu day, the Marquis of Jin entered Cao, seized the Earl of Cao, and handed him over to the men of Song. 〔Twenty-eighth year of Duke Xi〕
On the jiwei day, the duke met the Marquis of Jin, the Marquis of Wei, the Earl of Cao, and the Viscount of Zhu, and they jointly swore a covenant at Duandao. 〔Seventeenth year of Duke Xuan〕 In spring, the Marquis of Jin and Zang, heir apparent of Wei, attacked Qi. 〔Eighteenth year of Duke Xuan〕 In the sixth month, on the guiyou day, Jisun Xingfu, Zangsun Xu, Shusun Qiaoru, and Gongsun Yingqi led an army to join Xi Ke of Jin, Sun Liangfu of Wei, and Prince Shou of Cao. They fought the Marquis of Qi at An, and the army of Qi suffered a crushing defeat. 〔Second year of Duke Cheng〕
In autumn, Shi Yang of Jin, Yue Qili of Song, Beigong Xi of Wei, and men of Cao, Zhu, and Teng met at Hu. 〔Twenty-seventh year of Duke Zhao〕

punctuated:
故天生時而地生財，人其父生而師教之，四者君以正用之。
貴其質而已矣，所以交於神明者，不可同於所安，褻之甚也。如是而后宜。
此之謂大當。然後聖人作爲父子君臣，以爲紀綱。紀綱既正，天下大定；天下大定，然後正六律，和五聲，弦歌詩頌。
君子不以一日使其躬僨焉，如不終日。
第貳塲
論
天地中和之至。
詔誥表內科一道。
擬漢以高密侯禹爲太傅、東平王蒼爲驃騎將軍詔，中元二年。
擬唐命僕射裴冕、郭英乂等十三人於集賢殿待制誥，永泰元年。
擬禮部刋定《興都志》
translation_en:
Thus Heaven produces the seasons and Earth produces material resources; a person is begotten by his father and instructed by his teacher. The ruler puts these four to their proper use.

What is valued is simply their plain substance. The things used to communicate with divine spirits must not be the same as those used for personal comfort, for that would be extreme irreverence. Only in this way are they fitting.

This is called the great fitting order. Thereupon the sages established the relationships of father and son, ruler and minister, to serve as the governing framework. Once that framework was correctly established, all under Heaven became firmly settled. Once all under Heaven was firmly settled, they then regulated the six pitch standards, harmonized the five notes, and sang the poems and hymns to string accompaniment.

The gentleman does not allow himself to fall into ruin even for a single day, remaining watchful as though he could not last out the day.

Second Session

Discourse

Heaven and Earth: the utmost realization of equilibrium and harmony.

One topic from among imperial edicts, proclamations, and memorials [?].

Compose an imperial edict in the manner of the Han appointing Yu, Marquis of Gaomi, as Grand Preceptor, and Cang, Prince of Dongping, as General of Agile Cavalry. Second year of Zhongyuan.

Compose a proclamation in the manner of the Tang commanding the Vice Directors Pei Mian and Guo Yingyi and the others, thirteen men in all, to await imperial commands at Jixian Hall. First year of Yongtai.

punctuated:
太祖高皇帝肇造區夏，成祖文皇帝輯寧邦家，列聖嗣休，增其式廓，神謨懿範，咸五登三。區區貞觀之治，何暇置喙？顧天府所藏，未易窺測，而一時儒臣亦有倣唐臣之遺意而輯爲《皇明政要》者，採摭類列，足備鑒觀。今考其編，爲卷二十，爲目四十，固天下所共傳而諸士子所習見者。涵濡誦法之餘，不知可以悉數而陳之歟？抑其間大本大綱之所在，亦可以指言其要歟？聖天子法祖休烈，方隆熈洽之理，尚相與敷張之，以昭我明之政之所以盛。

問：農桑，王業根本，帝王祈天永命之道，莫先乎是。是故天子親耕以供齊盛，王后親蠶以供純服，豈唯崇報？盖以身教也。其說見於經、著傳者，可得聞與？說者謂
translation_en:
… Emperor Taizu Gao founded the realm of China; Emperor Chengzu Wen brought peace to the state; and the successive sage emperors carried forward their splendid legacy and further enlarged its scope. Their divine counsels and admirable models equaled those of the Five Emperors and attained the stature of the Three Sovereigns. Who, then, has leisure to speak of the comparatively modest government of the Zhenguan reign? Yet the writings preserved in the imperial repository are not readily accessible for examination. Some Confucian officials of the time, following the intention bequeathed by the Tang official, also compiled the Essentials of Government of the August Ming (Huang Ming zhengyao). Its collected materials, arranged by category, amply provide instruction and examples for reflection. Examining its arrangement, we find twenty juan and forty headings. It is certainly circulated throughout the realm and familiar to you candidates. Having steeped yourselves in it, recited it, and taken it as a model, can you enumerate and explain its contents fully? Or can you identify and state the essentials of its fundamental principles and main outlines? Our sage Son of Heaven takes the glorious achievements of his ancestors as his model and is now bringing harmonious government to ever greater flourishing. May you together expound these matters fully, to illuminate what makes the government of our Ming so splendid.

Question: Agriculture and sericulture are the foundation of kingly rule. Among the means by which emperors and kings pray to Heaven for an enduring mandate, none takes precedence over these. Thus the Son of Heaven ploughs in person to supply the grain for sacrificial offerings, and the queen tends silkworms in person to supply the silk for ritual garments. Is this merely to honor and requite the objects of sacrifice? It is also to teach by personal example. May we hear the explanations of these practices found in the Classics and set forth in their commentaries? Commentators say that …

punctuated: 唐虞尚矣，三代唯周世重穡事，故享年獨永，而其制亦獨詳。然則前乎周者，農桑顧弗重與？由周而降，多歷年所者曰漢、唐、宋，其君后耕蠶之舉，史不絶書，治何以弗三代若與？洪惟我聖祖高皇帝，聰明睿智，憂勤迪哲，踐阼之初，他務未遑，首耕藉田，爲天下勸；至於訓諭臣民，尤惓惓焉。猗與休哉！茲惟宗社億萬年無疆之慶，不但比隆成周已爾。其宏猷大旨，亦可頌言其萬一與？然嘗伏窺成憲，似於親蠶之制有所未備，豈固不能無待於今日與？恭惟皇上嗣登寶位，益隆繼述，嵗大駕親耕，皇后親蠶，鴻儀鉅典，翔洽宇宙，真足以考諸三
translation_en:
…Tang and Yu belong to remote antiquity. Of the Three Dynasties, only the Zhou gave weight to agriculture; hence its rule alone endured so long, and its institutions alone were so fully elaborated. But does this mean that before the Zhou, agriculture and sericulture were not valued? Among the dynasties after the Zhou, the Han, Tang, and Song endured for many years. Their rulers’ personal plowing and their empresses’ personal tending of silkworms are repeatedly recorded in the histories. Why, then, did their governance not equal that of the Three Dynasties?

We reverently reflect that our Sagely Ancestor, the Exalted Emperor, was discerning and wise, solicitous and diligent, guided by sagacity. At the beginning of his reign, before he had leisure for other affairs, he first plowed the imperial ritual field to encourage all under Heaven. In instructing and admonishing his officials and people, he was especially earnest. Ah, how splendid! This indeed secured boundless blessings for the ancestral temples and altars of state for countless ages, far exceeding merely matching the flourishing Zhou. Might you express in praise even a ten-thousandth part of his grand designs and great purposes?

Yet, having humbly examined the established institutions, we find that the provisions for the empress’s personal tending of silkworms seem somewhat incomplete. Could their completion necessarily have had to await the present day? We reverently consider how His Majesty, upon succeeding to the precious throne, further enhanced the continuation of his predecessors’ work. Each year His Majesty personally plows, and the empress personally tends silkworms. These magnificent ceremonies and grand rites extend throughout the universe, and truly suffice to be measured against the Three…

問：周官有職方氏，掌天下之圖與地，蓋凡以辨區域、知要害、審民風耳矣。不識畫野分州之制昉于何人？重圖籍以觀天下昉于何代？書稱堯憂洪水，使禹治之，別九州，定五服，其績偉矣。舜陟元后，肇州十二；夏氏受命，仍爲九州。其所損益，可得而聞與？及考職方氏所載，若所謂九州九服之制，視諸禹服，又不能無沿革廣狹之殊。豈聖人立極，固不嫌於紛更與？三代以下，若漢唐宋之撫有方夏，各數百年，其載諸圖籍者，寧無可考者與？我
translation_en:
…the Three Kings without error. May we ask whether there is an essential principle by which these rites carry forward the glory of the illustrious ancestors, establish a model for ten thousand generations, and render the Han, Tang, and Song so paltry as to be unworthy of mention? You assembled scholars have been steeped in the sagely transforming influence for years. Expound and extol these achievements for us, proclaiming their magnificence. And if you cherish some humble offering of advice—as one might offer celery or the warmth of the sun—why withhold a word? The officials conducting the examination can convey it to His Majesty.
Question: The Offices of Zhou records an Office of Territorial Administration, responsible for maps and the lands of the realm [?]. Its purpose was simply to distinguish territorial divisions, identify strategic places, and examine local customs. Who first instituted the demarcation of lands and their division into provinces? In what age did the practice begin of attaching importance to maps and registers as a means of surveying the realm? The Book of Documents states that Yao, troubled by the floods, commissioned Yu to bring them under control. Yu distinguished the Nine Provinces and established the Five Zones of Submission: his accomplishments were great indeed. When Shun ascended to supreme rulership, he established twelve provinces; when the Xia received the mandate, they reverted to nine provinces. May we hear what was removed or added in these changes? Furthermore, when we examine the account of the Office of Territorial Administration, its system of Nine Provinces and Nine Zones of Submission necessarily differs from Yu’s zones in what it retained or altered and in territorial extent. Could it be that, in establishing the supreme standard, the sages had no objection to repeated changes? text:
皇明用夏變夷奄有九有盖虞夏所不能臣職
方所不能載者莫不覃被聲教化爲文
物盖自生民来未有若此之盛者也及
若要害民風爲今日所宜亟講者亦可
舉其凡與洪惟
英宗睿皇帝嘗命儒臣纂輯
一統志頒布天下頃者
皇上嗣登寶位輔臣有撰輿地圖略以進者
特賜嘉納諸士子生長太平習聞其說舊矣
盍肆言之爲一道德以同俗之助
===
問易曰君子多識前言往行以畜其德故
知古知今儒者分内事也自有書契以
来史冊紀載之當明人物事爲之當辨
盖有更僕未易以數者姑舉一二與爾
諸士評之元聖如周公而有避毁居楚
之說何據睿聖如武公而有襲伯代侯
之文何稽不與驪言非簡也而不與楊
思勗交言者將無同獵較猶可非徇也

===
盍肆言之為一道德以同俗之助
問易曰君子多識前言往行以畜其德故
知古知今儒者分內事也自有書契以
來史冊紀載之當明人物事為之當辨

之說何據睿聖如武公而有襲伯代侯
之文何稽不與驩言非簡也而不與楊
思勗交言者將無同獵較猶可非徇也
punctuated:
皇明用夏變夷，奄有九有。盖虞夏所不能臣、職方所不能載者，莫不覃被聲教，化爲文物。盖自生民来，未有若此之盛者也。及若要害民風，爲今日所宜亟講者，亦可舉其凡與？洪惟英宗睿皇帝嘗命儒臣纂輯《一統志》，頒布天下。頃者皇上嗣登寶位，輔臣有撰《輿地圖略》以進者，特賜嘉納。諸士子生長太平，習聞其說舊矣，盍肆言之，爲一道德以同俗之助？

問：《易》曰：「君子多識前言往行，以畜其德。」故知古知今，儒者分内事也。自有書契以来，史冊紀載之當明，人物事爲之當辨，盖有更僕未易以數者。姑舉一二，與爾諸士評之。元聖如周公，而有避毁居楚之說，何據？睿聖如武公，而有襲伯代侯之文，何稽？不與驪言，非簡也，而不與楊思勗交言者，將無同？獵較猶可，非徇也，
translation_en:
…our august Ming dynasty has transformed the barbarians through Chinese civilization and possesses all the nine regions. Even those whom Yu and Xia could not bring into subjection, and lands that the Director of Territories could not record, have all come under the far-reaching influence of its teachings and been transformed by civilized institutions. Since humankind first came into being, there has surely never been such flourishing greatness. As for strategic locations and popular customs—matters urgently requiring study today—can you also set forth their main outlines? We reverently recall that Emperor Yingzong Rui once commanded his scholarly officials to compile the Comprehensive Gazetteer of the Realm and distribute it throughout the empire. Recently, when His Majesty succeeded to the precious throne, a Grand Secretary compiled and presented an Outline of Territorial Geography, which received his special commendation and acceptance. You candidates have grown up in an age of peace and have long been familiar with discussions of these matters. Why not expound them fully, helping to unify moral principles and thereby bring customs into accord?

Question: The Book of Changes says: “The gentleman acquaints himself widely with the words and deeds of the past, thereby nurturing his virtue.” Thus, knowledge of antiquity and the present belongs to the proper duties of a Confucian scholar. Since written records began, the historical accounts that require clarification, and the people and actions that require discrimination, have been so numerous that they could not readily be enumerated even through successive changes of attendants. Let us select one or two for you candidates to assess. Concerning even a supreme sage such as the Duke of Zhou, there is an account that he withdrew to Chu to escape slander: what is its basis? Concerning even a perspicacious sage such as Duke Wu, there is a passage stating that he attacked his elder brother and replaced him as marquis: what evidence supports it? Refusing to speak with Li [?] was not aloofness; might the person who refused to exchange words with Yang Sixu have acted in the same spirit? Even participation in competitive hunting could be permissible, without constituting unprincipled conformity…

title: 嘉靖二十二年順天府鄉試錄
text:
而迎觀音於郊外者將無異致恭桑梓
詩人義也下里門者孰與馬卿之侈大
義滅親春秋法也稱賣友者孰與石碏
之賢魯諸儒之歸陳未必是也而何孔
甲又為之博士魯兩生之辭漢未必非
也而何叔孫又為之奉常執筆螭頭若
直矣何以復上起居注乎薦韓歐陽若
公矣何以云欲免國謗乎王翬之出廩
粟得無與矯制開倉者似歟王丹之濟
===
軍乏得無與輸貲助邊者類歟自表求
見與章偕來裴度何以若此其急得詔
不發十日召見杜佑何以若是其遲鍾
離意之不拜賜何惡於名褚承亮之不
對策何嫌於義彗出寅艮耿南仲李光
之見孰優旦暮日赤紇石烈良弼之言
何驗高麗之讓謙益之亨也曷為其不
可讓遼左之征修攘之舉也曷為其不
可征吐蕃文籍之請何以當予通國胡

punctuated: 而迎觀音於郊外者，將無異？致恭桑梓，詩人義也，下里門者孰與馬卿之侈？大義滅親，春秋法也，稱賣友者孰與石碏之賢？魯諸儒之歸陳，未必是也，而何孔甲又為之博士？魯兩生之辭漢，未必非也，而何叔孫又為之奉常？執筆螭頭，若直矣，何以復上起居注乎？薦韓歐陽，若公矣，何以云欲免國謗乎？王翬之出廩粟，得無與矯制開倉者似歟？王丹之濟軍乏，得無與輸貲助邊者類歟？自表求見，與章偕來，裴度何以若此其急？得詔不發，十日召見，杜佑何以若是其遲？鍾離意之不拜賜，何惡於名？褚承亮之不對策，何嫌於義？彗出寅艮，耿南仲、李光之見孰優？旦暮日赤，紇石烈良弼之言何驗？高麗之讓，謙益之亨也，曷為其不可讓？遼左之征，修攘之舉也，曷為其不可征？吐蕃文籍之請，何以當予？通國胡
translation_en:
…Yet was the man who went out beyond the suburbs to welcome Guanyin any different? To show reverence for the mulberry and catalpa trees of one’s native place accords with the moral teaching of the Book of Odes. How did the man who dismounted at his village gate compare with the ostentation of Ma Qing? To let the greater demands of righteousness override affection for one’s kin is a principle of the Spring and Autumn Annals. How did the man accused of selling out a friend compare with the worthy Shi Que?

The scholars of Lu were not necessarily right to attach themselves to Chen; why, then, did Kong Jia nevertheless become his Erudite? The two scholars of Lu were not necessarily wrong to decline service under the Han; why, then, did Shusun nevertheless become its Chamberlain for Ceremonials? Wielding the brush beside the dragon-headed ornament seems an act of uprightness; why, then, were the Diaries of Activity subsequently submitted to the throne? Recommending Han and Ouyang seems impartial [?]; why, then, speak of wishing to escape the reproach of the realm?

Was Wang Hui’s distribution of granary grain not like opening the granaries under a falsely claimed imperial command? Was Wang Dan’s relief of the army’s shortages not like contributing private wealth to support the frontier? Submitting his own memorial to request an audience and arriving along with it—why was Pei Du in such haste? Receiving an edict yet not setting out, and being summoned to an audience after ten days—why was Du You so slow? When Zhongli Yi refused to bow in acknowledgment of a gift, what did he find objectionable in its designation? When Chu Chengliang declined to answer the policy questions, what scruple of righteousness did he have?

When a comet appeared in the yin and gen directions, whose interpretation was better, Geng Nanzhong’s or Li Guang’s? When the sun was red at dawn and dusk, what confirmation was there of Heshilie Liangbi’s words? Yielding Goryeo exemplified the success that comes from humility and bringing benefit; why, then, was it impermissible to yield it? The expedition against Liaozuo was an undertaking to put affairs in order and repel outsiders; why, then, was it impermissible to conduct it? Why should the request from Tubo for books have been granted? Tongguo, the Hu …

title: 嘉靖二十二年順天府鄉試錄
text:
□□子何以可歸凡此皆必有折衷之
道要非徒言而無當也願著于篇用觀
畜德之學
問古者大國三軍國方百里軍萬二千五
百人若周蓋千八百國較國之中大約
國得二軍何以若是眾歟嘗考今之郡
縣視周侯國亦略相當都司衞所所在
總其尺籍無慮百萬然視古兵數不啻
懸絕豈今則專力古則兼農故耶
===
國家京師團營桓桓貔虎諸邊甲士湯湯江
漢可謂盛矣獨郡縣之兵若所當議故
頃者本兵建策欲酌郡縣小大卽所設
壯快稍增其額豈其然乎昔漢置材官
騎士杜佑以為其制可采唐李抱真籍
丁教練或指其事遂謂民兵可用可得
聞乎然有兵則有將如有宋時一郡盡
行軍制施諸今之有司無乃不可乎或
□兵非難難于足食故昔人有謂給

punctuated:
□□子何以可歸？凡此皆必有折衷之道，要非徒言而無當也。願著于篇，用觀畜德之學。
問：古者大國三軍，國方百里，軍萬二千五百人。若周，蓋千八百國，較國之中，大約國得二軍，何以若是眾歟？嘗考今之郡縣，視周侯國亦略相當。都司衞所所在，總其尺籍，無慮百萬，然視古兵數，不啻懸絕。豈今則專力，古則兼農故耶？國家京師團營，桓桓貔虎；諸邊甲士，湯湯江漢，可謂盛矣！獨郡縣之兵，若所當議。故頃者本兵建策，欲酌郡縣小大，卽所設壯快稍增其額，豈其然乎？昔漢置材官騎士，杜佑以為其制可采；唐李抱真籍丁教練，或指其事，遂謂民兵可用，可得聞乎？然有兵則有將，如有宋時一郡盡行軍制，施諸今之有司，無乃不可乎？或□兵非難，難于足食，故昔人有謂給
translation_en:
…why could the □□ son [?] be sent back? In all these matters there must be a way to arrive at a balanced judgment; mere words without practical relevance will certainly not suffice. Please set this out in writing, so that we may assess your learning in the cultivation of virtue.
Question: In antiquity, a large state had three armies. Its territory measured one hundred li square, and each army numbered twelve thousand five hundred men. Under the Zhou there were some eighteen hundred states. Taking an average among the states, each would have had approximately two armies. How could their forces have been so numerous? I have examined the prefectures and counties of the present day: they are roughly comparable to the feudal states of the Zhou. Wherever Regional Military Commissions, guards, and battalions are established, their military registers total fully a million men. Yet compared with the troop numbers of antiquity, the disparity is immense. Is this because soldiers today devote themselves exclusively to military service, whereas in antiquity they also farmed?
The capital’s combined training camps have warriors valiant as bears and tigers; the armored troops along the frontiers are as mighty as the surging Jiang and Han rivers. These forces may indeed be called flourishing! It is specifically the troops of the prefectures and counties that seem to require discussion. Recently, therefore, the Minister of War proposed a plan to take account of the size of each prefecture and county and slightly increase the authorized numbers of the sturdy men and swift runners already established there. Is this indeed the right approach? Formerly, the Han established picked infantry and cavalry, and Du You considered their system worthy of adoption. Under the Tang, Li Baozhen registered adult men and trained them. Some cite these precedents and consequently maintain that militia can be employed. May we hear your views?
Yet where there are troops, there must also be commanders. If, as in Song times, an entire prefecture were placed under a military system, would it not be impracticable to apply this to the responsible officials today? Some □ [?] that providing troops is not difficult; the difficulty lies in ensuring sufficient provisions. Thus, people in the past proposed supplying them with…

可倣而行之否歟夫天下郡縣均之不
可無兵而西北為急諸士子燕趙之良

translation_en: …them idle farmland and assign them revenue from market taxes: in sum, those who proposed this must have had some insight. Could these measures also be emulated and put into practice? All prefectures and counties throughout the realm must have troops, but the need is most urgent in the northwest. You candidates are the outstanding men of Yan and Zhao and should long have studied these matters. Please set out your views fully in your essays, without reserve.

title: 嘉靖二十二年順天府鄉試錄
text:
第壹場
四書
子曰無爲而治者其舜也與夫何爲哉恭
己正南面而已矣
沈紹慶
同考試官教諭藍批氣象宏大真若親覩
有虞之廷者結尤能道聖人之心
同考試官教諭浦批講夫何爲處明净可
愛以恭己句爲申贊尤有見
===
考試官左贊善浦批莊重
考試官右中允泰批明盡
聖人以至神之化歸聖君而申贊其神也夫恭
己而天下化成非天下至神其孰能與於此此
舜之治所以獨盛夫子所以申贊之也歟其意
若曰治至聖人而極聖人之治至無爲而極是
故主靜立極而至仁之澤自爾其潜孚人見其
天地之位也所以彌綸之具不可得而窺也簡
易示人而德施之普于焉而黙運人見其萬物

第壹場
四書

沈紹慶
同考試官教諭藍批：「氣象宏大，真若親覩有虞之廷者，結尤能道聖人之心。」
同考試官教諭浦批：「講夫何爲處，明净可愛；以恭己句爲申贊，尤有見。」
考試官左贊善浦批：「莊重。」
考試官右中允泰批：「明盡。」
聖人以至神之化歸聖君，而申贊其神也。夫恭己而天下化成，非天下至神，其孰能與於此？此舜之治所以獨盛，夫子所以申贊之也歟！其意若曰：治至聖人而極，聖人之治至無爲而極。是故主靜立極，而至仁之澤自爾其潜孚；人見其天地之位也，所以彌綸之具不可得而窺也。簡易示人，而德施之普于焉而黙運；人見其萬物
translation_en:
First Session
Four Books
The Master said: “Was it not Shun who governed without action? What indeed did he do? He simply held himself reverently and sat facing due south.”
Shen Shaoqing
Comment by Associate Examiner Lan, Instructor: “Grand in its scope and spirit, as though he had personally beheld the court of Youyu [Shun]. The conclusion is particularly successful in expressing the sage’s mind.”
Comment by Associate Examiner Pu, Instructor: “The explanation of ‘What indeed did he do?’ is clear, lucid, and pleasing. Taking the phrase ‘held himself reverently’ as a further expression of praise shows particular insight.”
Comment by Examiner Pu, Left Assistant Adviser: “Dignified and weighty.”
Comment by Examiner Tai, Right Assistant Mentor: “Clear and exhaustive.”
The sage attributes transformation of the utmost spiritual efficacy to the sage ruler, and further praises that efficacy. To hold oneself reverently and thereby bring all under Heaven to a perfected state through transformation—who could attain this without possessing the utmost spiritual efficacy in the world? Is this not why Shun’s government was uniquely flourishing, and why the Master praised it further? His meaning might be expressed thus: Government reaches its highest perfection in the sage, and the sage’s government reaches its highest perfection in governing without action. Thus, by making stillness his guiding principle and establishing the supreme standard, the beneficence of his consummate humaneness naturally permeates unseen. People see Heaven and Earth in their proper places, but cannot discern the means by which he comprehensively orders them. He presents himself to others with simplicity and ease, while the universal bestowal of his virtue operates silently therein. People see his myriad things…

title: 嘉靖二十二年順天府鄉試錄
text:
之育也所以參贊之宜不可得而測也吾嘗由
百世之後等百世之王可以與此者其舜也與
盖天下之治唯萃于一人之身故雖聖人之治
盖難于泯大化之迹舜則玄德升聞而重華協
于帝凡時之所當爲者堯先之矣知人則哲而
岳牧唯其賢凡身之所欲爲者人代之矣是故
無爲之治非舜莫之能與也夫舜則何爲哉吾
見濬哲之蘊發而爲穆穆之容有孚顒若嚮離
明以聽治也允塞之恭形而爲作肅之貌嚴威
===
儼恪居九重以臨民也垂衣而百辟刑焉所以
示天下中正之觀唯此焉耳負扆而羣后覲焉
所以慰天下利見之誠盡在是矣盖外此而其
有爲之跡夫孰得而見之也耶夫曰無爲則化
之神可知顯諸仁者藏諸用也曰恭已則德之
盛可想本諸身者徵諸民也夫子以是賛舜所
以感慕之者至矣抑夫子賛堯曰蕩蕩乎民無
能名焉此賛舜之旨也然堯所可見者曰成功
文章而舜唯曰恭已豈唐虞之德固有間歟盖

punctuated: 之育也，所以參贊之宜，不可得而測也。吾嘗由百世之後，等百世之王，可以與此者，其舜也與！盖天下之治，唯萃于一人之身，故雖聖人之治，盖難于泯大化之迹。舜則玄德升聞，而重華協于帝，凡時之所當爲者，堯先之矣；知人則哲，而岳牧唯其賢，凡身之所欲爲者，人代之矣。是故無爲之治，非舜莫之能與也。夫舜則何爲哉？吾見濬哲之蘊，發而爲穆穆之容，有孚顒若，嚮離明以聽治也；允塞之恭，形而爲作肅之貌，嚴威儼恪，居九重以臨民也。垂衣而百辟刑焉，所以示天下中正之觀，唯此焉耳；負扆而羣后覲焉，所以慰天下利見之誠，盡在是矣。盖外此而其有爲之跡，夫孰得而見之也耶？夫曰無爲，則化之神可知，顯諸仁者藏諸用也；曰恭已，則德之盛可想，本諸身者徵諸民也。夫子以是賛舜，所以感慕之者至矣。抑夫子賛堯曰：「蕩蕩乎！民無能名焉。」此賛舜之旨也。然堯所可見者曰成功文章，而舜唯曰恭已，豈唐虞之德固有間歟？盖
translation_en:
…the nurturing of the myriad things; yet the fitting means by which he assists Heaven and Earth in their transforming and nourishing work cannot be fathomed. I have sought, from a hundred generations later, to rank the kings of those hundred generations. Surely it is Shun who can attain this!

The governance of all under Heaven is concentrated in the person of one man. Thus, even in a sage’s government, it is difficult to efface the traces of his great transforming work. In Shun’s case, his profound virtue became known on high, and his renewed brilliance accorded with that of the emperor Yao. Whatever the times required to be done, Yao had already undertaken. Shun was discerning in his knowledge of men, and the chiefs of the mountains and regional governors were all worthy. Whatever he wished to do himself, others performed in his stead. Thus none but Shun could attain government through nonaction.

What, then, did Shun do? I see his inner store of profound wisdom expressed in a solemn and reverent countenance. Sincere and august, he faced south toward the light to attend to government. His reverence, truly pervading his being, took form in a dignified bearing. Awe-inspiring, solemn, and respectful, he dwelt within the ninefold palace precincts and presided over the people. With his robes hanging loosely, he served as a model for the hundred lords: this alone was how he displayed centrality and rectitude to all under Heaven. With the ceremonial screen behind him, he received the assembled lords in audience: herein lay everything needed to satisfy the sincere longing of all under Heaven for the beneficial sight of a great man. Beyond this, who could discern any trace of deliberate action on his part?

To say ‘nonaction’ makes the wondrous power of his transformation intelligible: what is manifest in benevolence is concealed in its workings. To say ‘maintaining reverence in his own person’ allows us to conceive the fullness of his virtue: what is rooted in his person finds its evidence among the people. In praising Shun in these terms, the Master expressed the utmost admiration and yearning.

Moreover, when the Master praised Yao, he said: ‘So vast was he that the people could find no name for it!’ This is also the purport of his praise of Shun. Yet what could be seen in Yao was described as accomplished works and splendid cultural forms, whereas of Shun he said only that he maintained reverence in his own person. Even so, in establishing the boundaries of the mountains, dredging the rivers, punishing the wicked, and consulting the Four Peaks, did Shun ever for a single day forget the world? Precisely because he never forgot it, he could govern by following his heart’s desires. How apt are Master Cheng’s words: “Heaven and Earth have no deliberate intention, yet accomplish transformation; the sage has deliberate intention, yet acts without contrivance.”
The Book of Odes says: “Cutting an axe handle, cutting an axe handle: its pattern is not far away.” Yet when one holds an axe handle to cut another and looks askance at it, one still considers the pattern distant. title: 嘉靖二十二年順天府鄉試錄
text:
道不可離之意至此若曰知天下無性外之道
則知君子無道外之教詩不云乎伐柯伐柯其
則不遠蓋言人之伐木以爲柯者不必遠有所
法也而長短之則惟取諸所執之柯焉是固以
爲不遠矣然自今觀之所執一柯也所伐一柯
也在物者有彼此之别則伐者有睨視之勞其
猶以爲遠乎若乃人之有道猶物之有則也雖
裁成品節不無待于君子而降衷秉彞則各足
於斯人是又非伐柯者倫矣是故君子之治人
===
也方夫人之未易其惡未至于中也則因厥性
分之有責以職分之常迪之以知皆其人之良
知也庸之以能皆其人之良能也初未嘗取此
與彼而輙有所附益焉及夫人之既易其惡既
至于中也則嘉其遷善之益遂其並生之心蓋
曰彼能是是亦足矣彼知是是亦足矣又曷嘗
舍近圖遠而過爲之責望耶蓋其始非徇也緣
性以立教也其終非恕也過之則違道也觀此
則道不遠人人不可遠人以爲道豈不益可見

舍近圖遠而過爲之責望耶蓋其始非徇也緣
性以立教也其終非恕也過之則違道也觀此
則道不遠人人不可遠人以爲道豈不益可見
punctuated: 道不可離之意，至此若曰：知天下無性外之道，則知君子無道外之教。《詩》不云乎：「伐柯伐柯，其則不遠。」蓋言人之伐木以爲柯者，不必遠有所法也，而長短之則，惟取諸所執之柯焉。是固以爲不遠矣。然自今觀之，所執一柯也，所伐一柯也，在物者有彼此之别，則伐者有睨視之勞，其猶以爲遠乎？若乃人之有道，猶物之有則也。雖裁成品節不無待于君子，而降衷秉彞則各足於斯人，是又非伐柯者倫矣。是故君子之治人也，方夫人之未易其惡、未至于中也，則因厥性分之有，責以職分之常。迪之以知，皆其人之良知也；庸之以能，皆其人之良能也。初未嘗取此與彼，而輙有所附益焉。及夫人之既易其惡、既至于中也，則嘉其遷善之益，遂其並生之心。蓋曰：彼能是，是亦足矣；彼知是，是亦足矣。又曷嘗舍近圖遠，而過爲之責望耶？蓋其始非徇也，緣性以立教也；其終非恕也，過之則違道也。觀此，則道不遠人，人不可遠人以爲道，豈不益可見
translation_en:
…the meaning of the Way’s inseparability. At this point, it is as though he were saying: Once one understands that there is no Way outside human nature, one understands that the gentleman has no teaching outside the Way. Does the Book of Odes not say, “Carving an axe handle, carving an axe handle: its pattern is not far away”? This means that someone cutting wood to make an axe handle need not seek a distant model: the standard for its length is taken solely from the handle already in his grasp. This certainly seems near at hand. Yet, considered now, the handle he holds is one handle, and the handle he cuts is another. Since the objects are distinct, the woodcutter must take the trouble to glance from one to the other. Might this still be considered distant? Human beings possess the Way just as things possess their standards. Although shaping conduct and regulating its particulars require the gentleman’s guidance, the inner nature bestowed by Heaven and the constant norms people uphold are fully present in each person. This, then, is unlike the case of carving an axe handle.

Thus, when the gentleman governs people, while they have yet to reform their faults and attain the mean, he draws upon what their nature already possesses and holds them to the constant requirements of their duties. The understanding toward which he guides them is entirely their own innate moral knowledge; the abilities he puts to use are entirely their own innate capacities. From the outset, he has never taken something from one person and given it to another, thereby adding anything to them. Once they have reformed their faults and attained the mean, he commends their progress toward goodness and fulfills their wish to live alongside others [?]. It is as though he says: If they can do this, this is sufficient; if they understand this, this is sufficient. When has he ever abandoned what is near to seek what is distant, making excessive demands upon them? His initial approach is no mere indulgence: he establishes his teaching in accordance with human nature. His final approach is no mere leniency: to go beyond this would violate the Way. Viewed in this light, does it not become still clearer that the Way is not far from people, and that people must not depart from humanity in pursuing the Way…

title: 嘉靖二十二年順天府鄉試錄
text:
哉嗟夫道教之名不明于天下久矣子思子首
發明之而於篇章不一而足至此復以伐柯爲
喻盖曰知所以教則知所以學矣或者乃曰君
子之道費而隱語大天下莫能載焉而治人乃
爾不以姑息乎殊不知道無精粗學有漸次是
故夫婦之所能知能行以至聖人之所不能知
不能行事在不息而已學者能由是而緝煕其
功尚何高遠之不可企哉否則日用不知君子
之教荒矣
===
夫義路也禮門也惟君子能由是路出入
是門也詩云周道如底其直如矢君子
所履小人所視

…indeed! Alas, the meanings of the Way and instruction have long been obscure to the world. Master Zisi first elucidated them, addressing them repeatedly throughout his chapters. Here he again uses the cutting of an axe handle as an analogy, in effect saying: if one understands how to teach, one understands how to learn. Some, however, say: “The gentleman’s Way is all-pervasive yet hidden; speaking of its greatness, nothing in the world can contain it. If one governs people in this fashion, does this not amount to indulgence?” They utterly fail to understand that the Way has no division into refined and coarse, while learning proceeds by stages. Thus, from what ordinary husbands and wives can know and do, to what even sages cannot know and do, the task consists simply in never ceasing. If learners can proceed from this and continually develop and illuminate their achievement, what heights or distances could remain beyond their reach? Otherwise, people use the Way daily without knowing it, and the gentleman’s teaching falls into neglect.
“Righteousness is the road; ritual propriety is the gate. Only the gentleman can follow this road and pass in and out through this gate. The Book of Odes says: ‘The road of Zhou is like a whetstone, straight as an arrow. It is what the gentleman treads, and what the common people look upon.’”

text:
守矣
考試官左贊善浦批是知義禮者
考試官右中允秦批精確
大賢指人君見賢之道因言能守道者之義焉
夫禮義由賢者出而實人君所由以見賢者也
自非君子其孰能守哉宜孟子證其義以曉萬
章也意謂君之與士本以相成然恒相求而不
相遇者亦以未盡其道焉耳何則欲見賢而召
之孰不以為進賢之路也然有義焉夫義也者
===
宜也宜於義而後有可見之節上不諂而下不
瀆也以是登賢而賢無不進矣欲見賢而召之
又孰不以為來賢之門也然有禮焉夫禮也者
理也理於禮而後有可嘉之會儀不愆而則不
過也以是延賢而賢無不入矣夫義雖為進賢
之路然非其人則舍之而不由者多矣惟君子
則以義制事非其義也固無適也如其義也亦
無莫也而能由是路焉夫禮雖為來賢之門然
非其人則得其門者或寡矣惟君子則以禮制

大賢指人君見賢之道，因言能守道者之義焉。夫禮義由賢者出，而實人君所由以見賢者也。自非君子，其孰能守哉？宜孟子證其義以曉萬章也。意謂君之與士，本以相成，然恒相求而不相遇者，亦以未盡其道焉耳。何則？欲見賢而召之，孰不以為進賢之路也？然有義焉。夫義也者，宜也。宜於義，而後有可見之節，上不諂而下不瀆也。以是登賢，而賢無不進矣。欲見賢而召之，又孰不以為來賢之門也？然有禮焉。夫禮也者，理也。理於禮，而後有可嘉之會，儀不愆而則不過也。以是延賢，而賢無不入矣。夫義雖為進賢之路，然非其人，則舍之而不由者多矣。惟君子則以義制事，非其義也，固無適也；如其義也，亦無莫也，而能由是路焉。夫禮雖為來賢之門，然非其人，則得其門者或寡矣。惟君子則以禮制
translation_en:
…what he upholds.

Examiner Pu, Left Mentor, comments: “Here is one who understands righteousness and ritual propriety.”

Examiner Qin, Right Assistant Instructor, comments: “Precise and sound.”

The great worthy points out the way for a ruler to meet worthy men, and accordingly explains what it means to be someone capable of holding to the Way. Ritual propriety and righteousness proceed from worthy men, yet they are indeed the means by which rulers may meet worthy men. Who but a gentleman could uphold them? It is fitting that Mengzi should substantiate this principle to enlighten Wan Zhang. His meaning is that rulers and scholars are fundamentally meant to bring one another to fulfillment. Yet they constantly seek one another without meeting, simply because they have not fully followed the proper way. Why is this? When a ruler wishes to meet worthy men and summons them, who would not regard this as the road to advancing the worthy? Yet righteousness must govern it. Righteousness means fittingness. Only when conduct accords with righteousness can there be a proper occasion for meeting: one neither flatters those above nor treats those below disrespectfully. If the worthy are elevated in this way, none will fail to come forward. When a ruler wishes to meet worthy men and summons them, who, again, would not regard this as the gate through which to attract the worthy? Yet ritual propriety must govern it. Ritual propriety means principle. Only when conduct is ordered according to ritual propriety can there be a commendable meeting, with no fault in ceremony and no overstepping of standards. If the worthy are invited in this way, none will fail to enter.

Although righteousness is the road to advancing the worthy, many who are not the right sort of person abandon it and do not follow it. Only the gentleman regulates affairs by righteousness. If something does not accord with righteousness, he certainly has no fixed inclination toward it; if it does accord with righteousness, neither does he have any fixed opposition to it. Thus he can follow this road. Although ritual propriety is the gate through which to attract the worthy, among those who are not the right sort of person, perhaps few find that gate. Only the gentleman regulates by ritual propriety…

其有爲也，禮當行也；其不爲也，禮當止也，而能出入是門焉。然此豈我有譽於君子哉？詩不云乎？瞻彼周道，言乎其平，則如砥也；言乎其直，則如矢也。是惟君子能履之爲道，而有以盡人事之制焉；若小人，則視之爲法，而有以具民則之觀焉。夫義也，則亦禮也；路也，則亦門也。上之所行，下斯效之矣。觀此，則能由是路固有足徵，而其出入是門亦可例見。曾是而可召之乎？不可召而召之，宜乎其不往見也！嘅夫！時至孟子，利路啓矣，權門闢矣，滔滔者天下皆是矣。故騶衍也以擁篲矜，季子也以佩印侈，大率可覩矣。孟子重爲世道惜也，故揭義路禮門詔焉。其不欲人爲君子之棄而小人之歸也，明矣。噫！以此爲防，而猶有捷徑終南、足三及門者，何也？

易
制而用之謂之法，利用出入，民咸用之謂之神。
沈紹慶
translation_en:
…When he acts, ritual propriety calls for action; when he refrains, ritual propriety calls for stopping. Thus he can enter and leave through this gate. But am I merely praising the gentleman here? Does not the Book of Odes say, “Look upon that road of Zhou”? As to its evenness, it is like a whetstone; as to its straightness, it is like an arrow. Only the gentleman can tread it as his Way and thereby fulfill the standards governing human affairs. The petty man regards it as a rule, finding in it a model of the standards for the people. Righteousness is also ritual propriety; the road is also the gate. What those above practice, those below emulate. From this, there is ample evidence that the gentleman can follow this road; his entering and leaving through this gate can likewise be understood by analogy. How, then, could such a man simply be summoned? To summon someone who ought not to be summoned—surely it is fitting that he should refuse to go for an audience!

Alas! By the time of Mengzi, the roads to profit had opened, and the gates of power stood wide. The whole world was swept along in this current. Thus Zou Yan vaunted the honor of being received with a broom to clear his path, while Jizi flaunted the seals of office he wore. From these examples, the general tendency is plain. Mengzi deeply lamented the condition of the world. He therefore proclaimed righteousness as the road and ritual propriety as the gate, to instruct people. Clearly, he did not want them to become people whom gentlemen rejected and petty men welcomed. Alas! Even with this safeguard, there were still those who took the “shortcut through Zhongnan” to office and those whose “feet reached the gate three times” [?]. Why was this so?

Book of Changes
“To fashion it and put it to use is called a pattern. To make its use beneficial in going out and coming in, so that all the people employ it, is called the numinous.”
Shen Shaoqing.

大傳論神物之生，必原法立於聖人而用妙於天下也。夫聖人制蓍龜之法以教天下，而天下之用神矣。神物之興，不亦在是也邪？大傳論卜筮而及此，若曰：蓍龜之生，固有天地自然之序矣，而聖人制之則何如哉？盖聖人有見於蓍者，天地之所以顯其數也，於是因蓍而制之，以肇夫大衍五十之數焉。盖用之以筮，而十八變之相營出矣。有見於龜者，天地之所以示其兆也，於是因龜而制之，以立夫洪範五占之兆焉。盖用之以卜，而五行之生克著矣。若是者，何以謂之法邪？盖蓍龜具造化之理，而非卜筮以顯之，則固不能自致其用也。今則本乾坤闔闢之妙

Comment by Associate Examiner Lan, Instructor: “The writing is vigorous and forceful, and the understanding is true and exact. Should not an exposition of the meaning of the Changes be like this?”

Comment by Associate Examiner Pu, Instructor: “The discussion of method and spiritual efficacy [?] is naturally apt in its arrangement. Nothing matches this piece; it should be recorded as a model.”

Comment by Examiner Pu, Left Admonisher: “The meaning of the Changes is expounded with precision and pertinence.”

Comment by Examiner Qin, Right Rectifier: “Both expression and reasoning are fully accomplished.”

In discussing the emergence of spiritually potent objects, the Great Commentary necessarily traces their origin to the sages’ establishment of methods and to the wondrous efficacy of their use throughout the world. The sages devised methods for using milfoil stalks and tortoise shells to instruct the world, and the world’s use of them thereby became spiritually efficacious. Does not the rise of these spiritually potent objects lie precisely here? The Great Commentary reaches this point in its discussion of tortoise-shell and milfoil divination, as though saying: The generation of milfoil and tortoises certainly follows the natural order of Heaven and Earth; but how did the sages regulate their use? The sages perceived that milfoil was the means by which Heaven and Earth made their numbers manifest. Accordingly, they devised a method based on milfoil, instituting the number fifty of the Great Expansion. Through its use in milfoil divination, the coordinated operations of the eighteen transformations emerged. They perceived that the tortoise was the means by which Heaven and Earth revealed their signs. Accordingly, they devised a method based on the tortoise, establishing the signs of the five kinds of tortoise-shell prognostication in the Great Plan. Through its use in tortoise-shell divination, the mutual generation and conquest of the Five Phases became manifest. Why are such things called methods? Milfoil and tortoise shells embody the principles of the transforming processes of creation, but without divination to reveal these principles, they cannot of themselves realize their usefulness. Now, taking as their basis the wondrous closing and opening of Qian and Kun …

text:
而啟制作之原因象以□見之迹而立推行之
準蓋縁物以作則而因時以設教乃聖人脩道
之所爲也不謂之法而何由是法之宜於民也
出則足以變動而時行則行焉入則足以靜謐
而時止則止焉出入无疾而有以盡其利矣由
是民之用夫法也以之出王游衍而出無不用
焉以之嚮晦宴息而入無不用焉廣大悉備而
有以普其施矣若是者何以謂之神邪盖天下

情蓍龜之生天地之心也卜筮之制聖人之情

translation_en:
…and thereby opens up the source of their devising and establishment; following the images and their □ manifest traces [?], he establishes standards for putting them into practice. Drawing upon things to make rules and adapting instruction to the times are what the sage does in cultivating the Way. What could this be called but a model? Thus, in its suitability for the people, this model enables change and movement when they go forth: when it is time to act, they act. It enables quiet repose when they withdraw: when it is time to stop, they stop. Going forth and withdrawing without harm, they can fully realize its benefits. Thus, when the people employ this model, they use it in going abroad and roaming at leisure, so that none of their outward activities is without it; they use it in resting as dusk approaches, so that none of their inward activities is without it. Vast and complete in every respect, it can extend its operation everywhere.

Why should this be called numinous? The world contains incipient signs of good and ill fortune, but without divination by tortoise shell and milfoil to disclose them, people could not themselves grasp their subtle beginnings. Now they are stirred to action in pursuing the auspicious and avoiding the harmful, in ways that thought cannot fathom; they adapt to changing circumstances in their dealings with things, in ways that intellect and effort cannot accomplish. Following this Way without knowing it, conforming to the Supreme Lord’s rules without recognizing them—this is the common people’s spontaneous everyday practice. What could this be called but numinous? Thus we know that the model is how the sage brings his capacity to fulfillment, and the numinous is how the common people share in that capacity. Which of these does not fulfill the usefulness of images and implements [?] and complete the work of creation and transformation?

In essence, the numinous is not something refined, nor is the model something coarse: they merely receive different names according to the matter at hand. Moreover, the constant way of Heaven and Earth is to extend their heart to all things without deliberate intention; the constant way of the sage is to respond to all affairs through his feelings without partial feeling. The production of milfoil and tortoises is the heart of Heaven and Earth; the institution of divination by tortoise shell and milfoil is the feeling of the sage…

With above and below having their constant positions, do not Heaven and Earth establish their places? Gen occupies the northwest, and its image is the mountain; Dui occupies the southeast, and its image is the marsh. When Gen and Dui face one another, the mountain, through its emptiness, receives the marsh’s moisture, and its qi consequently descends; the marsh, through its moisture, responds to the mountain’s emptiness, and its qi consequently rises. When Zhen and Xun face one another, nothing moves the myriad things more swiftly than thunder: thunder arises and the wind grows fierce. Nothing stirs the myriad things more swiftly than wind: wind rises and thunder accelerates. Thunder and wind augment one another and thus impinge upon one another. Li occupies due east, and its image is fire; Kan occupies due west, and its image is water. When Kan and Li face one another, water moistens the myriad things, while fire checks its cold; fire dries the myriad things, while water checks its fierceness. 三者統言休徵之所感而其效大焉甚矣休徵
之效大也觀其所感而君臣省驗之情可見矣
箕子衍庶徵之疇以告武王至此若謂庶徵之
理雖出於天感應之機寔存乎人是故歲月日
以尊卑爲徵也誠使三者之間召以五事之得
道通於上下之交而天地泰德隆於應感之際
而陰陽和曰雨曰暘各以其叙而先後無愆期

箕子衍庶徵之疇以告武王，至此若謂：庶徵之理雖出於天，感應之機寔存乎人。是故歲月日以尊卑爲徵也。誠使三者之間，召以五事之得，道通於上下之交而天地泰，德隆於應感之際而陰陽和，曰雨曰暘，各以其叙而先後無愆期也；曰燠寒風，各以其時而有無非一極也。是則君身可徵其巳修，臣下可徵其交修矣。而其效當何如哉？

These three collectively describe what calls forth auspicious signs, and their effects are great. How great indeed are the effects of auspicious signs! By examining what calls them forth, one can discern the disposition of ruler and ministers to reflect upon themselves and examine the evidence.

When Jizi expounded the category of the various signs to instruct King Wu, at this point he seemed to say: Although the principle governing the various signs proceeds from Heaven, the workings of stimulus and response truly reside in human beings. Thus the year, month, and day serve as signs corresponding to higher and lower ranks. If, among these three, auspicious signs are indeed summoned by the proper performance of the Five Activities, the Way will flow through the interaction of those above and below, and Heaven and Earth will be at peace; virtue will flourish in the interplay of stimulus and response, and yin and yang will be harmonious. Rain and sunshine will each follow their proper sequence, neither arriving before nor after their appointed time. Warmth, cold, and wind will each occur in their proper season, neither their presence nor their absence going to an extreme. These signs will then attest that the ruler has cultivated himself and that his ministers have cultivated themselves together. What, then, must their effects be?

I know that the abundance or scarcity of the grains depends upon the seasons. When conditions are seasonable, Heaven sends down well-being; all fine plants share in the blessing of luxuriant growth, and farmers rejoice in the bounty of abundant harvests. Reckoned by years, there are plentiful crops; reckoned by months, there are harvests. Through these auspicious signs, fruition is achieved. The decline or flourishing of government likewise depends upon the times. When conditions are seasonable, all undertakings prosper. Faithful discharge of duties produces accomplishments renewed daily, and profound discernment advances enterprises to ample fruition. This becomes manifest in laws and institutions and evident in rites and music: through these auspicious signs, government is made illustrious. Are those who judge the times in deciding whether to enter office or withdraw not the outstanding men? Once auspicious signs are elicited, an enlightened ruler and worthy ministers meet, and it is auspicious for men to advance together. Worthies among the people conceive the wish to serve as reverent ministers; the virtuous and wise express their resolve to exert themselves in service. Those possessing virtue advance through their virtue, and those with something to say gain recognition through their words. Is it not through this that they become distinguished? 同考試官教諭方批：親賢並用，周道然也。此作獨得此意，其殆發周公之蘊者與？
同考試官教諭黃批：以同姓異姓立說，的
translation_en:
…and is it not the household that experiences adversity or prosperity as the times change? Once auspicious signs are elicited, members of the household live fittingly together and every kind of harmony gathers. A spirit of concord and reverence becomes manifest within the palace, and the inner chambers enjoy the blessings of peace. The state is tranquil, and families rejoice together. Is this not the means by which peace and well-being are achieved? Thus we know that when the Five Conducts have their confirmations in Heaven, all four blessings arrive in the state. It is fitting that ruler and ministers, those above and those below, should examine themselves together. Can those who wish to establish the Sovereign's Ultimate Standard and put the constant human relationships in order fail to know what they must keep in mind and put into practice?
Yet this discusses only the underlying principle; it is not a matter of deliberately producing these effects. For the stimulus arising from the Five Conducts occurs of itself, without any expectation of eliciting it; the response of the various signs likewise occurs of itself, without any expectation of that response. As the saying goes, when those above and below are united in reverence and respect, Heaven and Earth naturally take their proper places, the myriad things naturally flourish, and all vital energies are harmonious. This is the way of embodying trustworthiness and attaining accord. How, then, should one act at the point where Heaven and humanity interact? Simply fulfill what lies within one's own power and leave what rests with Heaven to Heaven. Let those who understand the Way take note of this.
“There were also men such as Guo Shu, such as Hong Yao, such as San Yisheng, such as Tai Dian, and such as Nangong Kuo.”
Yu Min

Comment by Associate Examiner Huang, Instructor: “It builds its argument around men of the same surname and men of different surnames, clearly …”

Examiner Pu, Left Admonisher, comments: “Grounding the argument in royal kinsmen and worthy men is entirely right.”
Examiner Qin, Right Mentor, comments: “The language has proper form and captures the essentials.”
The great minister recalled and enumerated the assistants of the king who founded the dynasty: among them were esteemed relatives of the same surname and worthy men of other surnames. How greatly a founding king depends upon having assistants! When suitable men are found among both kinsmen and worthies, can one say that royal achievement is not founded upon this? The Duke of Zhou spoke of this while urging the Duke of Shao to remain, as if to say: “The royal enterprise of our Zhou certainly arose magnificently under King Wen. Yet the many states were vast, and the myriad people numerous. How could one man alone have brought them into good order and harmony? He surely had men to assist him.”
At that time there was a man such as Guo Shu. As a branch of the richly blessed royal stock, he inherited the family tradition of brotherly affection. Though enfeoffed in the state of Guo, he actually held a place among the officers at court. In their official relationship they were ruler and minister, but in kinship he ranked among the king’s brothers. Thus the royal clan had its suitable man. Nor was this all: there were also Hong Yao and San Yisheng. Nor was this all: there were also Tai Dian and Nangong Kuo. All these men fled the cruelty of Xin of Shang and attached themselves to the benevolence of our Zhou at Qi. Some followed in the footsteps of Boyi and Shuqi and were numbered among the ten ministers who brought order; others arrived following Xin and Yu and were known as the four friends. Thus there were suitable men among those of other surnames.
These five men shared one virtue and one purpose: among them were those called men who draw others into allegiance and those who repel aggression. United in reverence and working together respectfully, they included those who guided and assisted, and those who hastened to carry out affairs. translation_en:
…Hong Yao and San Yisheng, then Tai Dian and Nangong Kuo provided the support of trusted lieutenants. The good order of the many states rested upon this foundation, as did the harmony of the myriad people. Otherwise, King Wen too would have stood alone; how then would his situation have differed from that of the Xia? Even King Wen, in his rise, relied so heavily on the assistance of these five ministers. Now, among kinsmen, only I, Dan, and among worthy men, only you, Shi, remain to assist his cultivated descendant. How, then, can you still seek to leave? Alas! Whether seasoned elders remain or depart has grave consequences for a state. Moreover, the Duke of Shao’s worthiness certainly matched that of Hong Yao, Tai Dian, Nangong Kuo, and their fellows, while King Cheng, preserving the inherited achievement and tending the beginnings of his reign, was especially far from matching King Wen’s abundant virtue. This was what the Duke of Zhou recognized [?]. Yet the poems praising King Wen speak either of “the splendid many officers” or of “the many officers in their imposing ranks.” We therefore know that King Wen’s assistants must have extended beyond these men. The Duke of Zhou merely singled out the most important: this is what is meant by abundant assistance from the ministers known as the Four Companions. Otherwise, why would even the achievements of Grand Preceptor Shangfu have gone unmentioned?

Book of Odes

Fang Shu led them forth;
the gong players beat the drums.
He arrayed the army and marshaled the troops—
illustrious and trustworthy Fang Shu.
The drums resounded deeply;
the ranks were ordered to their rolling thunder.

Ma Kuai

translation_en:
…the many scholars.

Associate Examiner Zheng, Instructor, comments: “The progression is exceptional and the discipline strict and orderly: it vividly resembles Fang Shu’s method of directing an army.”

Associate Examiner Liang, School Director, comments: “Its standards and proportions are orderly and strict; its language and meaning are lucid. It is precisely what military strategy calls combining orthodox methods with extraordinary ones. Include it.”

Examiner Pu, Left Admonisher, comments: “Mature and accomplished.”

Examiner Tai, Right Admonisher, comments: “Refined and correct.”

The poet praises the great general for maintaining strict measures governing advance and retreat in his command of the army. Advancing and retreating according to prescribed measures constitutes good military governance. Fang Shu possessed this quality; it was fitting that he could achieve victory while preserving his forces intact. In King Xuan’s time, the Man peoples of Jing rebelled, and the king ordered Fang Shu to campaign in the south. The poet composed a poem about this. At this point, he seems to say: military forces serve to give ordered expression to anger; supporting this with restraint and discipline is the foundation for confronting the enemy in righteous indignation.

Thus our Fang Shu, entrusted with weighty responsibilities beyond the palace gates, commanded three thousand chariots. His well-trained soldiers were certainly all fit for deployment in battle formations. Yet the army’s ears and eyes depended on bells and drums, which unified its movements and halts. Accordingly, there were bell players and drum players. Commands were conveyed through these instruments, each player attending to his assigned duty, so that, in advancing and retreating, the soldiers could not only watch one another but also respond to one another through sound.

Among the five forms of admonition is the oath, employed in the army to impress upon the soldiers the duty of obeying commands. Accordingly, the troops were drawn up and solemn instructions proclaimed, enforcing strict oaths and commands at the moment before battle…

title: 嘉靖二十二年順天府鄉試錄
text:
時而各恭其事使其進與退不愆于六步七步
不愆于四伐五伐也不惟是耳惟我顯允之方
叔當其進而會戰非曰可以銳而不整也一鼓
作氣而紀律之嚴明謹以立動動以進衆而雍
容之意常行於金革之中其聲則淵淵然有和
平而無暴怒也此其進也又不爲有節乎入而
振旅非曰可以散而無統也戢其餘勇而節制
之明信見其入猶見其出而介胄之間不失夫
舒緩之度其鼓亦闐闐然有從容而無急迫也
===
此其退也又不爲有節乎夫以方叔帥師可謂
有能之將而進退有節如此則又爲有制之兵
有不怔征必克矣豈徒以車馬之盛爲足恃哉
嘗觀易之師曰師貞丈人吉又曰長子帥師蓋
以一國之重數萬人之命授之一人其責重且
艱矣而可以輕慮淺謀者當之乎違良士任勇
夫此秦穆所以取悔於殽之後也宣王南征而
付之以元老壯猶之方叔其濟也宜矣後之將

punctuated:
時，而各恭其事，使其進與退不愆于六步七步，不愆于四伐五伐也。不惟是耳，惟我顯允之方叔，當其進而會戰，非曰可以銳而不整也。一鼓作氣，而紀律之嚴明，謹以立，動動以進衆，而雍容之意常行於金革之中。其聲則淵淵然，有和平而無暴怒也。此其進也，又不爲有節乎？入而振旅，非曰可以散而無統也。戢其餘勇，而節制之明信，見其入猶見其出，而介胄之間不失夫舒緩之度。其鼓亦闐闐然，有從容而無急迫也。此其退也，又不爲有節乎？夫以方叔帥師，可謂有能之將，而進退有節如此，則又爲有制之兵，有不怔征必克矣，豈徒以車馬之盛爲足恃哉？

嘗觀《易》之《師》曰：「師貞，丈人吉。」又曰：「長子帥師。」蓋以一國之重、數萬人之命授之一人，其責重且艱矣，而可以輕慮淺謀者當之乎？違良士，任勇夫，此秦穆所以取悔於殽之後也。宣王南征，而付之以元老壯猶之方叔，其濟也宜矣。後之將□法焉。
translation_en:
…at the moment before battle, each respectfully attending to his duties, so that in advancing and withdrawing they err neither in taking six or seven steps nor in delivering four or five blows. Nor is this all. Our illustrious and trustworthy Fang Shu, when advancing to join battle, does not suppose that his troops may be impetuous yet disorderly. At the first beating of the drum their courage rises; discipline is strict and clear. They stand with circumspection, and movement upon movement brings the host forward [?], yet an air of composure always prevails amid weapons and armor. The sound is deep and resonant, expressing harmony and calm rather than violent anger. Is not their advance thus regulated? When they return and marshal the troops, he does not suppose that they may disperse without control. They restrain their remaining ardor, and their regulations are clear and dependable: to see them come in is just like seeing them go out. Even amid helmets and armor, they retain a measured ease. Their drums likewise resound, conveying composure without haste. Is not their withdrawal thus regulated? With Fang Shu commanding the army, one may indeed speak of a capable general; and with advance and withdrawal so regulated, these are also disciplined troops. There is no campaign in which they will not conquer [?]. How could the abundance of chariots and horses alone be sufficient to rely upon?

I have read in the Book of Changes, in the hexagram “The Army”: “The army must be steadfast and correct; for a mature man, good fortune.” It also says: “The eldest son commands the army.” When the weight of an entire state and the lives of tens of thousands are entrusted to one man, his responsibility is both grave and difficult. Can someone whose deliberations are careless and whose plans are shallow discharge it? Rejecting worthy men and employing men of mere valor—this was why Duke Mu of Qin came to regret his actions after the battle at Yao. When King Xuan campaigned southward, he entrusted the undertaking to Fang Shu, a venerable minister whose counsels were vigorous. It was fitting that he succeeded. Generals of later ages □ take him as their model [?].

United with Heaven, King Wen’s virtue attained its fullest greatness. If, then, it enriched posterity, was it not something his descendants ought to preserve from generation to generation? title: 嘉靖二十二年順天府鄉試錄
text:
維天之命流通而迹不露運行而用愈藏可謂
穆矣而動靜無端混闢而不窮也陰陽無始循
環而不息也何不已如之維我文王衆善咸備
殆有充積乎其中者所謂德也於乎我文王之
德著之爲文明之象播之爲西土之光可謂顯
矣而仁義根於心真實而無妄也中正建其極
精粹而不雜也何純如之是則天之所以爲天
者不已也不已則純矣文王之所以爲文者純
也純亦不已矣文王與天何間然之有哉然其
===
蘊之則爲德措之則爲道今我以不聰之資纘
莫大之統正有賴於文王之道也而冥冥之中
將何以恤我乎盖必有啓佑之圖以爲敷錫之
休者矣夫既有以恤我豈但已哉我則當昭受
而大順之監于成憲而是則是行務竭其恢弘
之力凡所以御家邦涖天下無一事之敢違焉
爲曾孫者又當繼序而篤厚之繩其祖武而不
愆不忘益致夫率由之功凡所以治百官化萬
民無一時之或悖焉吁上配於天此天命之所

punctuated: 維天之命，流通而迹不露，運行而用愈藏，可謂穆矣。而動靜無端，混闢而不窮也；陰陽無始，循環而不息也。何不已如之！維我文王，衆善咸備，殆有充積乎其中者，所謂德也。於乎！我文王之德，著之爲文明之象，播之爲西土之光，可謂顯矣。而仁義根於心，真實而無妄也；中正建其極，精粹而不雜也。何純如之！是則天之所以爲天者，不已也；不已則純矣。文王之所以爲文者，純也；純亦不已矣。文王與天何間然之有哉？然其蘊之則爲德，措之則爲道。今我以不聰之資，纘莫大之統，正有賴於文王之道也。而冥冥之中，將何以恤我乎？盖必有啓佑之圖，以爲敷錫之休者矣。夫既有以恤我，豈但已哉？我則當昭受而大順之，監于成憲而是則是行，務竭其恢弘之力。凡所以御家邦、涖天下，無一事之敢違焉。爲曾孫者，又當繼序而篤厚之，繩其祖武而不愆不忘，益致夫率由之功。凡所以治百官、化萬民，無一時之或悖焉。吁！上配於天，此天命之所
translation_en:
…Heaven’s mandate flows everywhere without revealing its traces; it moves and operates, yet its workings remain all the more concealed. It may indeed be called profound. Activity and stillness have no endpoint; primal undifferentiation and the opening of the cosmos proceed without exhaustion. Yin and yang have no beginning; their cycles never cease. How unceasing it is! Our King Wen possessed every goodness in full. What filled and accumulated within him was what we call virtue. Ah! Our King Wen’s virtue manifested itself in the signs of cultural brilliance and spread as the radiance of the western lands. It may indeed be called illustrious. Benevolence and righteousness were rooted in his heart, genuine and free of falsity; centrality and correctness established his highest standard, refined and free of admixture. How pure it was! Thus, what makes Heaven Heaven is its ceaselessness; being ceaseless, it is pure. What makes King Wen worthy of the name Wen is his purity; being pure, he too is ceaseless. What distinction could there be between King Wen and Heaven?

Yet what he stored within was virtue, and what he put into practice was the Way. Now I, with my unenlightened capacities, have succeeded to this supremely great imperial line and must depend upon King Wen’s Way. How, from the unseen realm, will he care for me? Surely he has a plan to guide and protect me, bestowing his gracious blessings far and wide. Since he thus cares for me, could I simply leave matters there? I must receive his legacy with clear understanding and fully follow it, looking to the established statutes as my model and putting them into practice, striving with all my strength to extend and magnify it. In governing the royal house and the state and presiding over all under Heaven, I dare depart from it in no single matter. Those who are his descendants must likewise continue the succession and deepen this legacy, following their ancestor’s footsteps without error or forgetfulness and devoting still greater effort to following his course. In governing the hundred officials and transforming the myriad people, they must never depart from it for even a moment. Ah! Above, he matched Heaven: this is why Heaven’s mandate…

盛如此揄揚於登歌之頃不亦宜乎抑論天人
一道也仁孝一理也故仁以承天者必能孝以
事親而善法祖者斯善事天者也周人舉天道
聖德並言豈惟爲文王頌哉夫固有見於天人
之合一而仁孝之無二道也已雖然惟此文王

translation_en:
…is why the Mandate of Heaven came to him; bringing abundance to his descendants below is how the royal enterprise was accomplished. With his virtue so flourishing, was it not fitting to extol it when the hymn was sung in the hall? Moreover, Heaven and humanity share one Way, and benevolence and filial devotion share one principle. Thus one who serves Heaven with benevolence must also be able to serve his parents with filial devotion; one who takes his ancestors as models well also serves Heaven well. When the people of Zhou spoke of Heaven’s Way and the sage’s virtue together, were they merely praising King Wen? They surely perceived the unity of Heaven and humanity, and that benevolence and filial devotion are not two distinct Ways. Nevertheless, it was King Wen’s caution and reverence that enabled him to accord with Heaven; what his descendants preserved generation after generation as their family rule amounted to nothing beyond reverence alone. Must not those in later ages who take King Wen as their teacher likewise make reverence their abiding foundation?

title: 嘉靖二十二年順天府鄉試錄
text:
虐小而謀之譎者此襄文之圖霸俱始於曹春
秋惡之其諸原情以示法與且宋曷為而圍曹
也討不服也曷為惡之君子所以服乎人者惟
德焉耳是故愛人以仁治人以智行有不得者
亦惟反諸已而已也曹共背曹南之盟而惟貳
之懷毋亦宋德有闕莫之攸畏矣乎襄也不知
自反遽以兵圍之絕其往來之使禁其樵採之
徒則亦過矣意者合諸侯以圖霸也釋曹而不
治將無以示威耶吾聞欲速則不達見小利則
===
大事不成順事恕施王政之本也使襄聽子魚
之言而弗亟於兵戈之逞則因壘降崇文王焉
我師矣今也不然卒之兵敗身傷貽譏後世夫
尚誰懟哉春秋書之以見宋舍無威由其操心
之失也晉曷為而入曹也誅無禮也曷為惡之
君子所以喻諸人者惟政焉耳是故武不可觌
文不可匿序成而不至於是乎有攻伐之兵也
曹嬴負觀裸之咎而為兵之端毋亦晉政未狎
莫知所承矣乎文也不修文告遂以師入之分

虐小而謀之譎者。此襄、文之圖霸，俱始於曹，春秋惡之，其諸原情以示法與？且宋曷為而圍曹也？討不服也。曷為惡之？君子所以服乎人者，惟德焉耳。是故愛人以仁，治人以智，行有不得者，亦惟反諸已而已也。曹共背曹南之盟，而惟貳之懷，毋亦宋德有闕，莫之攸畏矣乎？襄也不知自反，遽以兵圍之，絕其往來之使，禁其樵採之徒，則亦過矣。意者合諸侯以圖霸也，釋曹而不治，將無以示威耶？吾聞欲速則不達，見小利則大事不成。順事恕施，王政之本也。使襄聽子魚之言，而弗亟於兵戈之逞，則因壘降崇，文王焉我師矣。今也不然，卒之兵敗身傷，貽譏後世，夫尚誰懟哉？春秋書之，以見宋舍無威，由其操心之失也。

晉曷為而入曹也？誅無禮也。曷為惡之？君子所以喻諸人者，惟政焉耳。是故武不可觌，文不可匿，序成而不至，於是乎有攻伐之兵也。曹嬴負觀裸之咎，而為兵之端，毋亦晉政未狎，莫知所承矣乎？文也不修文告，遂以師入之，分
translation_en:
…cruelty toward small states and duplicity in their designs. Both Duke Xiang and Duke Wen began their pursuit of hegemony with Cao. The Spring and Autumn Annals condemns them: does it not examine their motives to make the proper standard clear?

Why did Song besiege Cao? To punish its refusal to submit. Why condemn this? A gentleman secures others’ submission through virtue alone. Thus he loves others with benevolence and governs them with wisdom; whenever his actions fail to achieve their purpose, he merely turns back to examine himself. Duke Gong of Cao broke the covenant made south of Cao and harbored divided loyalties. Might this not have been because Song’s virtue was deficient, leaving him with no reason to stand in awe of it? Xiang did not know to examine himself. Instead, he abruptly besieged Cao, cutting off its envoys’ passage and preventing its woodcutters and gatherers from going out. This was excessive. Perhaps he intended to unite the feudal lords and seek hegemony, and thought that releasing Cao without punishment would leave him no means of displaying his might? I have heard that seeking haste prevents attainment, and that attending to small gains prevents great undertakings from succeeding. Acting in accordance with circumstances and treating others with consideration are the foundations of kingly government. Had Xiang listened to Ziyu and not rushed to assert himself through arms, he could have taken King Wen as his teacher—the king who secured Chong’s surrender by returning to his former siege works. Yet he did otherwise. In the end, his army was defeated and he himself wounded, exposing him to the ridicule of later ages. Whom else could he resent? The Spring and Autumn Annals records this to show that Song’s lack of authority [?] arose from the error in his disposition of mind.

Why did Jin enter Cao? To punish a breach of propriety. Why condemn this? A gentleman makes others understand through his government alone. Thus military force must not be displayed, and civil virtue must not be concealed. Only when the proper order has been established and others still fail to come over may troops be sent to attack them. Cao Ying [?] bore the blame for peeping at Duke Wen’s naked body, thereby furnishing a cause for war. Might this not have been because Jin’s government was not yet familiar to others, so that no one knew what they were expected to obey? Wen did not prepare a formal proclamation, but proceeded to enter Cao with his army and divide …

其田而壞疆理之防執其君以亂上下之分斯
亦暴矣意者服荆楚以圖霸也執曹而畀宋殆
將以致戰耶吾聞招携以禮懷遠以德鑿智自
私王道之累也使文拒先軫之謀而罔事夫狙
詐之術則次陘帖楚齊桓不足侔矣今也不然
卒之戰勝攻克遂主夏盟夫亦奚貴哉春秋書

書而襄文之所以失具不可掩如此其義精矣
或者乃曰襄慕仁義而亡文尚功利而興聖人
===

圍曹之舉夫固功利之心使之而服楚尊周晉

punctuated:
其田，而壞疆理之防；執其君，以亂上下之分，斯亦暴矣！意者服荆楚以圖霸也，執曹而畀宋，殆將以致戰耶？吾聞招携以禮，懷遠以德，鑿智自私，王道之累也。使文拒先軫之謀，而罔事夫狙詐之術，則次陘帖楚，齊桓不足侔矣。今也不然，卒之戰勝攻克，遂主夏盟，夫亦奚貴哉？《春秋》書之，以見晉功雖多，道不足尚也。噫！同一虐曹之書，而襄、文之所以失，具不可掩如此，其義精矣！或者乃曰：「襄慕仁義而亡，文尚功利而興，聖人槩以為貶，何足？」殊不知五霸假仁，一而已矣。觀圍曹之舉，夫固功利之心使之，而服楚尊周，晉未嘗不慕仁義也。其興亡之異，豈孟子霸必有大國之謂耶？噫！使《春秋》之義不明，則兹父為文王，而重耳之功不在周宣下矣！
