translation_en:
…its lands, thereby destroying the safeguards of territorial boundaries; he seized its ruler, thereby disrupting the distinctions between superior and subordinate. This too was brutality! Perhaps his intention was to subdue Jing-Chu and seek hegemony: by seizing Cao and handing it over to Song, was he trying to provoke a battle? I have heard that one draws in the estranged through ritual propriety and wins over distant peoples through virtue. Devising clever schemes for private advantage is a blight upon the Kingly Way. Had Duke Wen rejected Xian Zhen’s plan and refrained from deceitful stratagems, then even Duke Huan of Qi, who encamped at Xing and brought Chu to submission, could not have matched him. Yet this was not what happened. In the end, he won battles and conquered his opponents, and thus came to preside over the covenant assemblies of the Xia states. But what was so worthy of esteem in that? The Spring and Autumn Annals records this to show that, although Jin’s achievements were many, its way was unworthy of admiration. Alas! In these records of the same act of oppressing Cao, the failings of Dukes Xiang and Wen alike are laid bare and cannot be concealed. How subtle their meaning is!
Some nevertheless say: “Xiang admired benevolence and righteousness yet came to ruin; Wen prized achievement and profit yet rose to power. How can it suffice for the Sage to condemn both alike?” They fail to understand that the Five Hegemons were all alike in borrowing the guise of benevolence. Consider the siege of Cao: it was certainly motivated by a desire for achievement and profit. Yet in subduing Chu and honoring Zhou, Jin too professed admiration for benevolence and righteousness. Could their different outcomes—ascendancy and ruin—be what Mencius meant when he said that a hegemon must possess a great state? Alas! Were the meaning of the Spring and Autumn Annals not made clear, Zifu would be another King Wen, and Chong’er’s achievements would rank no lower than those of King Xuan of Zhou!
“In autumn, Shi Yang of Jin, Yue Qili of Song, Beigong Xi of Wei, and men of Cao, Zhu, and Teng met at Hu.” 〔The twenty-seventh year of Duke Zhao.〕
Tao Dazhuang

…the grounds for acceptance and rejection are insufficiently clear. This essay is precise in expression and refined in meaning; it should be included as a model.
Examiner Pu, Left Mentor, comments: “The analysis is thorough.”
Examiner Qin, Right Rectifier, comments: “Concise and rigorous.”
By observing how the Spring and Autumn Annals records in detail the high ministers’ efforts to establish friendly relations, we can discern its fundamental grounds for acceptance and rejection. The Sage weighs the relative importance of things in judging the world: his mind is impartial. Is this why the grandees who assembled at Hu are recorded individually and in detail rather than summarily?
Formerly, Zichao threw Zhou into disorder, and King Jing had only just secured his position; Jisun held power in Lu, and Duke Zhao had not yet been restored. The grandees of six states therefore assembled at Hu to confer, clarify the orders for garrisoning Zhou, and settle plans to restore the duke. Of this undertaking, I have heard that bribes arrived from Lu and Shi Yang acted out of private interest, so that the undertaking was left uncompleted. Yet the Spring and Autumn Annals lists the high ministers individually rather than summarily. Could yielding to private interest be unworthy of censure?
Now, affairs in the world differ in importance. There is a broad distinction between the weightier and the lesser, but their relative standing is not fixed; it must be carefully examined. To accomplish two good things in a single undertaking is certainly admirable. But if the lesser is abandoned while the greater is preserved, can one demand much more? To dispel everyone’s doubts at a single gathering is certainly admirable. But if the many see clearly while one alone remains benighted, can all be rejected?
Thus, had all the grandees at Hu been like Shi Yang, with no reputation for righteousness manifest and bribery openly practiced, what could I find to approve in them? As it was, cultivating good relations with neighboring states and settling troubles did initially arise from the impartial intentions of the assembled men. Their turning from rectitude toward wrongdoing [?] resulted merely from their inability to withstand a glib speaker’s arguments. Once Song and Wei had become afraid, the smaller states began to withdraw. Were they all submerged in the pursuit of profit?
Or again, had the meeting at Hu been concerned solely with restoring the ruler of Lu, then, having enlisted others’ efforts for a good purpose only to end in greed, I…

無貸焉耳乃今持危定傾計雖沮於友邦而輸
粟具戍令實行於周室疏附同心先後戮力豈
槩無可取耶聖人修經至此以為晉諸侯之盟
主也大國帥之小國畏威而從命非其所得已
也以鞅之罪而罪列卿何以服其心乎周天下
之共主也諸侯脩睦相與蕃衞乎王室義莫大
焉者也以魯之故而廢其功何示以不廣乎故
在會之大夫詳而不畧異於會扈之諸侯者其
取舍之輕重審矣而非可與權者烏足以語此
===
抑又論之子朝以邪奪正季孫以臣逐君士鞅
徇貨棄利其罪均也皆先王之所必誅也晉頃
世伯使能因會而竄鞅之奸執意如定魯位然
後大合諸侯同聲翼戴文公之功褊矣乃聽其
所為而不問焉僅有戍周一令其為聲實也亦
微矣君子謂六卿之分晉也有由然哉

四者君以正用之

punctuated:
無貸焉耳。乃今持危定傾，計雖沮於友邦，而輸粟具戍，令實行於周室。疏附同心，先後戮力，豈槩無可取耶？聖人修經至此，以為晉，諸侯之盟主也，大國帥之，小國畏威而從命，非其所得已也。以鞅之罪而罪列卿，何以服其心乎？周，天下之共主也，諸侯脩睦，相與蕃衞乎王室，義莫大焉者也。以魯之故而廢其功，何示以不廣乎？故在會之大夫詳而不畧，異於會扈之諸侯者，其取舍之輕重審矣。而非可與權者，烏足以語此？
抑又論之，子朝以邪奪正，季孫以臣逐君，士鞅徇貨棄利，其罪均也，皆先王之所必誅也。晉頃世伯，使能因會而竄鞅之奸，執意如，定魯位，然後大合諸侯，同聲翼戴，文公之功褊矣。乃聽其所為而不問焉，僅有戍周一令，其為聲實也亦微矣。君子謂六卿之分晉也有由然哉！
禮記
故天生時，而地生財，人其父生而師教之，四者君以正用之。
translation_en:
…I would grant no pardon. Yet in this instance, although the plan to sustain the endangered and stabilize the tottering was obstructed by an allied state, the orders to transport grain and provide a garrison were actually carried out for the royal house of Zhou. Those who brought the distant into allegiance and those who attached the near were of one mind; those who led and those who followed joined their efforts. Could there be nothing at all worthy of approval? In editing the Classic at this point, the Sage considered that Jin was the leader of the covenant among the feudal lords: the great states followed its lead, while the small states obeyed out of fear of its might, having no choice in the matter. If all the ministers were condemned for Yang’s offense, how could their hearts be won over? Zhou was the common sovereign of all under Heaven. For the feudal lords to cultivate harmony and together defend the royal house was an act of the highest righteousness. To disregard their achievement on account of Lu—why display such narrowness? Thus the great officers attending this meeting are recorded in detail rather than summarily, unlike the feudal lords who met at Hu. The relative weight assigned to approval and rejection was carefully judged. How could anyone incapable of weighing circumstances be qualified to discuss this?
Consider the matter further. Zichao wrongfully usurped the rightful succession; Jisun, a subject, expelled his ruler; and Shi Yang pursued bribes and abandoned the common benefit. Their offenses were equal, and all would assuredly have been punished by the former kings. Duke Qing of Jin inherited the hegemony. Had he used the meeting to banish the treacherous Yang, arrest Yiru, and restore the ruler of Lu to his position, and then assembled the feudal lords in a great gathering to support the royal house with one voice, even Duke Wen’s achievements would have seemed limited by comparison. Instead, he let them act as they pleased without calling them to account. There was merely a single order to garrison Zhou: how meager this was in both reputation and substance! The gentleman says that the six ministers’ partition of Jin indeed had its causes!
Record of Rites
Thus Heaven produces the seasons, and Earth produces wealth; a person’s father gives him life, and his teacher instructs him. These four the ruler employs properly.

The author of the Record discusses the wondrous workings of the Three Powers—Heaven, Earth, and humanity—and how the great ruler brings their capacities to fulfillment. His intention in holding the ruler responsible for their fulfillment is expressed to the utmost. How profoundly the ruler’s own person is the foundation of orderly government and moral transformation! Heaven’s seasons, Earth’s resources, fathers’ begetting, and teachers’ instruction all depend upon the ruler to employ them correctly. Such is the weight of his responsibility!

The “Evolution of Rites” discusses government and grounds it in the ruler’s own person. Its meaning is this: the sage has the responsibility to participate in and assist the transforming work of Heaven and Earth; unless he takes that work as his model, his achievements in government cannot be brought to completion. The transforming forces of nature possess spontaneous capacities; unless they depend upon the sage, their wondrous workings cannot become manifest. Nature’s transforming forces and the sage surely depend upon each other in carrying out their functions!

Thus, nothing is greater in bringing about change and adaptation than the seasons, and the seasons are produced by Heaven. The alternating movement of the two vital forces, yin and yang, is entirely an expression of the simple mastery exercised by the primal power of Qian, Heaven. Nothing is more urgent for gathering people together than material resources, and these resources are produced by Earth. The abundant growth of all goods is entirely an expression of the effortless capacity of the way of Kun, Earth. Without the people, the sovereign has no means to govern the four quarters; fathers bring those people into being. The affection arising from their sharing one body is indeed a cardinal human relationship throughout the world. Without instruction, the people have no means to distinguish themselves from birds and beasts; teachers instruct them. The teaching that cultivates the Way is indeed the proper accomplishment of those who awaken to it first.

title: 嘉靖二十二年順天府鄉試錄
text:
天地生之教之而功有所屬父不得以兼夫師
惟夫人君者稟聰明睿智之資為天地父師之
主以政不可徒為也聿修厥德以為之本而四
事之施無一不得其當以事不可以徒行也克
正爾躬以為之基而庶政之用無往不適其宜
皇極建而達道行明時以敬授也利用以厚生
也道在天地者有以範圍而不過矣經德立而
妙用著庶矣而富也富矣而教也事在父師者
有以曲成而不遺矣是非聖人有所增益於性
===
分之外也立天下之大本者可以知天地之化
育盡己之性者可以盡人之性也苟身之不正
其何能以致是哉吁為人君者可以自省矣抑
論政之時義大矣其用歸于正人其始本于自
正是故未有君立于無過而天下不寡過者也
周茂叔曰純心要矣用賢急焉然則人君之所
以自檢其身者亦孰有外於斯二者哉審能是
則內外交修天德立王道行天下之治粹然一
出於正矣不然若後世之雄才大略力行仁義

translation_en:
… Heaven and earth give life and provide instruction [?]; yet these achievements have their respective agents, and the father cannot also assume the teacher’s role. The ruler alone, endowed with intelligence and sagely wisdom, presides over the functions of heaven, earth, father, and teacher. Since government cannot be conducted without a foundation, he cultivates his virtue as its root, so that each of these four functions is properly discharged. Since affairs cannot be carried out without a basis, he rectifies his own person as their foundation, so that every measure of government fits its circumstances. When the sovereign standard is established and the universally applicable Way prevails, he distinguishes the seasons and reverently announces them to the people, and makes resources useful to enrich their livelihood. Thus he orders and encompasses the Way embodied in heaven and earth without overstepping it. When constant virtue is established and its subtle efficacy becomes manifest, he enriches the people once they are numerous, and instructs them once they are prosperous. Thus he brings the functions of father and teacher to fulfillment in every particular, leaving nothing neglected. This does not mean that the sage adds anything beyond what is allotted to his nature. One who establishes the great foundation of all under heaven can understand the transforming and nourishing work of heaven and earth; one who fully realizes his own nature can enable others fully to realize theirs. If his own person is not upright, how could he achieve this? Ah! Those who rule others should examine themselves.

Moreover, great indeed is the significance of government in relation to its proper time! Its practical purpose comes down to rectifying others; its beginning is rooted in rectifying oneself. Thus there has never been a ruler who remained free of faults without faults also becoming few throughout the realm. Zhou Maoshu said: “Purifying the heart is essential; employing the worthy is urgent.” How, then, could the ruler’s scrutiny of his own person extend beyond these two things? If he can truly accomplish this, cultivating both his inner life and outward conduct, heavenly virtue will be established and the Kingly Way will prevail. The realm’s good order will issue entirely from uprightness. Otherwise, take those men of later ages who possessed outstanding talent and grand strategies and vigorously practiced benevolence and righteousness …

title: 嘉靖二十二年順天府鄉試錄
text:
人當禮固有可制也然後聖人因其不可解者
作爲父子之親因其無所逃者作爲君臣之義
於以爲三綱之目焉彜倫之叙有以倡克綏之
猷也於以爲六紀之目焉人紀之脩有以敷維
皇之化也是其天叙之所惇罔非天秩之所庸
禮不於是制乎夫天下之治固視紀綱何如耳
及夫之綱之紀而弘敷之下舉秩乎其有條則
以親以遜而四海之民咸翕然而順治此其皇
極之敷錫殆未有一人之弗協者矣天下既定
===

乎相生損益之宜比六律以和聲曲盡乎清濁
高下之變被之爲絃歌詩頌於摶拊洋洋乎其
盈耳也協之爲歌咏詩頌於長言颯颯乎有遺
音也是其和聲之所發罔非和氣之所宣樂不
於是作乎噫禮必序於先樂斯和於後如此樂
之所由來者遠矣夫豈新樂之所能彷彿哉文
侯好彼厭此弗思甚矣抑考子夏之言夫固有
所本也易之履曰君子以辨上下定民志豫曰

Then the sage, drawing upon bonds that cannot be dissolved, establishes affection between father and son; drawing upon obligations from which there is no escape, establishes righteousness between ruler and minister. He thereby sets out the provisions of the Three Bonds: the ordering of enduring human relationships serves to promote the way of securing peace. He thereby sets out the provisions of the Six Relations: the cultivation of human relationships serves to spread the transforming influence of the sovereign. Thus, what strengthens Heaven’s ordering of relationships invariably puts Heaven’s prescribed ranks into practice. Is this not the point at which rites are instituted? Indeed, the good government of the realm depends upon the condition of its guiding bonds and relationships. Once these have been established and broadly extended, all below are arranged in orderly ranks. Through affection and deference, the people within the Four Seas unanimously submit to good government. With the sovereign’s supreme standard thus disseminated and bestowed, scarcely a single person fails to accord with it.

Once the realm is settled, music can assuredly be created. Then the sage draws upon primordial vital energy to rectify the pitch standards, comparing and combining the appropriate procedures for generating pitches from one another by diminution and augmentation. He aligns the six pitch standards to harmonize sounds, fully encompassing the variations of clear and turbid, high and low. He gives this expression in singing to strings, with poems and hymns accompanied by drums, their abundant sound filling the ears; he brings it into accord through song and chant, with poems and hymns voiced in sustained utterance, their rustling resonance lingering. Thus, whatever harmonious sound brings forth invariably expresses harmonious vital energy. Is this not the point at which music is created? Ah! Rites must first establish order, and only then does music bring harmony. Such being the case, music has origins reaching far back indeed. How could the new music even resemble it? 也而天地中和之至則不雜以氣不參以人純
乎其純而純之至矣夫道而至於至純非天下

translation_en:
…comes close to equilibrium and harmony.

Examiner Qin, Right Rectifier of the Heir Apparent, comments: “Its words are accessible, yet their meaning reaches far. This is the only essay of its kind I have seen; its author must be deeply accomplished in self-cultivation.”

The Way of the utmost sage is the Way in its utmost purity. Why? Nothing in the Way is purer than equilibrium and harmony. In Heaven and Earth, equilibrium and harmony reach their utmost: unmixed with material force (qi) and untouched by human interference, their purity is utterly pure and reaches its highest degree. When the Way attains such utmost purity, who can participate in it except the utmost sage under Heaven, whose Way is truly one with that of Heaven and Earth? Ah! This is why, throughout Heaven and Earth and across past and present, only Yao, Shun, Yu, Tang, King Wen, and Zhongni have put it into practice, and why all sages should look to it as their model.

Now equilibrium is the great foundation of all under Heaven, and harmony is the universally followed Way of all under Heaven. Yet these are simply the virtues of our nature and feelings. Everyone possesses this nature, and everyone possesses these feelings. Thus everyone ought to be capable of equilibrium, everyone capable of harmony, and everyone capable of bringing equilibrium and harmony to their utmost. Why, then, do we so grudgingly reserve this attainment for the great sage alone?

Alas! This speaks only in terms of principle, without recognizing that, although principle exists between Heaven and Earth, material force and human activity cannot be absent either. Principle is precisely the nature conferred by Heaven: it is nothing but purity, nothing but equilibrium and harmony at their utmost. As for material force, yin and yang and the Five Phases vary and are uneven; there must therefore be differences in the intermingling of hardness and softness. title: 嘉靖二十二年順天府鄉試錄
text:
無昏明强弱善惡之異焉氣以雜之人以參之
是故不中不和者皆是也或中矣而不能以無
不中或和矣而不能以無不和或庶幾中和矣
而不能以無不至愚不肖之不能爲士也士之
不能爲賢也賢之不能爲聖也職此之故也然
聖矣而或少有氣者人者以雜乎其間則亦不
得爲至純矣不得爲至純則亦不得與於天地
中和之至矣吁亦難矣是故自有天地以來吾
不知其幾千百歳也而唐始有堯焉虞始有舜
===

又五百餘歳也而始有周文焉又五百餘歳也
而始有仲尼焉之六聖人者其鍾之者則至靈
也其稟之者則至粹也其執之者則至精而至
一也一毫之氣不雜也而純乎理一毫之人不
參也而純乎天是故其蘊之爲德性其發之爲
事業而所以立大本行達道者莫非中和也非
徒中和而天地中和之至也自今觀之允恭克
讓而親睦時雍堯之道何道也温恭允塞而克

translation_en:
…there cannot but be differences in dullness and intelligence, strength and weakness, goodness and evil. Material force introduces admixture, and human activity intervenes; hence failures of equilibrium and harmony are everywhere. Some attain equilibrium, yet cannot avoid all departures from it; some attain harmony, yet cannot avoid all departures from it; some approach equilibrium and harmony, yet cannot avoid falling short of their utmost perfection. That the foolish and unworthy cannot become cultivated scholars, that scholars cannot become worthies, and that worthies cannot become sages—all is due precisely to this. Yet even one who has become a sage, if the slightest element of material force or human activity remains mixed within, cannot attain perfect purity. Without perfect purity, one cannot participate in the utmost equilibrium and harmony of Heaven and Earth. Ah, how difficult it is!

Thus, since Heaven and Earth first existed—I know not how many hundreds or thousands of years have passed—it was only with Tang that Yao appeared, only with Yu that Shun appeared, and only with Xia that Yu appeared. More than five hundred years later, Tang of Shang appeared; more than five hundred years later, King Wen of Zhou appeared; and more than five hundred years later, Zhongni appeared. In these six sages, what was concentrated was supremely numinous; what they received as their endowment was supremely pure; and what they held fast to was supremely refined and wholly single-minded. Not the slightest trace of material force adulterated them: they were pure in accordance with principle. Not the slightest trace of human contrivance intruded: they were pure in accordance with Heaven. Thus, what they harbored within constituted their virtuous nature, and what they manifested constituted their deeds and achievements. Everything by which they established the great foundation and practiced the universally followed Way was equilibrium and harmony. Nor was this merely equilibrium and harmony: it was the utmost equilibrium and harmony of Heaven and Earth.

text:
諧風動舜之道何道也聲律身度而文命四敷
禹之道何道也克寬克仁而敷政優優湯之道
何道也徽柔懿恭而修和有夏文之道何道也
温良恭儉讓而太和元氣之流行仲尼之道又
何道也一天地中和之至也非有取焉而後爲
之也非擬諸天地而求與之參也蓋天地之中
和如此其至聖人之中和如此其至天地一聖
人也聖人一天地也故曰純亦不已而不得但
以人之道目聖人也是道也其見於天地之間
===
者則爲雨暘之時若爲寒燠之適宜爲景星卿
雲醴泉甘露之瑞世而見於聖人者則自庸行
之常以至彌六合垂千禩莫非是物也宜其周
乎萬物通乎無窮日用而不可離也於乎此其
所以爲至也彼聖而未至者豈足以與於此聖
且不與而況於賢乎而況於士乎而況於衆人
乎雖然是道也固惟六聖人能之而六聖人者
初未嘗自以爲至也是故堯兢兢日行其道也
□□業日致其孝也禹一饋十起以勞天下之

…harmony was achieved and his influence spread like the wind: what was Shun’s Way? His voice was the pitch standard and his person the measure, while his civilizing instruction spread in all directions: what was Yu’s Way? Capable of generosity and benevolence, he administered government with ample ease: what was Tang’s Way? Admirably gentle and nobly reverent, he brought order and harmony to the lands of Xia: what was King Wen’s Way? Mild, kind, respectful, frugal, and yielding, he embodied the circulation of the primal vital force of supreme harmony: what, then, was Zhongni’s Way? All were the utmost realization of the equilibrium and harmony of Heaven and Earth. They did not first borrow something from elsewhere and then put it into practice; nor did they model themselves upon Heaven and Earth in an effort to stand alongside them as a third power. Rather, the equilibrium and harmony of Heaven and Earth are consummate in this way, and those of the sages are consummate in this same way. Heaven and Earth are a sage; a sage is Heaven and Earth. Thus it is said: “Pure, it likewise never ceases.” One therefore cannot characterize the sages solely in terms of the human Way.

When this Way manifests itself between Heaven and Earth, it becomes rain and sunshine arriving in due season, cold and warmth in proper measure, and auspicious stars, felicitous clouds, sweet springs, and sweet dew that bless the age. When it manifests itself in the sages, everything from ordinary daily conduct to what fills the six directions and endures for a thousand years is this same reality. Fittingly, it encompasses the myriad things, extends without limit, and cannot be departed from in daily life. Ah! This is what makes it consummate. How could those who are sages but have not attained this consummation qualify to participate in it? If even sages cannot participate, how much less the worthy, how much less scholars, and how much less ordinary people!

Nevertheless, although only the six sages could fully realize this Way, those six sages never regarded themselves as having attained its consummation. …the people. Cheng Tang kept his attention fixed upon this and renewed himself daily; King Wen sought the Way as though he had yet to perceive it; Zhongni loved antiquity and diligently sought it. Thus, already sages, they became ever more sage and attained the utmost purity. For those of later generations who have not attained this perfection but wish to seek it, can there be no way? There is. Equilibrium and harmony are not virtues beyond reach. Everyone can become a Yao or Shun. King Wen is my teacher, and my aspiration is to learn from Confucius. If I can truly fulfill my nature and give proper expression to my feelings, embody the example of Yao [Shun’s clan name] and emulate Si [Yu’s clan name], take Yu as my ancestor and carry forward Tang’s legacy, take King Wen as my teacher and bring these achievements together as Confucius did, then my mind and vital energy will be upright, and my mind and vital energy harmonious. The utmost purity of the Way will then reside not in Heaven and Earth, nor in the sages, but in me. Thus Master Zisi said: “Bring equilibrium and harmony to their fullest realization, and Heaven and Earth take their proper places, and the myriad things flourish.” Can this fail to be true? Otherwise, the perfect Way existing between Heaven and Earth would at times cease, and the virtues of our nature and feelings, together with our learning of equilibrium and harmony, would fall into neglect. How could this accord with the saying that one may await a sage a hundred generations hence without misgivings? This, too, cannot be discussed by clinging to a single fixed view.

…the imperial lineage adds lustre to the genealogical records. Fortunately, the writings and worthy witnesses provide ample testimony, revealing the inexhaustible scope of the institutions governing human relations [?]. We, your servants, rejoice and clap our hands, bowing our heads to the ground again and again.
We humbly reflect that the unfolding of destiny established the imperial standard, meeting the five-hundred-year cycle of Heaven and Earth; Heaven bestowed auspicious tokens, disclosing the thousand-year mysteries of the Yellow and Luo Rivers. Whenever a sage rises above all others, his house and state are surely about to flourish. A rainbow appeared at Yaoxu: Shun received the rule of Yu and assembled the jade tokens of investiture. A star streamed down at Shiniu: Yu established the sacrifices of Xia and was granted a jade tablet. Huazhu displayed auspicious signs, whereby Jintian came to govern the world; Danling nurtured exceptional excellence, whereby the ruler of Fire Virtue laid his foundations. These were indeed extraordinary conjunctions of cosmic cycles, yet their numinous origins had a source.
As for the land of Yingdu, it was from the outset comparable to a region that is Heaven’s storehouse. It has the Yangzi and Han Rivers marking its bounds as a moat, and extends to Yunmeng, bringing the region under orderly rule. Distantly connected with the two Shi peaks, it stands firm as a great rock for ten thousand years; nearer at hand, from Jiulong, its commanding natural defenses extend a thousand li. Truly, this happy land of today was a renowned domain in former times.

…Heaven, his flourishing virtue as broad as Earth [?]. And Empress Cixiao Zhenshun Renjing Chengyi Antian Dansheng Xian took reverence and harmony as her model; her earthlike generosity knew no bounds. Her tranquil renown in the princely palace surpassed former exemplars, and she continued the excellent reputation of Tai Si. She also fittingly advanced the transforming influence that spread through the southern regions, and in her later years ascended to the honored position of Empress Dowager. Both embodied the powers of Heaven’s strength and Earth’s compliance, thereby bringing forth the sage who followed. As yin and yang, they made their teachings manifest and inaugurated a great restoration. This was truly the foundation of the royal enterprise and the renewal of our august Ming dynasty.
Now we humbly find that Your Majesty the Emperor is pure and unalloyed, central and upright, accomplished in civil and military affairs, sagely and divinely perceptive. While your Shun-like virtue still lay hidden in obscurity, it already accorded with the auspicious portent of the Yellow River running clear. Once you grasped Heaven’s mandate, you duly brought about the blessed transformation that spreads like the wind.

translation_en:
…eminent scholars of extensive learning, drawing especially upon the traditions transmitted by local elders. We recorded these matters prominently and at length, making clear that the sacred vessel of sovereignty is not easily obtained; we examined auspicious signs and brought blessings to light, demonstrating the authenticity of Heaven’s mandate. Above, the account encompasses the full particulars of literary culture, ritual, and music; more broadly, it extends to the excellence of people, mountains, and rivers. Dividing the material into categories and analyzing it closely, setting out its main framework and arranging its particulars, we compiled a coherent work, which has already received Your Majesty’s perusal.

Yet Your Majesty’s sagacious plans are vast and far-reaching, far surpassing those of all your officials; your imperial reflections are profound and subtle, extending to ten thousand generations. You judged that matters pertaining to the dynastic history could not, according to the rules of compilation, be recorded together here, while passages concerning institutions and regulations must prize substance and essentials in their wording. You therefore issued a special command for detailed review, entrusting this responsibility to us, your officials charged with ritual affairs.

Ashamed of our meager and commonplace abilities, how could we claim to understand the art of historical revision? Though we devote our strength to brush and writing tablet, what contribution could we make, even as slight as a drop or a speck of dust? Opening the jade treasury and beholding its precious jades, we can only congratulate ourselves on our good fortune; looking up at the azure heavens and contemplating the celestial patterns, we truly cannot exhaust their praise.

Reverently embodying your profound intentions, we have ventured to abridge and settle the text. translation_en:
…Your Majesty’s august presence. We humbly hope that you will graciously peruse this work in your tranquil leisure, take account of our humble views as those of grass-cutters and wood-gatherers, and distribute it to those holding office, thereby making manifest Your Majesty’s boundless filial devotion. May you entrust it to the court historians, so that it may help complete the enduring authoritative record of this dynasty. We further wish that you may secure the dynastic tripods of the venerable Zhou, preserving abundance and prosperity as the sun stands at its zenith; uphold the imperial design of the Yellow Emperor, laying the foundations of profound and unobtrusive rule morning and night; show devoted care for those nearby and raise up those afar, circulating the vital force of the great cosmic potter’s wheel throughout the eight reaches of the world; and establish states and sustain noble houses, bequeathing plans for the peace and protection of your descendants through a hundred generations. Looking toward Heaven and reverently up to Your sagely Majesty, we, your servants, are overcome with fervent emotion and trembling awe. We respectfully submit the edited Gazetteer of Xingdu (Xingdu zhi) together with this memorial for Your Majesty’s attention.
Third Session
Five Policy Questions

translation_en:
First Policy Question
Lu Guangzuo 陸光祚

Comment by Associate Examiner Fang, Instructor: The great foundations and guiding principles of government under our sagely ancestors and divine forebears—the mutual admonitions of Heaven and humanity, and the joint flourishing of virtue and learning—truly matched the admirable examples of the ancient emperors and kings. His Majesty, carrying forward their glorious achievements and fulfilling every human relationship and institution, has further made manifest the brilliant light of the successive sage sovereigns. None of this can be fathomed by later students looking reverently upward. This policy essay is uniquely comprehensive in its praise: a masterpiece. It is therefore recorded as a model.

Comment by Associate Examiner Huang, Instructor: The sagely virtue and wondrous transforming influence of our Two Founders and Three Ancestral Emperors, and His Majesty’s equal greatness in carrying on their work and creating anew, are glorious blessings that inspire rejoicing everywhere within and beyond the seas, yet defy description. The government of the Zhenguan era scarcely merits mention beside them. This policy essay draws upon accounts of the past to extol this abundant excellence. It also reverently probes the great foundations and guiding principles, encompassing them in its discussion of virtue and learning, Heaven and humanity. How profound! A Continuation of Sagely Government is something we shall soon look to you to produce.

Comment by Examiner Pu, Left Mentor: This policy essay succeeds in recounting the admirable examples and grand designs of our Two Founders and Three Ancestral Emperors. It also elucidates His Majesty’s combined greatness and manifold flourishing, and at its conclusion returns to the foundation …

title: 嘉靖二十二年順天府鄉試錄
text:
純皇所不屑於貞觀之治者可謂誦法
聖政而識其要矣古曰薦何忝
考試官右中允泰批考據不遺對揚有體
祖
宗膏澤子其覃沐最深者邪錄之
大哉
聖人之政也以作則謂聖而有以神治功於前
以述則謂明而有以裕治法於後作之聖
故盡善盡美而博厚高明之業樹焉述之
===
明故丕顯丕承而悠久無疆之盛引焉樹
之而博厚高明則推無不準動無不化而
治功之在當時者神矣引之而悠久無疆
則言爲世法行爲世則而治法之在萬世
者裕矣然作述一道也明聖一德也治法
之裕者即其治功之神者也盛德大業至
矣哉執事教諸生而以儒臣所編
皇明政要爲問盖欲藉是以揄揚我
列聖之盛于萬一也愚雖未獲覩

punctuated:
純皇所不屑於貞觀之治者，可謂誦法聖政而識其要矣。古曰：「薦何忝？」
考試官右中允泰批：考據不遺，對揚有體。祖宗膏澤，子其覃沐最深者邪？錄之。
大哉，聖人之政也！以作則謂聖，而有以神治功於前；以述則謂明，而有以裕治法於後。作之聖，故盡善盡美，而博厚高明之業樹焉；述之明，故丕顯丕承，而悠久無疆之盛引焉。樹之而博厚高明，則推無不準，動無不化，而治功之在當時者神矣；引之而悠久無疆，則言爲世法，行爲世則，而治法之在萬世者裕矣。然作述一道也，明聖一德也。治法之裕者，即其治功之神者也。盛德大業，至矣哉！執事教諸生，而以儒臣所編《皇明政要》爲問，盖欲藉是以揄揚我列聖之盛于萬一也。愚雖未獲覩
translation_en:
…Emperor Chun’s reasons for disdaining the governance of the Zhenguan era: this may indeed be called studying and emulating sagely government while grasping its essentials. As an ancient saying puts it, “What shame could there be in recommending him?” [?]
Examiner Tai, Right Mentor, comments: Your examination of historical evidence leaves nothing out, and your response fittingly extols imperial virtue. Of those who have received the abundant beneficence of the imperial ancestors, are you perhaps among the most deeply steeped in it? Include this essay.
Great indeed is the government of the sage! In founding, he is called sagely, possessing the means to make the achievements of government wondrous in his own time; in carrying on, he is called enlightened, possessing the means to leave ample methods of government to posterity. Because the founder is sagely, his work is wholly good and wholly beautiful, and an enterprise of breadth, depth, loftiness, and brilliance is established. Because the successor is enlightened, he illustriously manifests and grandly continues that work, extending its flourishing for an eternity without bounds. Once established in such breadth, depth, loftiness, and brilliance, its application never fails to accord with the standard, and every action transforms the people: thus the achievements of government in that age are wondrous. Extended for an eternity without bounds, its words become models for the world and its deeds become standards for the world: thus its methods of government amply provide for ten thousand generations. Yet founding and carrying on constitute one Way; enlightenment and sageliness constitute one virtue. The ample provision of those methods of government is precisely the wondrous efficacy of those achievements. How consummate are such flourishing virtue and such a great enterprise!
You gentlemen, in instructing us students, have posed a question concerning the Essentials of Government of the August Ming, compiled by Confucian officials. Surely you wish thereby to extol some tiny fraction of the greatness of our successive sage emperors. Though I, in my ignorance, have not yet had the opportunity to behold…

translation_en: …the holdings of the imperial repository; yet I have reverently read the imperially composed canonical works whose authority is unalterable, and thus have gained a glimpse of their greatness. Allow me respectfully to set this forth. From the time when Heaven bestowed its favor upon our Ming, Emperor Taizu Gao settled all under Heaven through divine martial prowess and founded the realm; Emperor Chengzu Wen established enduring peace through civil governance and brought tranquility to the imperial house and state. They were succeeded by Emperor Renzong Zhao, who firmly resolved to achieve good government; Emperor Xuanzong Zhang, who upheld established norms and secured the imperial enterprise; and Emperor Yingzong Rui, who exercised the firmness of Heaven and decided matters on his own authority. These two founding ancestors and three ancestral sovereigns added brilliance upon brilliance and prosperity upon prosperity. Their grand designs and exemplary standards were equally wondrous from generation to generation. What they held within constituted heavenly virtue; what they expressed in action constituted the Way of the True King. Truly, they were lofty and luminous like Heaven, sheltering all things; broad and substantial like Earth, supporting all things; enduring without limit, bringing all things to fulfillment. In the entirety of their virtue and its wondrous operation, not a single undertaking was less than good, just as the primordial vital force of supreme harmony never ceases to pervade everything. Even the Canons, Counsels, Instructions, and Announcements…

translation_en:
…even the writings comprising the Canons, Counsels, Instructions, and Announcements, and the volumes in the Tianlu and Shiqu imperial libraries, would be insufficient to record the fullness of their magnificent achievements. How much less could a single compilation or record aspire to portray them! Nevertheless, gathering these deeds together to encompass their full scope presents the entirety of the emperors’ sagely government; condensing them to bring out their essence presents its essentials. These approaches illuminate one another, and neither can dispense with the other.

Now, examining what is recorded in Essentials of Government of the August Ming (Huang Ming Zhengyao), we find its volumes arranged by category and its headings divided according to a consistent scheme. Origins and outcomes are systematically presented, and its overall organization is orderly. It begins with “Honoring Moral Nature,” showing the purity, singleness, and ceaselessness of imperial sagely virtue. Next comes “Pursuing Inquiry and Learning,” showing the continuing brilliance of imperial sagely learning. Next comes “Rectifying Preferences,” through which the steadfastness of the imperial sagely resolve can be examined. Next comes “Guarding against Appetites and Desires,” through which the restraint of imperial sagely feelings can be discerned. Since what the emperors revere is Heaven’s majesty, next comes “Standing in Awe of Heaven’s Admonitions.” Since what concerns them is the people’s hidden suffering, next comes “Taking Pity on People in Distress.”

They follow established ordinances to preserve the enduring norms of the realm; accord importance to the heir apparent to set the foundation of the realm aright; establish filial piety and reverence to strengthen familial affection throughout the realm; and extend benevolence and kindness to relieve urgent needs throughout the realm. They draw Confucian officials close to honor civil learning, and open channels for remonstrance to broaden the resources of government. ===

…and rigorously evaluating officials’ performance: these are the means of selecting worthy men and seeking good government. Promoting schools, nurturing talent, and strengthening moral instruction: these are the means of cultivating people and improving customs. Lightening taxation enriches the people’s livelihood; overseeing agriculture attends to the foundation; establishing rites and music regulates and harmonizes all under Heaven; and conducting sacrifices with care establishes communion with the spirits. Preparing military defenses puts the armed forces in order; remaining vigilant when no danger is apparent checks indulgence in ease and pleasure. Securing the frontiers makes plans for internal peace comprehensive; resisting the non-Chinese peoples puts measures for repelling external threats in order. All such measures employ the heart of a true sage-king to carry out the government of a true sage-king. Outwardly, they realize the full grandeur of its scope; inwardly, they exhaust the particulars of its provisions. Sage succeeds sage, and successive enlightened rulers continue to shine. Their methods and achievements of government are wondrous and abundant. Is this not magnificent!
Moreover, this compilation reveals the great foundation of sagely government: honoring moral nature and pursuing inquiry and learning. It also reveals the great guiding principles of sagely government: standing in awe of Heaven’s warnings and taking pity on people in distress. Virtue and learning are where all goodness converges. Only when virtue and learning flourish together does the work of refinement and singleness of purpose become pure; applied throughout the realm, it is then fitting in every instance. Heaven and humanity are the source of all transformations. Only when both Heaven and human affairs furnish admonitions is government marked by reverence and compassion put into practice; extended to the myriad affairs of state, it leaves nothing unattended to with care. … As for the sagely virtue of Taizu, the Gao Emperor, he was born with divine understanding and uniquely endowed with complete wisdom. There was a pavilion for observing the mind and a record for preserving the mind. He instructed Zeng Lu that he wished to seek the mind of Yao and Shun, and admonished Song Lian to exercise care in holding fast to and preserving the mind. As for the sagely virtue of Chengzu, the Wen Emperor, he was generous, benevolent, and magnanimous, and precise and meticulous in ordering affairs. He instructed the Imperial Heir Apparent that what Yao and Shun transmitted to one another lay solely in sincerely holding fast to the mean. He instructed the academicians that, when sitting silently after withdrawing from court, they should consider how to keep this mind under control. As for the sagely virtue of Renzong, the Zhao Emperor, his natural endowment was pure and luminous, and his innermost nature was filial and brotherly. He often said that a ruler should rest in benevolence, and therefore took the benevolent mind alone as his guiding foundation. Were not such things the essentials of the sages’ honoring their virtuous nature, practiced with unceasing purity and singleness of purpose?
As for the sagely learning of Taizu, the Gao Emperor, he laid aside his spear to discuss the Way and applied himself tirelessly to learning. He elucidated the Great Plan, making clear the principles of portents and responses between Heaven and humanity; he wrote out the Extended Meaning of the Great Learning, making manifest the sources of order and disorder, past and present. As for the sagely learning of Chengzu, the Wen Emperor, he promoted the Six Classics and promulgated the Instructions for the Inner Quarters. He compiled the Precious Mirror of Literary Splendor, broadening the principles by which illuminating precedents serve as a mirror, and compiled the Methods of the Mind in Sagely Learning, enlarging the learning of emperors and kings. As for the sagely learning of Emperor Yingzong Rui, he delighted in reading the Book of Documents and declared that its Two Canons and Three Counsels truly contained excellent words. He reflected continually upon the Way, which becomes clear only through study. Were these not examples of the sage’s essential practice of inquiry and learning, through which his brilliance was continually renewed?

When a solar eclipse occurred, he cancelled the New Year’s Day court audience; when disaster struck the Three Halls, he dispensed with the ceremonies for the Imperial Birthday. Such was Chengzu’s reverence for Heaven. When a solar eclipse was not visible, he rejected Hu Ying’s request to offer congratulations; when the rites to rescue the moon during an eclipse were not performed, he punished Feng Xu for his failure to predict it. Such was the reverence for Heaven of Xuanzong and Yingzong.
Mindful of the region where he had crossed the Yangzi and laid the foundations of his rule, he remitted the land taxes of Taiping, Yingtian, and the other circuits. 以不能純耳於乎數言之間衮鉞具在真
萬世不易之定論哉使太宗而有聞將不
靦然心服乎是宜我

後聖一而已矣，又豈臣下之所能仰窺其盛者乎？乃若唐臣吳兢輯太宗遺事為《貞觀政要》四十篇，獻之中宗，而置諸無用。後雖有文宗者盥手熟讀，雅志服行，太和初政庶幾可觀，然權綱不振，國是日非，終亦何補？
洪惟我憲宗純皇帝，心涵千古，妙契百王，玄覽之餘，超然有得，而特製序于篇端，蓋帝堯稽眾之仁、大舜用中之智也。且謂：「太宗濟世康民，偉有成績。所可惜者，惟正心修身有愧於二帝三王之道，此其治所以不能純耳。」於乎！數言之間，衮鉞具在，真萬世不易之定論哉！使太宗而有聞，將不靦然心服乎？是宜我純皇之德之政，上則同符二祖，次則媲美三宗，有以光於前，有以裕於後，而陋貞觀之治
translation_en:
…and the later sages are one and the same. How could we, his subjects, possibly look up and comprehend the fullness of his greatness? As for the Tang minister Wu Jing, he compiled accounts of Taizong’s deeds into the forty chapters of Essentials of Government of the Zhenguan Reign (Zhenguan zhengyao) and presented them to Zhongzong, who left them unused. Later, Wenzong washed his hands before studying the work closely and earnestly aspired to put it into practice. The government of the early Taihe reign thus came close to being worthy of admiration. Yet sovereign authority failed to assert itself, and affairs of state went increasingly astray. What benefit, in the end, did it bring?
We reverently reflect upon our Emperor Xianzong Chun, whose mind encompassed the ages and subtly accorded with the hundred kings. Through his profound contemplation, he attained a transcendent understanding and personally composed a preface for the beginning of this work. This indeed embodied Emperor Yao’s benevolence in consulting the multitude and the great Shun’s wisdom in applying the Mean. He further stated: “Taizong rescued his age and brought well-being to the people, achieving great results. The sole cause for regret is that, in rectifying his mind and cultivating himself, he fell short of the Way of the Two Emperors and Three Kings. This is why his government could not be wholly pure.” Ah! Within these few words, both the ceremonial robe of praise and the axe of censure are present. Truly, this is a definitive judgment that will remain unchanged for ten thousand generations! Were Taizong able to hear it, would he not blush and inwardly submit? Fittingly, then, the virtue and government of our Emperor Chun matched those of the Two Progenitors above and rivaled those of the Three Ancestral Emperors who followed them, bringing glory to his predecessors and leaving abundant provision for his successors, while regarding the government of the Zhenguan reign as inferior…

punctuated:
於不屑也。然則其說雖不得遇於李唐，而猶獲伸於昭代，豈非幸歟？雖然，祖宗以来，聖神繼作，英廟而後，謨烈承休，帝德已隆而益隆，治道已盛而益盛。億萬載有道之長，方與天無極，則所以倣吳兢之遺意，以成聖政之續編者，將不有待於人乎？愚也不揆，竊有志焉，而未之敢也。惟執事其與進之。
第二問
翟汝孝
同考試官教諭陳批：周家八百年根本，正於憂勤中得之。我皇祖奠基，首惟農務是重。逮我皇上懋隆繼述，制作大備，而子能鋪張揚厲，末復拳拳於敬天。陳是誠有驟於中者，錄之不獨以其文也。
translation_en:
…as beneath consideration. Thus, although these views found no acceptance under the Li house of Tang, they have nevertheless found fulfillment in our illustrious dynasty. Is this not fortunate? Yet since our dynastic ancestors, sage and divine rulers have arisen in succession. From Yingzong onward, their plans and achievements have carried forward this glorious legacy. Imperial virtue, already exalted, has grown still more exalted; the way of governance, already flourishing, has flourished still further. The enduring rule of the Way, lasting hundreds of millions of years, is to be as boundless as Heaven. Will not the task of following the intention bequeathed by Wu Jing and compiling a continuation recording sagely government therefore await someone to undertake it? Without measuring my own abilities, I privately aspire to this, but have not yet dared attempt it. I ask you, honored sir, to encourage me in this endeavor.
Second Policy Question
Zhai Ruxiao
Comment by Associate Examiner Chen, Instructor: The foundation of the Zhou house’s eight hundred years was established precisely through anxious care and diligence. When our imperial ancestor laid the dynasty’s foundations, he gave foremost importance to agriculture. By the time of our present emperor, who has magnificently continued and developed that legacy, institutions and regulations have become fully established. You have expounded and extolled these achievements at length, and at the end return with earnest devotion to reverence for Heaven. This truly expresses an inward conviction [?; the transcription 陳是誠有驟於中者 is doubtful]. I select this essay for more than its literary merit.

translation_en:
Comment by Associate Examiner Zheng, Instructor: Nowadays, candidates writing policy essays concern themselves only with stock formulas. Although agriculture and sericulture are the practical basis of the people’s daily livelihood and the foundation of the former kings’ benevolent government, candidates carelessly give them no consideration. This answer expounds its subject clearly and in detail. Moreover, it fully elucidates the essential methods for transmitting the teachings of the mind from the sagely founder to our Emperor. This is sufficient evidence of learning suited to practical use.

Comment by Associate Examiner Liang, School Instructor: On the policy question concerning agriculture and sericulture, candidates generally manage to do little more than gather up familiar sayings. This essay probes the foundations and grasps the essentials, amply celebrating the excellence of our Emperor’s efforts to petition Heaven for an enduring mandate. It deserves to be recorded and circulated.

Comment by Examiner Pu, Left Mentor: This policy essay concerns the illustrious plans by which our imperial ancestor laid the foundations of his great enterprise, and the magnificent institutions through which the sagely Son of Heaven follows his predecessor’s footsteps and leaves guidance for posterity. The depth and sources of their achievements and virtue surpass those of Shun and the Zhou. That you can extol these in your answer surely marks you as an outstanding talent. Accordingly, we record it as an offering to the reigning sovereign.

Comment by Examiner Qin, Right Admonisher: Our Emperor has revived rites and music, matching the flourishing age of Zhou. As for the great ceremonies of plowing and sericulture, these indeed accord with those of antiquity despite the difference in ages. Ultimately, this must have a foundation. This essay is uniquely able to respond to and extol imperial favor and excellence; moreover, it concludes by offering counsel on reverent concentration on the One. Its author must be no ordinary scholar and truly deserves recommendation in first place.

title: 嘉靖二十二年順天府鄉試錄
text:
知聖王有致治之首務當知聖王有傳心
之要法何謂要法勵憂勤以恤民之隱是
已何謂首務重農桑以厚民之生是已心
以出治而其本立治以達心而其仁溥是
故其始也以一人先天下而不知其勞也
其既也以天下奉一人而克享其逸也此
古先哲王祈天永命之道我
聖祖
皇上所以遠紹千古垂法萬世而
===
國家胤祚之長不獨比隆成周已爾執事發
策秋闈首以王業根本下詢承學愚雖不
敏竊嘗有槩於中矣敢不掇述以對夫人
一日不再食則饑終歲不製衣則寒是衣
食者生民之大命也匪耕則何以資食匪
蠶則何以資衣是農桑者衣食之所自出
也然民之命君實制之是故君知其艱而
先之則靡不以為先矣君忽其艱而後之
則靡不以為後矣茲唯教化之所由以隆

punctuated: 知聖王有致治之首務，當知聖王有傳心之要法。何謂要法？勵憂勤以恤民之隱，是已。何謂首務？重農桑以厚民之生，是已。心以出治，而其本立；治以達心，而其仁溥。是故其始也，以一人先天下，而不知其勞也；其既也，以天下奉一人，而克享其逸也。此古先哲王祈天永命之道，我聖祖、皇上所以遠紹千古、垂法萬世，而國家胤祚之長，不獨比隆成周已爾。執事發策秋闈，首以王業根本下詢承學。愚雖不敏，竊嘗有槩於中矣，敢不掇述以對？夫人一日不再食則饑，終歲不製衣則寒，是衣食者生民之大命也。匪耕則何以資食？匪蠶則何以資衣？是農桑者衣食之所自出也。然民之命，君實制之。是故君知其艱而先之，則靡不以為先矣；君忽其艱而後之，則靡不以為後矣。茲唯教化之所由以隆
translation_en:
To know that the sage kings had a foremost task in bringing about good government, one must also know that they had an essential method for transmitting their moral purpose. What was this essential method? To exert themselves in anxious diligence and attend to the people's hidden sufferings: that was all. What was their foremost task? To give weight to agriculture and sericulture so as to enrich the people's livelihood: that was all. When government proceeds from the heart, its foundation is established; when government gives expression to the heart, its benevolence extends everywhere. Thus, at the outset, the ruler alone leads all under Heaven without feeling his toil; afterward, all under Heaven support the ruler, enabling him to enjoy repose. This was the way by which the wise kings of antiquity prayed to Heaven for an enduring mandate. It is also how our sagely dynastic founder and His Majesty have carried forward the legacy of distant antiquity and bequeathed a model to ten thousand generations, so that the duration of our dynasty's succession and blessings will do more than merely rival the glory of the Zhou.

You gentlemen have issued policy questions for the autumn Provincial Examination, first condescending to ask us students about the foundations of kingly achievement. Though I am slow of understanding, I have privately formed some thoughts on this matter. How could I dare not gather and present them in reply? If a person does not eat twice in a day, he goes hungry; if no clothing is made throughout the year, he suffers from cold. Clothing and food are thus the great necessities upon which the people's lives depend. Without plowing, how could food be supplied? Without raising silkworms, how could clothing be supplied? Agriculture and sericulture are therefore the sources of clothing and food. Yet the people's livelihood is in fact governed by their ruler. Hence, if the ruler understands the difficulties of these pursuits and gives them priority, everyone will likewise give them priority; if he disregards their difficulties and puts them last, everyone will likewise put them last. This is what causes moral instruction to flourish…

title: 嘉靖二十二年順天府鄉試錄
text:
替國祚之所由以修短而敬忽一念實始
基之此聖王之所為兢兢而不能自已者
也粤自神農教耒耜黃帝製衣裳農桑之
重駸駸乎開其原矣而其說獨詳於周祭
統曰天子親耕於南郊以共齊盛吾嘗考
其制矣穜稑載種甸師率屬昭其時也為
藉千畝秉耒三推昭其分也元辰而有祈
穀之典終事而有勞酒之賜其為禮也重
矣又曰王后蠶於北郊以共純服吾嘗求
===
其制矣公桑蠶室近川為之宫也獻繭稱
絲隨事為之節也伐柘之禁嚴於仲春蠶
器之修預於將事其為義也協矣夫以天
子之尊非莫耕也必親耕以共齊盛王后
之貴非莫蠶也必親蠶以共純服者豈好
逸惡勞與人殊好哉敬
天勤民不遑暇逸聖賢傳心要法端在乎是且
周自后稷以穡事基命公劉亶父益從而
培溉之歷世相傳其君子非稼穡之事不

For all the Son of Heaven’s exalted rank, it was not that there was no one else to plow, yet he had to plow personally to supply sacrificial grain. For all the queen’s noble status, it was not that there was no one else to raise silkworms, yet she had to do so personally to supply silken ceremonial robes. title: 嘉靖二十二年順天府鄉試錄
text:
務其室家非織紝之勞不親吾嘗觀之成
王踐阼周公惓惓乎豳風無逸之陳及宣
王不藉虢父則諫之曰匱神之祀困民之
財又何嚴也后妃恭儉率下蓋見諸葛覃
諸篇而幽王惑褒姒之溺詩人則刺之曰
婦無公事休其蠶織又何切也即其君臣
內外之間相與咨嗟而告戒如此是列聖
相傳心法其子孫蓋世守以為家法矣此
周之治所以獨盛而其制所以為獨詳也
===
雖然豈唯成周商之三宗無逸嘗舉以告
成王矣說者以為獨稱商者繼世之君也
然則由商以觀夏可知矣盡力溝洫荒度
土功典則之詒顧嘗不在是哉嗣是以降
於漢吾得文景焉得明章焉憫農重穀詔
旨頻仍東郊之蠶先後輝映此所以衍為
四百年之緒也於唐吾得太宗焉得玄宗
焉敦復古制必示躬親先蠶之祠歲勤內
苑此所以衍為三百年之祀也若宋則以

務，其室家非織紝之勞不親。吾嘗觀之，成王踐阼，周公惓惓乎《豳風》《無逸》之陳；及宣王不藉，虢父則諫之曰：「匱神之祀，困民之財。」又何嚴也！后妃恭儉率下，蓋見諸《葛覃》諸篇；而幽王惑褒姒之溺，詩人則刺之曰：「婦無公事，休其蠶織。」又何切也！即其君臣內外之間，相與咨嗟而告戒如此，是列聖相傳心法，其子孫蓋世守以為家法矣。此周之治所以獨盛，而其制所以為獨詳也。
雖然，豈唯成周？商之三宗，《無逸》嘗舉以告成王矣。說者以為獨稱商者，繼世之君也。然則由商以觀，夏可知矣。盡力溝洫，荒度土功，典則之詒，顧嘗不在是哉？嗣是以降，於漢吾得文景焉，得明章焉。憫農重穀，詔旨頻仍；東郊之蠶，先後輝映。此所以衍為四百年之緒也。於唐吾得太宗焉，得玄宗焉。敦復古制，必示躬親；先蠶之祠，歲勤內苑。此所以衍為三百年之祀也。若宋，則以
translation_en:
…pursued, and their households undertook no labor other than spinning and weaving. I have considered this: when King Cheng ascended the throne, the Duke of Zhou earnestly presented the Airs of Bin and Against Idleness. When King Xuan failed to perform the ceremonial plowing, Guo Fu remonstrated with him, saying: “You impoverish the sacrifices to the spirits and exhaust the people’s resources.” How stern this was! That queens and consorts led those below them through reverence and frugality is evident in such poems as The Spread of the Kudzu. But when King You became infatuated with Bao Si, the poet censured him, saying: “Women have no public business; let them attend to their silkworms and weaving.” How pointed this was! Between ruler and ministers, and between the inner and outer spheres, they thus admonished and warned one another with earnest concern. This was the essential teaching transmitted from one sage king to another; their descendants preserved it generation after generation as the rule of their house. This is why Zhou’s government was uniquely flourishing and its institutions uniquely detailed.
Yet was this true only of Zhou? Against Idleness cited the three exemplary Shang kings to admonish King Cheng. Commentators explain that it singled out these Shang rulers because they were heirs to an established dynasty. Looking back from Shang, we can therefore understand Xia as well. Devoting every effort to irrigation channels and surveying the land for public works—were these not precisely what its bequeathed standards and rules concerned? In later ages, under the Han, I find Emperors Wen and Jing, and Emperors Ming and Zhang. Edicts expressing solicitude for farmers and esteeming grain followed one another repeatedly; successive observances of sericulture in the eastern suburbs added luster to one another. This enabled the dynasty’s succession to extend for four hundred years. Under the Tang, I find Taizong and Xuanzong. They earnestly restored ancient institutions and insisted on setting an example through personal participation; each year, worship of the First Sericulturalist was diligently performed in the inner imperial gardens. title: 嘉靖二十二年順天府鄉試錄
text:
三不盡之仁而綿三百年之統盖自顯德
以来耕耤之典斯備自紹興以後蠶桑之
制始荒其見諸史策者可考也總之無關
雎麟趾之意而行周官之法度治迄小康
又何惑耶洪惟我
太祖高皇帝以聰明睿智之資肇旋乾轉坤之
業身歷艱難念切民隱
踐阼之初首耕耤田為天下勸至於
訓諭臣民不一而足是故
===
出觀
圜丘則命世子遍歷農家觀其居處服食為之
諭曰夫農勤四體所居不過茅茨草榻所服
不過練裳布衣所飲食不過菜羹糲飯而國
家經費皆其所出故欲令汝知之
駕幸鍾山則憫田者冒暑而耘由獨龍岡步至
淳化門語侍臣曰農為國本百需皆其所出
夫衣帛當思織女之勤食粟當念農夫之苦
朕為此故不覺惻然於心他如

洪惟我太祖高皇帝，以聰明睿智之資，肇旋乾轉坤之業。身歷艱難，念切民隱。踐阼之初，首耕耤田，為天下勸。至於訓諭臣民，不一而足。是故出觀圜丘，則命世子遍歷農家，觀其居處服食，為之諭曰：「夫農勤四體，所居不過茅茨草榻，所服不過練裳布衣，所飲食不過菜羹糲飯，而國家經費皆其所出，故欲令汝知之。」

…through the benevolence of the “three things not exhausted” [?], prolonged its dynastic rule for three hundred years. From the Xiande era onward, the ceremonial arrangements for plowing the imperial field were fully established; after the Shaoxing era, the institutions governing sericulture began to fall into neglect. What is recorded in the histories can be examined. In sum, when the regulations of the Offices of Zhou are implemented without the spirit of “The Ospreys Cry” (Guanju) and “The Qilin’s Hooves” (Linzhi), why should it be surprising that government attains only modest well-being?
We reverently reflect that our Emperor Taizu Gao, endowed with intelligence and sagely wisdom, inaugurated an undertaking that turned Heaven and Earth around. Having personally endured hardship, he deeply concerned himself with the people’s suffering. At the beginning of his reign, he took the lead in plowing the imperial field to encourage all under Heaven. His instructions and admonitions to officials and commoners were too numerous to recount individually. He instructed him: “Farmers toil with all four limbs. He has diligently planned the pavilions for inspecting the harvest and inspecting the ploughing, and from time to time has graciously visited the structures named “Against Idleness” (Wuyi) and “Airs of Bin” (Binfeng). Moreover, the flourishing of rites and music requires a hundred years; excellence in carrying forward and completing one’s predecessors’ work is what merits the name of great filial piety. Our Emperor’s resolve to make freedom from idle ease his abiding concern is profoundly sincere. I humbly hope that Your Majesty will continue to illuminate your sagely learning, remaining consistent from beginning to end: nurture it in stillness to preserve the full substance of Heaven’s virtue, and examine it in activity to realize the workings of the Kingly Way. title: 嘉靖二十二年順天府鄉試錄
text:
考試官右中允秦批考古之學適用之才即此
具見子其以天下為已任者耶
帝王者聯屬天下以成其身者也是故育
之以仁而運之以智仁也者體也大德之
敦化也智也者仁之用也小德之川流也
夫人之於身也無尺寸之膚不愛焉則無
尺寸之膚不養也而後吾身安矣苟或五
官四體之間一失其職元氣周流未能無
間此其為病不為偏痺必為踸𨇾矣其謂
===
身何故曰知所以治身則知所以治天下
國家矣執事以
皇明輿地之盛策諸生且欲聞要害民風之畧
斯忠愛無已之盛心也顧愚曲士也使之
語宇宙之大猶責井蛙以語海其不取笑
於大方之家也鮮矣請試言之以就正焉
粵自元胎無象太素流形三皇之世即人
為治封域之廣狹未暇論矣黃帝建萬國
以親諸侯顓頊定九州以配星野斯皆仰

帝王者，聯屬天下以成其身者也。是故育之以仁，而運之以智。仁也者，體也，大德之敦化也；智也者，仁之用也，小德之川流也。夫人之於身也，無尺寸之膚不愛焉，則無尺寸之膚不養也，而後吾身安矣。苟或五官四體之間，一失其職，元氣周流未能無間，此其為病，不為偏痺，必為踸𨇾矣。其謂身何？故曰：「知所以治身，則知所以治天下國家矣。」執事以皇明輿地之盛策諸生，且欲聞要害民風之畧，斯忠愛無已之盛心也。顧愚曲士也，使之語宇宙之大，猶責井蛙以語海，其不取笑於大方之家也鮮矣。請試言之，以就正焉。

translation_en:
Comment by Examiner Qin, Right Mentor: Your learning in the study of antiquity and your talent for practical application are both fully apparent here. Are you perhaps one who takes responsibility for all under Heaven upon himself?

An emperor or king links all under Heaven together to constitute his own body. Thus he nurtures it through benevolence and directs it through wisdom. Benevolence is the substance: it is the ample transforming power of great virtue. Wisdom is benevolence in operation: it is the flowing forth of lesser virtues like streams. In caring for his body, a person cherishes every inch of skin and therefore nourishes every inch; only then is his body at ease. If any of the five sense organs or four limbs fails in its function, the circulation of vital energy cannot remain uninterrupted. The resulting illness will be either paralysis on one side or an inability to walk properly. What, then, becomes of the body? Hence the saying: “Knowing how to govern oneself, one knows how to govern all under Heaven, the state, and the family.” You, honored examiners, have set the candidates a policy question concerning the vast territory of our august Ming dynasty, and wish also to hear an outline of its strategic locations and popular customs. This manifests your profound and unceasing loyalty and concern. Yet I am an ignorant scholar of narrow experience. To have me discuss the immensity of the universe is like requiring a frog in a well to speak of the sea: seldom could it avoid being laughed at by those of broad understanding. Permit me nevertheless to attempt an account and submit it for correction.

From the time when the primordial germ was without perceptible form and primal substance unfolded into shapes, through the age of the Three Sovereigns, government was established in accordance with the people; there was as yet no leisure to discuss the extent of territorial boundaries. Huangdi established the myriad states to bind the regional lords to him; Zhuanxu defined the Nine Provinces to correspond to the celestial divisions. All these rulers looked upward…

title: 嘉靖二十二年順天府鄉試錄
text:
觀俯察章厥順治非用其私智以鑿天下
者也夫封建之法行而幅員難於統一巡
狩之典稀而風俗難于周知帝王端拱穆
清欲致天下於同仁之化斯亦艱矣是故
周官職方氏之職設焉內之都鄙城邑外
之蠻貊戎夷大之人民財用纖之九穀六
畜盖按圖之間而數要利害可一覽而得
矣是地圖之制寔重於周夫亦省方觀民
之遺意也夫堯憂洪水禹言厎績別九州
===
叙五服地平天成萬世永賴矣若乃冀北
創并部之名燕齊起幽營之號肇州十二
舜實任之當是時中國之地方五千里東
漸於海西被流沙朔南暨聲教唐虞之際
於斯盛焉夏制復於唐堯殷因無所損益
惟周公以元聖之資成文武之德體國經
野其法特詳若見諸職方氏所掌可覆也
是故以九州言之東南曰揚州正南曰荆
州河南曰豫州正東曰青州河東曰兗州

觀俯察，章厥順治，非用其私智以鑿天下者也。夫封建之法行，而幅員難於統一；巡狩之典稀，而風俗難于周知。帝王端拱穆清，欲致天下於同仁之化，斯亦艱矣。是故《周官》職方氏之職設焉。內之都鄙城邑，外之蠻貊戎夷，大之人民財用，纖之九穀六畜，盖按圖之間，而數要利害可一覽而得矣。是地圖之制寔重於周，夫亦省方觀民之遺意也。
夫堯憂洪水，禹言厎績，別九州，叙五服，地平天成，萬世永賴矣。若乃冀北創并部之名，燕齊起幽營之號，肇州十二，舜實任之。當是時，中國之地方五千里，東漸於海，西被流沙，朔南暨聲教，唐虞之際，於斯盛焉。夏制復於唐堯，殷因無所損益。惟周公以元聖之資，成文武之德，體國經野，其法特詳，若見諸職方氏所掌，可覆也。是故以九州言之，東南曰揚州，正南曰荆州，河南曰豫州，正東曰青州，河東曰兗州。
translation_en:
…observed above and examined below, making manifest their orderly governance; they did not use their private ingenuity to impose artificial arrangements upon the world. When the system of enfeoffment operated, the territory was difficult to bring under unified rule; when royal inspection tours were infrequent, local customs were difficult to know comprehensively. For emperors and kings, seated with folded hands in the serene purity of their courts, bringing all under Heaven within the transforming influence of impartial benevolence was indeed difficult. Thus the office of Director of Territorial Administration was established in the Offices of Zhou. Within lay domains, towns, and cities; beyond lay the Man, Mo, Rong, and Yi peoples. Matters of broad scope included population, wealth, and expenditure; matters of detail included the nine grains and six domestic animals. By consulting maps, the essential figures, advantages, and disadvantages could all be grasped at a glance. Thus the system of geographical maps was indeed accorded great importance under the Zhou; it also preserved the intent of touring the regions and observing the people.
Yao was troubled by the floods, and Yu reported the completion of his work: he distinguished the Nine Provinces and ordered the Five Zones of Service. The land was brought into order and Heaven’s work accomplished, to the lasting benefit of countless generations. As for establishing the name of Bing Province in northern Ji, and introducing the names You and Ying in Yan and Qi, thereby instituting twelve provinces, Shun himself undertook this. At that time, the territory of the central realm measured five thousand li on each side. Eastward it reached the sea; westward it extended to the Flowing Sands; north and south, its civilizing instruction reached everywhere. In the age of Yao and Shun, its extent attained this flourishing state. The Xia system reverted to that of Yao, and the Yin followed it without addition or subtraction. Only the Duke of Zhou, endowed with the qualities of a supreme sage, brought the virtue of Kings Wen and Wu to fulfillment. In laying out the capital and organizing the countryside, his regulations were especially detailed, as can be verified from the responsibilities assigned to the Director of Territorial Administration. Thus, speaking of the Nine Provinces, the southeast was called Yangzhou; due south, Jingzhou; south of the Yellow River, Yuzhou; due east, Qingzhou; and east of the Yellow River, Yanzhou…

正西曰雍州東北曰幽州河內曰冀州正
北曰并州封山及川以辨區域是即禹之
九州也蓋彼以治水利導而言故先冀而
後雍此以王化遠近而言故先南而後北
獨其合徐梁於雍青分冀州為幽并是不
能無沿革之殊耳以九服言之方千里曰
王畿其外五百里曰侯服又其外曰甸服
曰男服曰采服曰衛服曰蠻服曰夷服曰
鎮服曰藩服設儀衛辨以等邦國是即禹
===
===
之五服也蓋五服各五百里自一面而言
九服各五百里合二面而言獨其藩服之
制於九州外地增五百里是不能無廣狹
之殊耳夫聖人以一人治天下不以天下
奉一人體天之心因地之利順人之情先

或九服不過與時損益通變宜民焉耳豈

之廣日侈于前而先王之制蕩無遺跡漢

translation_en:
…Directly west was Yongzhou; northeast was Youzhou; within the bend of the Yellow River was Jizhou; directly north was Bingzhou. Mountains and rivers were designated as boundaries to distinguish the regions: these were Yu’s Nine Provinces. The earlier account concerned controlling the waters and guiding their flow to advantage, and therefore began with Ji and ended with Yong; this account concerns the reach of royal civilizing influence, from near to far, and therefore begins in the south and ends in the north. Only in incorporating Xu and Liang into Yong and Qing, and dividing Jizhou to form You and Bing, were there necessarily differences of continuity and change. As for the nine zones of service, the territory a thousand li square was called the royal domain. The five hundred li beyond it was called the lords’ zone; farther out were, successively, the domains’ zone, the barons’ zone, the allotments’ zone, the guards’ zone, the Man zone, the Yi zone, the garrisons’ zone, and the outer dependencies’ zone. Ceremonial and defensive distinctions were established [?] to grade the states: these corresponded to Yu’s Five Zones of Service. The five zones, each five hundred li, were described from one side; the nine zones, each five hundred li, were described by combining two sides. Only the institution of the outer dependencies’ zone added five hundred li of territory beyond the Nine Provinces, so there were necessarily differences in extent.
The sage employs one person to govern all under Heaven; he does not employ all under Heaven to serve one person. Embodying Heaven’s intent, making use of the advantages of the land, and accommodating human feelings, the earlier and later sages followed the same standard. Whether there were nine provinces or twelve, five zones of service or nine, they merely made additions and reductions suited to the times, adapting to change for the people’s benefit. How could they have sought difference for its own sake? After the Three Dynasties, this intent gradually faded. Although the territorial extent grew ever greater than before, the institutions of the former kings vanished without a trace. The Han…

title: 嘉靖二十二年順天府鄉試錄
text:
承乎秦者也時則分天下爲十三部焉唐
承乎隋者也時則分天下爲十五道焉宋
承乎五代者也時則分天下爲二十六路
焉要之兩漢四履之盛比跡夏周唐雖東
不及漢西寔過之若宋則北無燕雲西無
寧夏斯不足言矣
明興混一函夏削平僭亂體
上天好生之德無利人土地之心並建
兩京分置十三省蓋虞夏所不能臣職方所
===
不能載者靡不歸我版圖覃被德化是故
今之
京師即古冀州地而山西亦其境也今之
南京即古揚州地而浙江江西亦其境也今
之山東即古青州地而陝西則雍州也今
之河南即古豫州地而湖廣則荆州也今
之四川即古梁州地而雲南則其裔境也
今之福建即古閩越地而廣東廣西則百
粤也今之貴州即古西南夷地所謂羅施

translation_en:
…succeeded the Qin, and at that time divided the realm into thirteen regions. The Tang succeeded the Sui, and at that time divided the realm into fifteen circuits. The Song succeeded the Five Dynasties, and at that time divided the realm into twenty-six circuits. In sum, the territorial extent of the Western and Eastern Han rivaled that of the Xia and Zhou. Although the Tang did not reach as far east as the Han, it actually extended farther west. As for the Song, it possessed neither Yan and Yun in the north nor Ningxia in the west; its extent scarcely merits discussion.
When the Ming arose, it unified the Chinese realm and suppressed usurpers and rebels. It embodied Heaven’s virtue of cherishing life, harboring no desire to profit by taking others’ lands. It established the two capitals and separately organized thirteen provinces. Even lands that Yu and Xia could not bring into submission, and that the Director of Territorial Administration could not record, have all entered our territorial registers and received the far-reaching influence of our virtuous governance. Thus, today’s capital occupies the territory of ancient Jizhou, whose bounds also encompassed Shanxi. Today’s Nanjing occupies the territory of ancient Yangzhou, whose bounds also encompassed Zhejiang and Jiangxi. Today’s Shandong occupies the territory of ancient Qingzhou, while Shaanxi corresponds to Yongzhou. Today’s Henan occupies the territory of ancient Yuzhou, while Huguang corresponds to Jingzhou. Today’s Sichuan occupies the territory of ancient Liangzhou, with Yunnan forming its outlying borderlands. Today’s Fujian occupies the territory of ancient Minyue, while Guangdong and Guangxi correspond to the lands of the Hundred Yue. Today’s Guizhou occupies the ancient territory of the southwestern non-Chinese peoples, the so-called Luoshi…

title: 嘉靖二十二年順天府鄉試錄
text:
鬼國者也猗與休哉自生民來未有盛於
今日者也肆我
英宗睿皇帝命纂一統志以時備觀覽
皇上嗣位因輔臣輿圖之獻
特賜嘉納仁育智運罔非宅中圖大保泰持
盈之至意也執事復以要害民風導之使
言豈亦以諸生之中有治安之賈生乎夫
古今異宜盛衰不同運今海内之大非不
陶然治也顧為萬世深長之慮蓋不無可
===
言者是故扆山帶海
京師形勢尊矣然居庸之外蔽甚微畿甸之
遺戎未徙順天馬政河間水潦不思為之
所乎防江備海
南都根本固矣然廬鳳之民惰而地不盡利
徽寧之民細而俗用以偷田賦蘇松河流
豐沛不思為之恤乎由
京師而推之齊魯之絃歌弗聞歲苦河役南
盡于邳徐矣三晉之民勞日甚寇在門庭

皇上嗣位因輔臣與圖之獻
特賜嘉納仁育智運罔非宅中圖大保泰持
盈之至慮也執事復以要害民風道之使
言豈亦以諸生之中有治安之實生乎夫
古今異宜盛衰不同運今海內之大非不
肅然治也顧為萬世深長之慮蓋不無可
===
言者是故處山帶海
京師形勢尊矣然居庸之外蔽甚微畿甸之
遺戎未徙順天馬政河間水潦不思為之
所乎防江備海
南都根本固矣然廬鳳之民情而地不盡利
徽寧之民細而俗用以偷田賦蘇松河流
豐沛不思為之恤乎由
京師而推之齊魯之絃歌弗聞歲苦河徙南
盡于邳徐矣三晉之民勞日甚冦在門庭
punctuated:
鬼國者也。猗與休哉！自生民來，未有盛於今日者也。肆我英宗睿皇帝命纂一統志，以時備觀覽。皇上嗣位，因輔臣輿圖之獻，特賜嘉納。仁育智運，罔非宅中圖大、保泰持盈之至意也。執事復以要害民風導之使言，豈亦以諸生之中有治安之賈生乎？夫古今異宜，盛衰不同運。今海内之大，非不陶然治也。顧為萬世深長之慮，蓋不無可言者。
是故扆山帶海，京師形勢尊矣。然居庸之外蔽甚微，畿甸之遺戎未徙，順天馬政、河間水潦，不思為之所乎？防江備海，南都根本固矣。然廬鳳之民惰而地不盡利，徽寧之民細而俗用以偷，田賦蘇松、河流豐沛，不思為之恤乎？由京師而推之，齊魯之絃歌弗聞，歲苦河役，南盡于邳徐矣。三晉之民勞日甚，寇在門庭
translation_en:
…the “Kingdom of Ghosts.” Ah, how splendid! Since humankind first existed, there has never been prosperity greater than today’s. Thus our Emperor Yingzong Rui ordered the compilation of the Gazetteer of the Unified Realm (Yitong zhi), to be available for his inspection from time to time. After His Majesty succeeded to the throne, he graciously accepted and commended the maps presented by his assisting ministers. His benevolent nurturing and wise governance alike express his utmost commitment to occupying the center and planning for greatness, preserving peace and sustaining prosperity at its height. You, honored examiners, have further prompted us to speak about strategic locations and popular customs. Might you suppose that among us students there is a Master Jia Yi, ready to discuss good government and security? What is appropriate differs between antiquity and the present; flourishing and decline do not follow the same course. Today, the vast realm within the seas certainly enjoys contentment and good order. Yet, considering its enduring welfare for ten thousand generations, there are surely matters worth discussing.
Thus, with mountains at its back and the sea as its girdle, the capital occupies a commanding strategic position. Yet the outer defenses beyond Juyong are very slight, and the remaining Rong peoples within the metropolitan domain have not been relocated. As for horse administration in Shuntian and flooding in Hejian, should we not consider how to deal with them? With the river defended and the coast guarded, the southern capital has a secure foundation. Yet the people of Lu and Feng are indolent, and their land’s productive potential is not fully realized; the people of Hui and Ning are petty, and their customs have consequently become lax. As for land taxes in Su and Song and the river’s course through Feng and Pei, should we not consider how to provide relief? Extending our view outward from the capital, in Qi and Lu the sounds of strings and singing—the signs of cultivated instruction—are no longer heard. Year after year, the people suffer under river labor service, extending southward as far as Pi and Xu. The people of the Three Jin regions grow more overburdened by the day, while raiders stand at their very gates…

title: 嘉靖二十二年順天府鄉試錄
text:
矢達於太原矣關陜之間昔號陸海今則
烽火時乘土魯番之内侵亦不刺之殘孽
皆腹心之隱憂也河洛之地古稱形勝今
則輻輳趨利土地未盡闢教令未盡馴此
奸宄之自出也由
南都而推之民緣山谷爲利亦藉之以爲奸
此江浙之同患也況並海倭夷南贛盜賊
是可弛凶器之除乎楚俗剽輕而人訾窳
蜀地肥沃而民淫泆此統治之異宜也若
===
力役之殷征需之急是可無息肩之惠乎
若夫嶺南蠻獠始事芟夷而廣右猺獞方
勤誅討閩粤之間素號難治而粤則非閩
中比矣時恬則蜂屯蟻聚有事則禽駭獸
奔雲貴之治舊稱雜夷是又非諸省比矣
嗚呼廣谷大川異制民生其間異俗事理
固然無足怪者是故聖人不易民而成化
王公必設險以守國興利除害移風易俗
庸非

punctuated: 矢達於太原矣。關陜之間，昔號陸海，今則烽火時乘，土魯番之内侵、亦不刺之殘孽，皆腹心之隱憂也。河洛之地，古稱形勝，今則輻輳趨利，土地未盡闢，教令未盡馴，此奸宄之自出也。由南都而推之，民緣山谷爲利，亦藉之以爲奸，此江浙之同患也。況並海倭夷、南贛盜賊，是可弛凶器之除乎？楚俗剽輕而人訾窳，蜀地肥沃而民淫泆，此統治之異宜也。若力役之殷、征需之急，是可無息肩之惠乎？若夫嶺南蠻獠，始事芟夷，而廣右猺獞，方勤誅討。閩粤之間，素號難治，而粤則非閩中比矣。時恬則蜂屯蟻聚，有事則禽駭獸奔。雲貴之治，舊稱雜夷，是又非諸省比矣。嗚呼！廣谷大川異制，民生其間異俗，事理固然，無足怪者。是故聖人不易民而成化，王公必設險以守國。興利除害，移風易俗，庸非
translation_en:
…Arrows have reached Taiyuan. The region of Guanzhong and Shaanxi was once called a “sea on land” for its abundance; now warning beacons repeatedly flare. Incursions from Turfan and the surviving followers of Yibula are all latent threats to the heart of the realm. The region of the Yellow and Luo rivers was anciently praised for its strategic terrain. Now people converge there in pursuit of profit, yet the land is not fully brought under cultivation, nor are the people fully responsive to instruction and commands. This is where wrongdoing and disorder arise.

Extending our view outward from the Southern Capital, the people draw their livelihoods from mountains and valleys, but also use them to commit wrongdoing. This is a shared affliction of Jiangsu and Zhejiang. Moreover, with Japanese marauders along the coast and bandits in southern Jiangxi, can efforts to eliminate them by force of arms be relaxed? The customs of Chu are fierce and frivolous, and its people idle and indolent; the land of Shu is fertile, but its people dissolute and unrestrained. These differences require different approaches to government. As for heavy labor service and urgent demands for levies and supplies, can the people be denied the kindness of relief from their burdens?

As for the Man and Liao peoples south of the Ling mountains, their suppression has only just begun, while punitive campaigns against the Yao and Zhuang of Guangxi are now being vigorously pursued. Fujian and Guangdong have long been known as difficult to govern, but Guangdong cannot be compared with Fujian. In quiet times they gather like swarms of bees and ants; when trouble comes, they scatter like startled birds and fleeing beasts. The territories governed in Yunnan and Guizhou have long been described as inhabited by a mixture of non-Han peoples; these, again, cannot be compared with the other provinces.

Alas! Broad valleys and great rivers differ in their configurations, and the people living among them differ in their customs. This is the natural order of things and gives no cause for surprise. Thus the sage transforms the people without replacing them, and kings and dukes must establish defenses at strategic barriers to safeguard their states. To promote benefits and eliminate harms, to reform prevailing practices and change customs—are these not…

title: 嘉靖二十二年順天府鄉試錄
text:
今日之急務乎竊又有聞焉天險不可升也
地險山川丘陵也夫險至于不可升則必
有出於山川丘陵之外者矣今
天下一家深仁厚澤又足以相維於不壞要
害非所先也顧風俗侈靡士習澆漓識者
有深慮焉敦儉朴以明好惡之端振紀綱
以祛積習之弊而行之必自
京邑始則道德一風俗同天下至險伏之於
大順矣雖然亦在乎任人耳賈生曰移風
===
===
易俗使天下回心向道要非俗吏之所能
爲是故文翁任而蜀化常衮治而閩興况
天下之俗未至閩蜀天下之吏有賢於文
衮者乎善乎孟軻氏之言曰堯舜之智而
不徧物急先務也堯舜之仁不徧愛人急
親賢也此其所以能通天下爲一身也謹
對
第四問
李最

有出於山川丘陵之外者矣今
天下一家深仁厚澤又足以相維於不壞要
害非所先也顧風俗侈靡士習澆漓識者
有深慮焉敦儉朴以明好惡之端振紀綱
以袪積習之弊而行之必自
京邑始則道德一風俗同天下至險伏之於
大順矣雖然亦在乎任人耳賈生曰移風
===
易俗使天下回心向道要非俗吏之所能
爲是故文翁任而蜀化常袞治而閩興況
天下之俗未至閩蜀天下之吏有賢於文
袞者乎善乎孟軻氏之言曰堯舜之智而
不徧物急先務也堯舜之仁不徧愛人急
親賢也此其所以能通天下爲一身也謹
對
第四問
李最
punctuated:
今日之急務乎？竊又有聞焉：「天險不可升也，地險山川丘陵也。」夫險至于不可升，則必有出於山川丘陵之外者矣。今天下一家，深仁厚澤又足以相維於不壞，要害非所先也。顧風俗侈靡，士習澆漓，識者有深慮焉。敦儉朴以明好惡之端，振紀綱以祛積習之弊，而行之必自京邑始，則道德一，風俗同，天下至險伏之於大順矣。雖然，亦在乎任人耳。賈生曰：「移風易俗，使天下回心向道，要非俗吏之所能爲。」是故文翁任而蜀化，常衮治而閩興，况天下之俗未至閩蜀，天下之吏有賢於文衮者乎？善乎孟軻氏之言曰：「堯舜之智而不徧物，急先務也；堯舜之仁不徧愛人，急親賢也。」此其所以能通天下爲一身也。謹對。

第四問
李最
translation_en:
…are these not urgent tasks for today? Your servant has also heard it said: “Heaven’s heights cannot be ascended; earth’s natural defenses are mountains, rivers, hills, and ridges.” If a defense is so formidable that it cannot be ascended, there must be something that surpasses mountains, rivers, hills, and ridges. Now that all under Heaven forms one family, and profound benevolence and abundant beneficence suffice to hold it together without collapse, strategic strongpoints are not the first priority. Yet customs are extravagant and wasteful, and the habits of scholars have grown shallow and insincere; discerning men are deeply concerned. Foster frugality and simplicity to make clear the grounds for approval and disapproval; reinvigorate the governing order to eliminate the evils of entrenched habits. These measures must begin in the capital. Then moral principles will be unified and customs made uniform, and the gravest dangers throughout the realm will be subdued within a condition of general harmony. Even so, this depends upon appointing the right men. Master Jia said: “To transform customs and cause all under Heaven to turn their hearts toward the Way is certainly beyond the ability of ordinary officials.” Thus, when Wen Weng held office, Shu was transformed; when Chang Gun governed, Min flourished. How much more can be achieved when the customs of the realm have not deteriorated to the condition of Min and Shu, and there are officials in the realm worthier than Wen Weng and Chang Gun! Well did Meng Ke say: “Even the wisdom of Yao and Shun did not encompass every affair: they attended urgently to what came first. Even the benevolence of Yao and Shun did not extend equally to every person: they attended urgently to drawing worthy men close.” This is how they could unite all under Heaven into a single body. Respectfully submitted in reply.

Fourth Question
Li Zui

title: 嘉靖二十二年順天府鄉試錄
text:
同考試官教諭藍批是策淹貫諸史𤼵越
千百年人物剖析疑似灼有卓見以若學識而致諸
用焉徃不達薦寘首列豈獨以文巳也
同考試官教諭浦批博物窮理固吾儒蓄
德之資也此篇條析無遺品評不爽讀之令人灑然
晉臣之多聞子產之博物又奚足侈哉健羨健羨
考試官左贊善浦批於考據見子之學於品
隲見子之識
考試官右中允秦批博洽而不淆於衆見盖尚
===
友古人者錄之
知所以博物者可以語窮理矣知所以窮
理者可以語畜德矣知所以畜德者可以
語尚論矣何則物也者理之所由以寓者
也理也者德之所由以成者也物有不博
理不可得而窮矣理有未窮德不可得而
蓄矣德之不畜則其學也或失則陋或失
