Comment by Associate Examiner Lan, Instructor: This policy essay displays comprehensive mastery of the histories and brings to light figures spanning hundreds and thousands of years. It analyzes doubtful and seemingly similar cases, showing unmistakably outstanding insight. If learning and discernment such as these are put to practical use, success will follow wherever one goes [?]. In recommending its placement among the foremost, could we be judging solely by literary accomplishment?

Comment by Associate Examiner Pu, Instructor: Broad knowledge of things and exhaustive investigation of principle are indeed resources through which we Confucians cultivate virtue. This essay analyzes each matter without omission and evaluates without error; reading it leaves one refreshed. What further cause is there to extol the extensive learning of the minister of Jin or Zichan’s broad knowledge of things? Most admirable, most admirable!

Comment by Examiner Pu, Left Admonisher: In your examination of evidence I see your learning; in your evaluations I see your discernment.

Comment by Examiner Qin, Right Mentor: Broadly learned without being confused by the multitude of opinions, he is surely one who reaches back to make friends with the ancients. Accept him.

One who understands how to acquire broad knowledge of things may be engaged in discussion of investigating principle to its utmost. One who understands how to investigate principle to its utmost may be engaged in discussion of cultivating virtue. One who understands how to cultivate virtue may be engaged in discussion of judging the ancients. Why is this? Things are that in which principle resides; principle is that through which virtue is brought to completion. If knowledge of things is not broad, principle cannot be investigated to its utmost. If principle has not been fully investigated, virtue cannot be cultivated. If virtue is not cultivated, one’s learning will err either through shallowness or through narrowness. If, on this basis, one seeks to judge the deeds of the ancients, I see only confusion and error. How could such a person comprehend the causes of affairs throughout the world and illuminate its transformations …

title: 嘉靖二十二年順天府鄉試錄
text:
而能折衷往聖哉於乎此君子所以唯學
之爲貴而畜德則其要也執事以古今紀
載人物事爲之當擬議者下策諸生愚固
知非導之以徒博而已也請具陳之公孫
碩膚赤舄几几周公所爲居東也觀之鴟
鴞九罭之詩則可徵矣而魯世家乃謂人
或譖公公避奔楚噫此果是膺是懲之訓
乎史氏之附會其甚哉恪恭箴儆威儀抑
抑武公所爲君國也觀之淇澳懿戒之詩
===
則可占矣而衛世家乃謂襲殺共伯立和
爲侯噫此果有斐君子之事乎史遷之所
聞其誣哉孟子之待王驩所謂不惡而嚴
也楊思勗以內侍而迎宋璟於西京則亦
驩之類耳璟肯與之交言乎此其持正當
不在泰山壁立下矣孔子之亦獵較所謂
小同於俗也尹和靜以從班而迎觀音於
郊外則非獵較之比矣尹何爲亦與之往
乎此其作用殆難以語大賢以上事矣開

…and be able to judge matters by the standards of the sages of old? Ah! This is why the gentleman prizes learning above all, with the cultivation of virtue as its essential purpose. You, honored examiners, have set the candidates a policy question concerning people and events recorded in ancient and modern times that call for deliberation. I know well that your intention is not merely to lead us toward wide learning. Allow me to explain fully.
“The duke withdrew, yet great was his merit; his red shoes were stately”: this concerns the Duke of Zhou’s residence in the east. The poems “The Owl” (Chixiao) and “The Nine-Netted Fishing Net” (Jiuyu) provide evidence for it. Yet the “Hereditary House of Lu” says that someone slandered the duke and that he fled to Chu to escape. Ah! Does this truly accord with the teaching, “These he struck, these he chastised”? How extreme the historian’s contrived account is! “Reverently attentive to admonition and warning, dignified and restrained in bearing”: this concerns Duke Wu’s rule over his state. The poems “The Bend of the Qi” (Qi’ao) and “Admonitions” (Yijie) allow us to discern this. Yet the “Hereditary House of Wei” says that an attack killed Gongbo and that He was installed as marquis. Ah! Is this truly the conduct of the “accomplished gentleman”? How false were the reports heard by the historian Sima Qian!
Mencius’s treatment of Wang Huan exemplifies what is called being stern without hostility. When Yang Sixu, a palace eunuch, welcomed Song Jing at the Western Capital, he was simply another of Wang Huan’s kind. Would Song Jing consent to converse with him? In his adherence to rectitude, he surely stood no lower than the sheer face of Mount Tai. Confucius’s participation in the hunting contest exemplifies what is called conforming to customary practice in minor matters. But when Yin Hejing, as a member of the court retinue, went outside the city to welcome Guanyin, this was not comparable to the hunting contest. Why did Yin also accompany them? Such conduct can hardly be discussed as belonging to the affairs of a great worthy or anyone higher. Opening up…

title: 嘉靖二十二年順天府鄉試錄
text:
西南夷逢君病國矜夸貴盛負弩前驅司
馬相如之鄙行也其視萬石君家父子醇
謹致恭桑梓者夐不侔矣而卓王孫顧猶
有喜眩之色暴富遷虜何足齒哉産祿擅
兵寄與友善謀誅呂氏劫而後從商寄之
罪均也其視州吁好兵石碏誅厚大義滅
親者有餘辜矣而班固乃爲洗賣友之穢
固之於義一何陋哉陳涉之王也事至微
淺而魯諸儒抱祭器歸之豈非積百年之
===
憾而發憤於陳王猶曰秦民之湯武乎然
而見亦愚矣矧孔甲又爲之博士與涉俱
斃果用舍行藏之家法邪史記列之儒林
可嗤也夫朝儀之起也機會可乘而魯兩
生乃設辭以拒之豈必其能傳孔孟之道
而知禮樂之所由興乎然而行則高矣乃
叔孫通則爲之綿蕞焉秦儀雜就果夔作
大章之遺意乎君子鄙其器小有以也夫
史以記君舉也欲自觀焉以冀免過於將

…opening up the lands of the southwestern peoples, pandering to the ruler and harming the state, and ostentatiously displaying wealth and eminence, with crossbow bearers leading the way: these were Sima Xiangru’s contemptible deeds. Compared with Lord Wanshi’s household, where father and sons were sincere and circumspect and showed reverence for their native place, he fell far short. Yet Zhuo Wangsun still looked delighted and dazzled. A suddenly enriched descendant of forcibly resettled captives—how could he merit mention!

Lü Chan and Lü Lu monopolized military power, and Li Ji was on friendly terms with them. When the plot to destroy the Lü clan was made, he joined only under coercion. Li Shang and Li Ji were equally culpable. Compared with Shi Que, who, when Zhouxu pursued warfare, executed his own son Hou, destroying a kinsman for the sake of the greater right, their guilt more than warranted punishment. Yet Ban Gu sought to cleanse them of the stain of betraying a friend. How deficient was Gu’s understanding of righteousness!

When Chen She became king, his undertaking was exceedingly slight and shallow. Yet the Confucian scholars of Lu carried their sacrificial vessels and rallied to him. Was this not because they had accumulated a century’s resentment and gave vent to their indignation through King Chen, virtually calling him a Tang or a Wu for the people of Qin? Yet their judgment was foolish indeed! Moreover, Kong Jia became his Erudite and perished alongside She. Was this truly the rule handed down in his family: to act when employed and withdraw when set aside? That the Records of the Grand Historian included him among the Confucian scholars is laughable!

When court ceremonial was being established, there was an opportunity to seize, yet the two scholars of Lu offered reasons for refusing. Must this mean that they could transmit the Way of Confucius and Mencius and understood how rites and music arise? Nevertheless, their conduct was lofty. Shusun Tong, however, marked out the ceremonial positions with cords and bundles of thatch, assembling a mixture incorporating Qin ceremonial. Did this truly preserve the intent of Kui’s composition of the Great Zhang? The gentleman has reason to scorn the narrowness of his capacity!

title: 嘉靖二十二年順天府鄉試錄
text:
来得無起人顧慮而開隱諱之端與鄭朗
有執筆螭頭之直而乃亦為之則其於文
宗也未免失之徇矣相為天下置也使姑
用馬以求免國謗於後世得無異於迪知
忱恂告教厥后與韓琦有薦相歐陽修之
公而乃亦言之則其於仁宗也未免待之
淺矣王望便宜出粟以活所部之民而朝
廷赦其專命之罪君人之度也汲黯持節
開倉以賑河南之饑而自請伏矯制之罪

虛秏而卒享三公之富商賈之道也其心

待報恐不及也故與章偕来以示其切盖

涉於彊邪杜佑欲明李藩撼軍之誣而詔

…to come—might this not arouse misgivings and open the way to concealment? Zheng Lang possessed the integrity of a court diarist wielding his brush beside the dragon-carved steps, yet he too did this. In his dealings with Emperor Wenzong, therefore, he could not escape the fault of undue accommodation. Chief councillors are appointed for the sake of all under Heaven. If one were provisionally to employ Ma [?] merely to spare the state the censure of later generations, would this not depart from sincerely guiding and instructing one’s sovereign? Han Qi showed impartiality in recommending Ouyang Xiu as chief councillor, yet he too made such a statement. In his dealings with Emperor Renzong, therefore, he could not escape the fault of expecting too little of him.

Wang Wang exercised discretion in distributing grain to save the people under his jurisdiction, and the court pardoned his crime of acting without authorization: this was a ruler’s magnanimity. Ji An, bearing his envoy’s credentials, opened the granaries to relieve famine in Henan, and himself requested punishment for falsely invoking an imperial command: this was a subject’s deference. Were their underlying principles really so far apart? Wang Dan led his clansmen in contributing wheat to meet military needs in Guanzhong, yet ultimately declined appointment as Governor of Fengyi: this was the scrupulous restraint of a scholar-farmer. Bu Shi contributed his wealth to support the frontier, thereby furthering the depletion of resources throughout the realm [?], and ultimately enjoyed the wealth of one of the Three Dukes: this was the way of a merchant. How could their motives be considered the same?

Pei Du wished to stop Emperor Jingzong’s journey to the Eastern Capital, but feared that waiting for a response would leave him too late. He therefore came in person along with his memorial to demonstrate his urgency. This was simply an adaptation of ritual propriety to circumstances. Such action is permissible when one has Du’s intentions; otherwise, would it not verge on coercion? Du You wished to expose the false accusation that Li Fan had incited unrest in the army [?], and knew that the imperial order for his execution was unjustifiable. 以廉之義鍾離意委地而不拜賜可謂清
白不自汚矣但謂盜泉勝母而惡於其名
無乃爲皎乎金人策士而詆及上皇本非
先資自獻之日褚米亮長揖而辭主文可
謂威武不能屈矣彼以富貴之圖而忍忘
故國亦獨何心哉大君天下之主有分野
無分氣也彗出寅艮之間而謂應在外夷
===

證而勸人主恐懼修省斯得之矣日爲衆
陽之宗無私照無偏應也旦暮日色皆赤
而謂應在四夷金良弼之言直偶驗耳惟
謂人君修德應天則災變自弭斯近之矣
高麗之貢方物可以讓可以無讓讓則弱
唐高祖惟知自強故能納溫彥博之言而
无咎遼左之違詔命可以征可以無征征
則黷唐太宗不知自戢故不能聽褚遂良

translation_en: …was merely a matter of seeing truly. Yet this was permissible for someone with Du You’s wisdom; otherwise, would one not incur suspicion of partisan collusion? When Zhang Hui was convicted of corruption and an edict bestowed his illicit gains upon the assembled ministers, this certainly did not accord with the principle of teaching people integrity. Zhongli Yi laid his share on the ground and refused to bow in acknowledgment of the gift: he may be called pure and upright, unwilling to sully himself. But to invoke Robber’s Spring and Shengmu—“Surpassing One’s Mother”—and abhor them for their names: was this not excessively fastidious? When the Jin held policy examinations for scholars and disparaged the retired emperor, this was surely no occasion to advance oneself and offer one’s services [?]. Chu Miliang [?] made a deep bow with clasped hands and took his leave of the chief examiner: he may be said to have remained unbowed by force and might. As for those who, in pursuit of wealth and rank, could bear to forget their former country—what sort of hearts did they have? The sovereign is lord of all under Heaven: celestial regions have their corresponding terrestrial divisions, but vital force has no such divisions. When a comet appeared between the yin and gen directions, to say that its portent concerned foreign peoples was simply nonsense on Geng Nanzhong’s part. Li Guang alone got it right when he cited the Spring and Autumn Annals as evidence and urged the ruler to respond with fear, self-cultivation, and self-examination. The sun is the chief of all manifestations of yang; its illumination is impartial, and its portents do not apply selectively. When the sun was red both morning and evening, Jin Liangbi’s assertion that the portent concerned the peoples of the four quarters was merely borne out by coincidence. Only his statement that, if a ruler cultivates virtue in response to Heaven, calamities and anomalies will subside of themselves came close to the truth. Gaoli’s tribute of local products could have been declined or accepted; declining it would have shown weakness. Emperor Gaozu of Tang understood the need to strengthen his own position, and thus could accept Wen Yanbo’s advice without fault. Liaozuo’s defiance of imperial commands could have prompted a punitive expedition or been left unpunished; an expedition would have meant excessive resort to arms. Emperor Taizong of Tang did not know how to restrain himself, and thus could not heed Chu Suiliang…

title: 嘉靖二十二年順天府鄉試錄
text:
之諫而有悔春秋名分之書尊攘之道於
是焉在彼謂頒經而捨春秋果何見歟裴
光庭因吐蕃之請而勸帝與之可謂通於
遠略而得善變之術矣通國胡婦之子華
夷之辨於是焉分然以蘇卿而使無後獨
何忍歟漢宣帝因平恩侯之請而詔特許
之可謂明於大體而有王者之風矣凡此
皆執事所謂必有折衷之道而非徒言無
當者但古今之事變靡常史冊之疑似匪
===
一苟非多聞而擇之以會其博多見而識
之以要其中則往蹟紛然渺如烟海亦將
何所紀極哉是故周公之不居楚固矣而
謂召公致疑於踐阼亦豈事實衛武之不
襲兄似矣而謂光義可疑於燭影亦豈名
言郊迎觀音固非崇正黜邪也而謂傅奕
非聖者亦何損於蕭瑀之朴忠受劫賣友
信非直道事人也而謂師友違君者亦何
悖於左儒之大義孔甲之死於陳勝誠愚

一苟非多聞而擇之以會其博多見而識
之以要其中則往蹟紛然渺如烟海亦將
何所紀極哉是故周公之不居楚固矣而
謂召公致疑於踐阼亦豈事實衛武之不
襲兄似矣而謂光義可疑於燭影亦豈名
言郊迎觀音固非崇正黜邪也而謂傳奕
非聖者亦何損於蕭瑀之朴忠受劫貴友
信非直道事人也而謂師友違君者亦何
悖於左儒之大義孔甲之死於陳勝誠愚
punctuated:
之諫而有悔。《春秋》，名分之書，尊攘之道於是焉在。彼謂頒經而捨《春秋》，果何見歟？裴光庭因吐蕃之請而勸帝與之，可謂通於遠略而得善變之術矣。通國，胡婦之子，華夷之辨於是焉分。然以蘇卿而使無後，獨何忍歟？漢宣帝因平恩侯之請而詔特許之，可謂明於大體而有王者之風矣。凡此皆執事所謂必有折衷之道，而非徒言無當者。但古今之事變靡常，史冊之疑似匪一。苟非多聞而擇之以會其博，多見而識之以要其中，則往蹟紛然，渺如烟海，亦將何所紀極哉？

是故周公之不居楚固矣，而謂召公致疑於踐阼，亦豈事實？衛武之不襲兄似矣，而謂光義可疑於燭影，亦豈名言？郊迎觀音，固非崇正黜邪也，而謂傅奕非聖者，亦何損於蕭瑀之朴忠？受劫賣友，信非直道事人也，而謂師友違君者，亦何悖於左儒之大義？孔甲之死於陳勝，誠愚
translation_en:
…and came to regret not heeding his remonstrance. The Spring and Autumn Annals is a book about proper titles and distinctions of status; within it lies the Way of honoring the sovereign and repelling the barbarians. What understanding, then, lay behind the proposal to distribute the Classics but omit the Spring and Autumn Annals? When Pei Guangting, in response to a request from Tubo, urged the emperor to grant it, he could be said to have understood long-range strategy and mastered the art of adapting appropriately to circumstances. Tongguo was the son of a non-Han woman: here the distinction between Chinese and barbarian was drawn. Yet how could one bear to leave a man such as Su Qing [Su Wu] without descendants? When Emperor Xuan of Han, in response to the request of the Marquis of Ping’en, issued an edict granting special permission, he could be said to have understood the larger considerations and displayed the bearing of a true king. All these are instances of what you, honored examiners, call the necessity of finding a sound resolution, rather than merely making statements that miss the mark. Yet events, past and present, change without constancy, and ambiguities in the historical records are numerous. Unless one hears much and selects from it to bring together a broad understanding, and sees much and remembers it to grasp what is sound, the tangled traces of the past will stretch as far as a sea of mist. How, then, could one ever set them in order or fathom their limits?

Thus, it is certain that the Duke of Zhou did not reside in Chu; but is the claim that the Duke of Shao became suspicious of his assumption of the throne actually historical fact? It seems plausible that Duke Wu of Wei did not attack his elder brother; but is the claim that Guangyi falls under suspicion because of the candle shadows really a sound pronouncement? Going out to the suburbs to welcome Guanyin was certainly no way to exalt orthodoxy and reject heterodoxy; yet how did calling Fu Yi a denigrator of the sages detract from Xiao Yu’s simple loyalty? Yielding to coercion and betraying a friend is indeed no way to serve another with integrity; yet how did the statement about defying one’s ruler for teachers and friends [?] conflict with Zuo Ru’s great righteousness? Kong Jia’s dying for Chen Sheng was truly foolish…

title: 嘉靖二十二年順天府鄉試錄
text:
矣然魯以禮義之國而亦爲項籍死守□
謂智乎叔孫之狃於秦儀誠鄙矣然賈□
以文帝之賢而亦不能復漢古制奚庸愈
乎給州帑錢以安東川之軍則黃震之權
宜又不啻王望諸人已矣閉玉門關以謝
西域之質則光武之深略又不啻唐祖之
讓已矣彗見而請罷郊禮杜鎬之迂幾何
而不爲耿南仲邪河清而謂失常性楊珪
之偏幾何而不爲金良弼邪李藩之罪可
===
赦矣而杜兼之誣亦可赦乎蘇武之子可
歸矣而蔡琰之子亦可歸乎引而伸之觸
類而長之誠有更僕不能終其物者然統
而會之其要在乎蓄德其究存乎反約所
謂同歸而殊塗一致而百慮言天下之至
賾而不可惡也言天下之至動而不可亂
也近之足以表裏人物遠之足以進退古
今舉宇宙内事皆吾分内事矣苟爲不然
則雖讀史成誦如謝顯道亦適以取玩物

之偏幾何而不爲金良輔邪李播之罪可

歸矣而蔡琰之子亦可歸乎引而伸之觸
類而長之誠有更僕不能終其物者然統
而會之其要在乎蓄德其究存乎反約所

也近之足以表裏人物遠之足以進退古
今舉宇宙內事皆吾分內事矣苟爲不然
則雖讀史成誦如謝顯道亦適以取玩物
punctuated: 矣。然魯以禮義之國，而亦爲項籍死守，□謂智乎？叔孫之狃於秦儀，誠鄙矣。然賈□以文帝之賢，而亦不能復漢古制，奚庸愈乎？給州帑錢以安東川之軍，則黃震之權宜，又不啻王望諸人已矣。閉玉門關以謝西域之質，則光武之深略，又不啻唐祖之讓已矣。彗見而請罷郊禮，杜鎬之迂，幾何而不爲耿南仲邪？河清而謂失常性，楊珪之偏，幾何而不爲金良弼邪？李藩之罪可赦矣，而杜兼之誣亦可赦乎？蘇武之子可歸矣，而蔡琰之子亦可歸乎？引而伸之，觸類而長之，誠有更僕不能終其物者。然統而會之，其要在乎蓄德，其究存乎反約。所謂「同歸而殊塗，一致而百慮」，「言天下之至賾而不可惡也，言天下之至動而不可亂也」。近之足以表裏人物，遠之足以進退古今，舉宇宙内事，皆吾分内事矣。苟爲不然，則雖讀史成誦如謝顯道，亦適以取玩物
translation_en:
…was indeed foolish. Yet Lu, a land of ritual propriety and righteousness, also defended itself to the death for Xiang Ji: could this be called wise [?]? Shusun’s attachment to Qin ceremonial was indeed base. Yet Jia □ [?], even with an emperor as worthy as Emperor Wen, likewise could not restore ancient institutions for the Han. In what respect was he better? In supplying money from the prefectural treasury to pacify the troops of Dongchuan, Huang Zhen’s expedient measures went beyond those of Wang Wang and the others. In closing the Yumen Pass to decline hostages from the Western Regions, Emperor Guangwu’s far-reaching strategy went beyond even the concessions of the Tang founder. When a comet appeared, Du Hao requested that the suburban sacrifice be suspended: how far was his pedantry from making him another Geng Nanzhong? When the Yellow River ran clear, Yang Gui said that it had lost its normal nature: how far was his one-sidedness from making him another Jin Liangbi? Li Fan’s offense might be pardoned, but could Du Jian’s false accusation also be pardoned? Su Wu’s son could return, but could Cai Yan’s sons also return?

Extend these examples and develop them through analogous cases, and there are indeed more matters than one could finish discussing even through successive changes of attendants. Yet, brought together into a coherent whole, their essential point lies in cultivating virtue, and their ultimate purpose in returning to what is simple and essential. As it is said: “The destination is the same, though the paths differ; the outcome is one, though the deliberations are a hundred.” And: “They speak of the utmost intricacy of the world without giving cause for aversion; they speak of the utmost movement of the world without giving cause for disorder.” Applied close at hand, this suffices to comprehend people and things inside and out; applied more broadly, it suffices to judge what should be advanced or rejected, past and present. Everything within the universe thus falls within my own sphere of responsibility. If this is not so, then even if one reads history until one can recite it from memory, as Xie Xiandao did, one merely invites the charge of toying with things…

title: 嘉靖二十二年順天府鄉試錄
text:
喪志之誚而已奚貴哉蠡見如斯不識執
事以為然否
第五問
劉體乾
同考試官教諭劉批五策條答無遺篇皆
可式而足兵一策尤考究精詳確有定見殆非徒談兵者

===

知今盖記誦可襲取而識時務者非俊傑不能也此作
不迂不佞鑿鑿可行豈胸中有甲兵者邪

punctuated:
喪志之誚而已，奚貴哉？蠡見如斯，不識執事以為然否？

第五問
劉體乾

同考試官教諭劉批：五策條答無遺，篇皆可式，而足兵一策尤考究精詳，確有定見，殆非徒談兵者。表此以例其餘耳。敬服！敬服！

考試官左贊善浦批：能劑量民兵利便之故，而為經畫疆圉之宜，必非昧於世務者，可以入彀矣。

考試官右中允秦批：儒生不難於博古，而難於知今，盖記誦可襲取，而識時務者非俊傑不能也。此作不迂不佞，鑿鑿可行，豈胸中有甲兵者邪？

酌內外輕重之大勢，可以語制兵矣；攷古今兵農之大較，可以語給兵矣。世之言兵者曰：「兵坐食國農也。」率不加察而和其聲，至議推行，以農之故而寢者亦多矣。是故，不酌內外輕重之勢，不攷古今兵農之實，以奢語政經與難事於通變，皆在□□人
translation_en:
…the reproach of losing one's resolve through preoccupation with things, and nothing more. What is there to esteem in that? Such is my narrow view; I do not know whether you, sir, consider it correct.

Fifth Question
Liu Tiqian

Comment by Associate Examiner Liu, Instructor: All five policy questions are answered point by point, with nothing omitted, and every essay can serve as a model. The essay on ensuring sufficient troops is especially meticulous and precise in its investigations, displaying firmly established judgments. Its author is surely no mere armchair discussant of military affairs. I single this out as representative of the others. Admirable! Admirable!

Comment by Examiner Pu, Left Mentor: He can weigh the factors affecting the interests and convenience of the people and the troops, and devise appropriate plans for the frontier. He is certainly no stranger to practical affairs and may be selected.

Comment by Examiner Qin, Right Companion to the Heir Apparent: For a Confucian scholar, broad knowledge of antiquity is not difficult; understanding the present is difficult. What one memorizes and recites can be borrowed from others, but only outstanding men can understand the affairs of their own time. This essay is neither impractical nor glib: its proposals are definite and feasible. Could its author be one who carries armies within his breast?

Only after weighing the overall balance of power between the interior and the frontier can one discuss organizing troops. Only after examining the broad relationship between soldiers and farmers in ancient and modern times can one discuss provisioning troops. Those who discuss military affairs nowadays say, “Soldiers sit idle and consume what the country's farmers produce.” Most echo this claim without examining it; even when proposals come up for implementation, many are shelved on account of agriculture. Thus, without weighing the balance of power between the interior and the frontier, or investigating the actual circumstances of soldiers and farmers in ancient and modern times, they speak extravagantly of the principles of government and raise difficulties about adapting to change; all rests with □□ people [?]…

title: 嘉靖二十二年順天府鄉試錄
text:
遽議足兵未有能濟者也執事慨郡縣之
不可無兵而謂西北爲急訏謨遠矣顧鉛
槧末學何足與議軍旅請試陳所聞惟執
事察焉夫今之天下即古之天下今之土
壤即古之土壤古者百里之地爲千乘之
國有兵三萬七千五百人周有天下諸侯
之國千有八百雖不皆方百里而絶長補
短國宜有兵二萬五千人總之得兵四千
五百餘萬而餘夫之爲羨卒者又不與也
===
今之郡縣大者非特百里而已其爲數亦
不下千八百也士徒之衆或數邑而無聞
豈其爲民者盡縁南畝盡輸公賦而不可
以爲兵耶抑可以兵而未求也愚嘗考之
古者三時耕稼一時閲武其于蒐田又率
之以從事盖農之用力於兵嵗六十日則
今專力之兵一當古兼農之兵六若舉千
八百國之常數較今日都司衛所之尺籍
姑以百萬爲率幾五十倍少于古矣苟即

…to hastily propose making the troops sufficient has never brought success. You, sir, deplore the fact that prefectures and counties cannot do without troops and judge the northwest to be the most urgent concern: your grand planning is far-reaching indeed. The realm today is the same realm as in antiquity; its land is the same land as in antiquity. In ancient times, a territory one hundred li square constituted a state of a thousand chariots and had 37,500 troops. When the Zhou possessed the realm, there were 1,800 states of the regional lords. Although not all were one hundred li square, if the larger and smaller were averaged out, each state should have had 25,000 troops. Altogether, this yields more than 45 million troops, without counting the additional adult males who served as reserve soldiers.

Today, the larger prefectures and counties extend well beyond one hundred li, and their total number is likewise no fewer than 1,800. Yet across several counties one may hear of no substantial body of troops. Can it be that their people all work in the fields and all pay public taxes, but cannot serve as soldiers? Or could they serve, but no attempt has been made to seek them out? I have examined this matter. In antiquity, people cultivated crops for three seasons and underwent military reviews for one; they were also led out to take part in hunting exercises. title: 嘉靖二十二年順天府鄉試錄
text:
古之兵數焉今之農數是以五十力農之
夫供一荷戈之卒用人之力費人之財不
可謂不省矣古者兵由農出凡干戈車乘
馬牛之屬皆取具於民而國無預焉今兵
由國出凡干戈車乘馬牛之屬皆取具於
國而民無預焉今日兵之於民又不可謂
不便也夫其費省于古其便多于民宜乎
兵不可勝用矣而郡縣以乏告非愚所知
也且今郡縣之相距或六七十里而近或
===
百里而近日出而發日中而至是故倉卒
之變奸宄之萌譬諸釜中苙內使有兵焉
南北聲援如響應也東西掎角如左右手
也宜若易易然無難矣惟其兵或不足故
往年霸州之警剽掠南北疾如迅飈州縣
或窘于城守之未備近年迤北之虜再歷
晉關突若奔豕村堡多潰于壁野之未堅
若是者謂不可不責之郡縣固也然亦豈
可以盡責耶蓋

且今郡縣之相距，或六七十里而近，或百里而近，日出而發，日中而至。是故倉卒之變、奸宄之萌，譬諸釜中苙內，使有兵焉，南北聲援，如響應也；東西掎角，如左右手也。宜若易易然無難矣。惟其兵或不足，故往年霸州之警，剽掠南北，疾如迅飈，州縣或窘于城守之未備；近年迤北之虜，再歷晉關，突若奔豕，村堡多潰于壁野之未堅。若是者，謂不可不責之郡縣，固也；然亦豈可以盡責耶？蓋

…the troop numbers of antiquity [taken as] the number of farmers today [?]: thus fifty men working at farming support one soldier bearing a spear. In its demands on people’s labor and expenditure of their wealth, this cannot be called uneconomical. In antiquity, soldiers came from the farming population. Weapons, chariots, horses, cattle, and the like were all supplied by the people, and the state had no part in providing them. Today, soldiers are provided by the state. Weapons, chariots, horses, cattle, and the like are all supplied by the state, and the people have no part in providing them. The present military arrangements cannot, then, be said to offer the people no advantage. Since their expense is smaller than in antiquity and their advantages to the people greater, troops ought to be available in inexhaustible numbers. Yet prefectures and counties report shortages. This is something I, in my ignorance, cannot understand.
Moreover, the distances between prefectural and county seats today may be as little as sixty or seventy li, or about a hundred li. Setting out at sunrise, one can arrive by midday. Thus, sudden disturbances and emerging outbreaks of lawlessness are like things caught in a cauldron or an enclosure. If troops were available, support from north and south would come as promptly as an echo answers a sound; coordinated action from east and west would be like that of the left and right hands. This ought to be perfectly easy, presenting no difficulty. But because troops are sometimes insufficient, during the alarm at Bazhou in earlier years, raiders plundered north and south as swiftly as a violent whirlwind, and some subprefectures and counties were hard pressed because preparations for defending their cities were incomplete. In recent years, the northern barbarians twice passed through the passes of Jin, charging like wild boars, and many villages and forts fell because their fortifications and measures to secure the countryside were inadequate [?]. In such cases, it is certainly right to say that prefectures and counties must be held accountable. Yet how can all the blame be laid upon them? For …

title: 嘉靖二十二年順天府鄉試錄
text:
國家健卒多集九邊正德初年之寇調宣大
遊擊之兵入而收海口狼山之捷王師制
之師盡在
京營近歳虜警之故簡官廳聽征之卒往而
屯紫荆諸關之隘矣若是者謂兵家調發
所不廢固也然抑豈可以爲常邪胡安國
曰自古及今內外之勢適平則安偏重則
危不可不深省也應劭曰兵發當有不及
講其射御用其警戒一旦驅之以即強敵
===
是以每戰常負又曰殊方之兵忿鷙縱橫
多僵良善以爲已功不可不深省也盖聞
西漢之制矣郡國有材官騎士毎歳八月
太守都尉令長丞尉會都試課殿最水處
爲樓船邊郡行障塞有事以羽檄徵發各
因其地此非郡縣之兵歟厥後光武除兵
制於是郡國罷都尉之官太守無都試之
役警備既撤實啓戎心張角之亂說者諉
罪焉有由然也杜佑曰兵制可采惟有漢

translation_en:
…the state's sturdy soldiers are mostly concentrated in the Nine Frontier Garrisons. During the bandit troubles early in the Zhengde reign, mobile troops from Xuanfu and Datong were brought into the interior and won victories at Haikou and Langshan. The troops of the imperial military establishment [?] are all stationed in the capital camps. Because of recent alarms concerning the northern invaders, soldiers awaiting expeditionary service under the military headquarters were selected and sent to garrison the strategic approaches to Zijing and the other passes. It is certainly true that military mobilization and dispatch cannot be dispensed with; but can this be made the regular practice? Hu Anguo said: “From antiquity to the present, when the balance of power between the interior and the frontier is even, there is security; when either side is disproportionately strong, there is danger.” This demands deep reflection. Ying Shao said: “When troops are mobilized, there may be insufficient time to train them in archery and charioteering and to have them practice vigilance. Suddenly they are driven forward to confront a powerful enemy; thus they regularly suffer defeat whenever they fight.” He also said: “Troops from distant regions are fierce and unruly, frequently killing innocent people and claiming these deaths as their own military achievements.” This demands deep reflection.
Now, I have heard of the Western Han system: the commanderies and kingdoms maintained selected infantry and cavalry. Each year in the eighth month, the governors, commandants, magistrates, chiefs, assistant magistrates, and defenders assembled for a general military review, grading performance from worst to best. In places with waterways, men served aboard towered warships; in frontier commanderies, they patrolled fortified posts and frontier defenses. When an emergency arose, they were called up by dispatches bearing feathers, with service adapted to each locality. Were these not troops of the commanderies and counties? Later, Emperor Guangwu abolished this military system. The office of commandant was consequently abolished in the commanderies and kingdoms, and governors no longer had responsibility for the general military reviews. Once these defensive precautions had been withdrawn, this indeed encouraged thoughts of armed rebellion. There is reason why commentators lay the blame for Zhang Jue's rebellion upon this measure. Du You said: “Among military systems worthy of adoption, there is only that of the Han…”

translation_en:
…the Han dynasty”—presumably this was what he meant. Today, men born in Yan and Zhao, Ying and Ping, Qi and Lu, and Yong and Jin are generally imposing and broad in spirit, high-minded, composed, and resolute. In peaceful times they are all ordinary commoners; in times of trouble they can become strong soldiers. If we followed the surviving practices of the Han, implementing them first in these regions and taking one region as a model, it would then be easy to extend them throughout the realm.
I have also heard of Li Baozhen’s administration of Huaizhou. He considered Ze and Lu to be thoroughfares where troops passed and assembled, and sought to guard beforehand against disturbances in Shandong. He therefore registered the households, selected two out of every three adult males, supplied them with bows and arrows, and had them practice archery in groups and pairs. At the end of each year he held a general review, personally checked the registers, graded their abilities, and announced rewards and reprimands. After two years they had all become skilled soldiers, yielding a trained force of twenty thousand. Was this not also an army raised from prefectures and counties? There was thus good reason why its reputation subsequently spread throughout the realm, why everyone ranked the Zhaoyi infantry foremost among all the armies, and why it was able to dominate Shandong and render distinguished service to the Tang ruling house. Li Zhaoliang said, “Militia can be employed effectively; recent times have furnished clear proof.” Presumably he was referring to this. Today, the people of the garrisons along the six frontiers are generally hardy by disposition and accustomed to toil. They have repeatedly faced incursions by northern foes; their livelihoods and property are mostly situated in the borderlands, and their customs and temper are little different from those of the desert. If we followed Baozhen’s surviving practices and implemented them first in these regions, then, once they had proved effective in the frontier garrisons, extending them to the interior would likewise be easy.
Recently, the Minister of War proposed adjusting recruitment to the size of each prefecture and county, expanding the existing complements of constables and local militiamen to one thousand men in large counties and half that number in small ones. This is indeed a sound plan. Yet in my humble opinion…

…consider that selection must be exacting. Thus, recruits must be skilled in mounted archery and proficient in military techniques [?]; the frail, the elderly, and the very young must not be allowed to participate. Supplies for them must also be ample. Thus, their weapons must be made effective and their equipment provided, while expenditure on wages and recruitment must not be begrudged. Only then should the responsible officials be charged with meeting the standards proposed. By taking the two methods mentioned above and appropriately supplementing or modifying each with the other, it would seem unnecessary to seek further measures elsewhere.

…why should this not be possible? If it is argued that leaders must be provided to command, instruct, and train the troops, prefects and county magistrates, together with their assistant officials, should not all be regarded as mere bookish scholars. Once responsibility has been assigned exclusively to them, neither the number of officials nor their stipends need be increased. This could also strengthen the bonds between fathers and elder brothers, sons and younger brothers, and establish a relationship of command like that of the body directing the arms and the arms directing the fingers. Under the Song, the prefectures and commanderies employed military arrangements throughout, under military commissioners, surveillance commissioners, defense commissioners, military training commissioners, and prefects. Even the titles of assistant prefects necessarily included responsibility for military and prefectural affairs; lower down, section officials were also called military staff officers. If this could be practiced under the Song, can it not be practiced today? Meng Ke said: “Qi is what fills the body.” Soldiers are like qi, and prefectures and counties are the four limbs. Postface to the Record of the Shuntian Prefecture Provincial Examination

The twenty-second year of His Majesty’s reign is the guimao year of Jiajing [1543]. His rule has now extended through two twelve-year cycles [?]. The Way pervades all, government is well ordered, and civil culture has brought about transformation. The hundred institutions have been set right, and the myriad spirits all flourish. Auspicious signs respond in harmony [?]; the people and all things prosper. States throughout the realm offer precious tribute, Jiaonan demonstrates its allegiance, and even the distant northern wastes and the lands north of the desert approach the frontier gates and come to court. Within there is peace; beyond there is tranquility. His influence spreads like wind and flows like the sea. …the earlier and later sages followed a single standard. Thus today our sagely Son of Heaven, with an undivided heart, summons outstanding men, diligently selects them, and invites them with careful consideration. His great achievements and brilliant virtue are manifest and exalted without wavering; he devotes particular attention to the examinations for selecting the worthy. Could he merely be following these old statutes and performing elaborate formalities? Surely he comprehensively understands how the sage employs both civil and military means together, so that mere men in armor and helmets cannot take precedence over us in scholars’ caps.
Reverently we reflect that our Emperor Taizu Gao united the realm under Heaven and inaugurated dynastic rule in the south, while Emperor Chengzu Wen established the capital and enlarged the dynastic foundations in the north. Taking civil governance as the warp and military affairs as the weft, they preserved the greatness of their dominion and secured their achievements. The foretold duration of the dynasty was already as boundless as Heaven. The successive sage emperors carried forward this excellence, applying themselves ever more diligently to plans and strategies, nourishing all with benevolence and steeping them in righteousness, as successive brilliance…

濯靈俾昌俾熾程
功選
德真尤有
集大成以臻至理者

之裒然願充賦于有司是故斯
舉也臣等竊尤有厚望焉蓋謂

translation_en: …joined to rectitude. Now [?] our Emperor, endowed with sagely and divine qualities [?] and presiding over an age of resurgence, makes his renown resplendent and his spiritual power manifest, bringing prosperity and flourishing. In assessing achievements and selecting the virtuous, he has indeed brought together the accomplishments of his predecessors to attain consummate governance. The brilliance of his civil counsels shines forth in authoritative statutes; the favor conveyed by his imperial pronouncements does not prize mere elaboration in words. Recently, following proposals from his servants, he has again eliminated superfluous personnel and dismissed the frivolous, clearing the paths of official service. Through the standards of accomplishment he has set forth [?], he has established an exemplary influence. Thus all who lay claim to talent and aspire to order the world hasten to rally to him, gathering in numbers and wishing to be presented as candidates by the responsible authorities. title: 嘉靖二十二年順天府鄉試錄
text:
其慶感遭逢之下或不徒以詞
章記誦爲文而必將有偉器長
材詩書禮樂之懿者出於其間
以翊我
偃武陳常之治即進而惠疇亮采
思皇譽髦之賢亦庶幾由此其
選内而訏謨外而甸宣以上媲
堯舜禹文王之德之文之盛豈
非主司之所榮願於爾諸士者
乎矧順天爲古燕趙域其地素
稱多賢豪人而司馬子長獲從
燕趙士游故其文豪宕有竒氣
則其人不啻沉鷙茂材力而有
文事焉久矣乃今乘大氣而出

punctuated: 其慶感遭逢之下，或不徒以詞章記誦爲文，而必將有偉器長材、詩書禮樂之懿者出於其間，以翊我偃武陳常之治。即進而惠疇亮采，思皇譽髦之賢，亦庶幾由此其選，内而訏謨，外而甸宣，以上媲堯舜禹文王之德之文之盛，豈非主司之所榮願於爾諸士者乎？矧順天爲古燕趙域，其地素稱多賢豪人，而司馬子長獲從燕趙士游，故其文豪宕有竒氣，則其人不啻沉鷙茂材力，而有文事焉久矣。乃今乘大氣而出
translation_en:
…that, rejoicing in and grateful for their fortunate encounter with this age, they may compose writings that go beyond literary ornament and memorized learning. Surely among them will emerge men of outstanding capacity and enduring talent, possessing the excellences of the Odes, Documents, rites, and music, to assist our government in laying aside arms and establishing enduring norms. When they advance to office, bringing harmony to their colleagues and assisting in government, we may hope that illustrious and renowned worthies will likewise be selected from their ranks. At court they will devise grand plans; beyond it they will administer the regions and spread the transforming influence of government, thereby helping our sovereign match the flourishing virtue and culture of Yao, Shun, Yu, and King Wen. Is this not the honorable aspiration that we who preside over the examination cherish for you scholars?
Moreover, Shuntian occupies the territory of ancient Yan and Zhao, a land long renowned for its many worthy and heroic men. Sima Zichang had the opportunity to associate with the scholars of Yan and Zhao, and thus his writing became bold and unrestrained, possessed of an extraordinary spirit. The people of this region, then, have long distinguished themselves not merely by their resolute fierceness and abundant talent and strength, but also by literary accomplishment. Now, borne upon this mighty spirit, they come forth…
